questions.stem: Two flats on different floors of the same block share an identical layout, yet the one facing a park sells for noticeably more than the one facing a car park. Which characteristic of real estate best explains why no two properties are priced alike?
options: Heterogeneity: each property differs in view and surroundings
Indestructibility: land survives even after the building is demolished
Indivisibility: a property cannot be sold in separate small pieces
Illiquidity: a sale takes time to complete
questions.explanation: Real estate is heterogeneous, so even apparently identical units differ in view, floor level and surroundings, which leads to different values. Illiquidity concerns time to convert to cash, not why prices differ.
questions.common_trap: Confusing price differences between similar units with how long a sale takes.

questions.stem: Because a property cannot be moved to a better area, which physical characteristic makes location the single most important influence on its value?
options: Indivisibility
Indestructibility
Heterogeneity
Immobility
questions.explanation: Land is fixed in place, so its value is bound to the surrounding location and its amenities. Heterogeneity says units differ but does not itself explain why location dominates.
questions.common_trap: Picking heterogeneity because location is one reason units differ.

questions.stem: An old terrace house is demolished to make way for a new project, yet the site remains valuable. Which characteristic does this illustrate?
options: Immobility of the property itself
Indestructibility of the underlying land
Scarcity of land supply
High cost of transaction
questions.explanation: The building can be destroyed but the land endures, so the value of a landed site rests largely on the land itself. Scarcity explains why land is valuable but not why it survives.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up why land is valuable (scarcity) with why it lasts (indestructibility).

questions.stem: Why is a private property usually harder to turn into cash quickly than a basket of SGX-listed shares?
options: Property sales can only be completed during fixed months set by law
A sale needs marketing, negotiation, legal work and loan approval
Banks do not lend against private properties in any circumstances
Property prices are fixed by the Government at the start of each quarter
questions.explanation: A property deal involves finding a buyer, agreeing a price, financing and conveyancing, and the market has no central exchange. Prices are set by the market, not by a Government schedule.
questions.common_trap: Assuming Government price setting is what slows down a property sale.

questions.stem: Farhan buys a resale condo and sells it a year later. The price rose only slightly, and after paying agent fees, legal fees and stamp duties he is out of pocket. Which characteristic of real estate does this show?
options: Inelastic supply
Area preference
Indivisibility
High cost of transaction
questions.explanation: Buying and selling property involves fees and duties that eat into short-term gains, which is why quick in-and-out trading is rarer than in shares. Inelastic supply relates to how supply reacts to price, not to costs.
questions.common_trap: Blaming the loss on supply conditions instead of the cost of dealing.

questions.stem: When demand for new private homes jumps, why can supply not rise quickly in response?
options: Land is limited and building takes years from site purchase to completion
Developers are legally banned from building whenever prices rise
Banks lend to developers only once in every five years
Buyers must wait for HDB to release every private housing site
questions.explanation: Supply is inelastic because land is scarce and development has long lead times. Neither a legal ban on building nor a bank lending cycle is the cause.
questions.common_trap: Thinking regulation, rather than lead time and land scarcity, makes supply inelastic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is classed as an economic (rather than physical) characteristic of real estate?
options: Immobility
Indestructibility
Area preference
Heterogeneity
questions.explanation: Area preference is about how people value locations, which is an economic matter. Immobility, indestructibility and heterogeneity all describe the physical nature of land.
questions.common_trap: Treating every property characteristic as physical.

questions.stem: A buyer is willing to pay a premium for a 3-bedroom unit in District 10 compared with a similar unit in District 22, even though both are equally new. Which economic characteristic is at work?
options: Improvement of the building
Indivisibility of the unit
High cost of transaction
Area preference
questions.explanation: Buyers consistently prefer certain locations because of prestige, schools and convenience, and pay more for them. Indivisibility only says a unit cannot be sold in parts.
questions.common_trap: Reading a location premium as a building-quality effect.

questions.stem: Compared with buying a shop unit directly, which feature is true of investing in a Singapore REIT?
options: The investor holds legal title to one particular unit in the portfolio pool
Units are listed on the exchange and a professional manager runs the properties
The investor is personally liable for repairs to the REIT's buildings
The investor can only sell units after a compulsory minimum holding period
questions.explanation: A REIT pools income-producing properties, is managed professionally and is listed so units can be bought or sold on the exchange. Unitholders do not own any specific unit.
questions.common_trap: Believing a REIT unitholder owns a specific property in the portfolio.

questions.stem: To enjoy tax transparency in Singapore, a REIT is generally expected to distribute at least what share of its taxable income to unitholders each year?
questions.explanation: The usual condition is distributing at least 90% of taxable income, so tax is dealt with at the unitholder level. It need not pay out all of it.
questions.common_trap: Remembering a rounder figure such as 100% or 50% instead of 90%.

questions.stem: Hui Min holds shares in a listed property developer, while her brother holds units in a retail-mall REIT. Which statement about their income is MOST accurate?
options: The developer pays dividends at its discretion, but a REIT is expected to pay out most of its income
Both are legally required to pay out at least 90% of their profits each year
Only the developer's shares can be bought and sold on the stock exchange
The REIT pays out distributions only in a year when a property is sold
questions.explanation: Property stocks pay dividends at the company's discretion, and some pay none, but a REIT distributes most of its rental income to keep tax transparency. Both are listed.
questions.common_trap: Assuming property stocks and REITs are required to distribute income in the same way.

questions.stem: An investor says: "I like that I can see, renovate and personally use my investment." Which advantage of direct property investment is this?
options: Diversification across many different buildings
A very low cost of entry for small investors
Tangibility, with physical control of the asset
High liquidity, as units sell quickly
questions.explanation: A physical property can be seen, improved and occupied by its owner, which stocks and REIT units do not offer. Direct ownership is typically costly and illiquid.
questions.common_trap: Crediting direct property with the liquidity or low cost that belong to REITs.

questions.stem: Why is property often described as a hedge against inflation?
options: Property values and rents tend to rise with general prices over time
Property loan interest rates are fixed by law for the whole loan term
Property prices are guaranteed never to fall in any period
Rental contracts must be indexed to the price level by statute
questions.explanation: Over time, property values and rents tend to keep pace with or exceed general price increases, which protects real purchasing power. This is a tendency, not a guarantee.
questions.common_trap: Treating a long-run tendency as a guarantee that prices never fall.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur is house-hunting and finds listings in property portals, newspaper ads and agents' WhatsApp groups, with no single place showing all sales. Which feature of the real estate market does this show?
options: It is a perfectly competitive market
Prices are set by a single regulator
Every unit is identical
There is no central marketplace
questions.explanation: Property is traded through many channels rather than one exchange, so information is scattered. Fragmentation and heterogeneity are the reverse of a perfect market.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a market with many listings must be perfectly competitive.

questions.stem: Why is the real estate market called an imperfect market?
options: Only the Government is allowed to buy and sell property
Trades are infrequent, products differ and information is uneven
Prices never change over time because they are regulated
All units are priced from a published Government tariff
questions.explanation: Few transactions, unique products and uneven information stop a single, transparent price from emerging. The market does set prices that move with supply and demand.
questions.common_trap: Thinking imperfection means regulated or fixed prices.

questions.stem: What is the main economic function of the real estate market?
options: To guarantee a minimum yearly return to every owner
To allocate scarce property among users through prices
To fix rents at the same level across all of Singapore
To ensure every household owns exactly one property each
questions.explanation: Through the price mechanism, scarce space goes to those who value it most, and price changes signal developers to speed up or slow down supply. The market offers no return guarantee.
questions.common_trap: Confusing allocation through prices with guaranteed outcomes.

questions.stem: Which of these is classified as non-landed private housing?
options: A semi-detached house on its own land title
A terrace house on freehold land
A bungalow on a large plot
A condominium unit held on a strata title
questions.explanation: Non-landed private housing is strata-titled, such as condominiums and apartments. Bungalows, semi-detached and terrace houses are landed forms.
questions.common_trap: Assuming any private home with a good address and facilities is landed.

questions.stem: Under URA guidelines, what is the minimum plot size for a bungalow within a designated Good Class Bungalow Area?
options: 400 sqm
800 sqm
questions.explanation: Inside a GCB Area the plot must be at least 1,400 sqm (with a minimum width of 18.5 m). 400 sqm is the minimum for an ordinary bungalow outside the GCB Area.
questions.common_trap: Using the ordinary bungalow minimum of 400 sqm for GCBs.

questions.stem: Raj is considering a 900 sqm detached house on a street that is outside every area designated for Good Class Bungalows. How would it be classified?
options: A GCB, because its plot is larger than the 400 sqm bungalow minimum
A GCB, because the plot is held on a freehold title
An ordinary detached house, as a GCB needs a designated area and larger plot
A semi-detached house, because its plot is under 1,000 sqm
questions.explanation: A GCB must lie within a designated GCB Area and meet the GCB plot minimums, so this house is simply a detached house. Size alone does not create GCB status.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a large detached house is automatically a GCB.

questions.stem: Which set correctly gives URA minimum plot sizes for a detached house outside GCB Areas, a side-to-side semi-detached house and a Type I intermediate terrace house?
options: 400 sqm, 150 sqm, 80 sqm
1,400 sqm, 400 sqm, 200 sqm
200 sqm, 150 sqm, 80 sqm
400 sqm, 200 sqm, 150 sqm
questions.explanation: The URA minimums are 400 sqm for a detached house, 200 sqm for a semi-detached house and 150 sqm for a Type I intermediate terrace house. The 80 sqm figure belongs to Type II terrace houses.
questions.common_trap: Shifting every landed type down one step on the plot-size ladder.

questions.stem: What minimum site area does URA require before a residential development can be a condominium (with communal facilities) rather than a flat development?
questions.explanation: A condominium needs at least 4,000 sqm, to provide room for communal and recreational facilities. 1,000 sqm is the minimum for a flat development.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the flat minimum site area with the condominium minimum.

questions.stem: A foreign professional wants to buy a strata-titled cluster house in a landed housing development. What is required?
options: None, because a strata title makes it an unrestricted condominium
Approval from the HDB, because it is a type of public housing flat
Approval from the Singapore Land Authority, as it is a landed housing form
Approval from the CPF Board, because the unit is held on freehold title
questions.explanation: Strata-titled cluster houses count as landed housing under the Residential Property Act, so a foreigner needs SLA approval. A strata title does not turn it into an unrestricted condominium.
questions.common_trap: Treating any strata-titled home as an unrestricted condominium for foreign buyers.

questions.stem: Which description best fits an Executive Condominium (EC)?
options: A hybrid built by private developers for eligible buyers, later fully private
A subsidised flat built and sold directly by HDB on a lease
A private condominium open to any buyer, without conditions
A rental-only residence for low-income families under HDB
questions.explanation: ECs are built and sold by private property developers, but only to eligible households, who must meet a minimum occupation period before the unit can be sold on the open market. HDB does not build them; HDB describes them as units bought from a property developer.
questions.common_trap: Believing ECs are built by HDB, like BTO flats.

questions.stem: What lease term does HDB typically grant for the flats it sells?
options: 30 years
60 years
99 years
999 years
questions.explanation: New HDB flats are sold on 99-year leases, so buyers own the rights to the flat for 99 years. The other terms are not the standard HDB flat lease.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the 99-year housing lease with a 999-year or shorter lease term.

questions.stem: How are commercial and industrial properties typically valued, compared with homes bought for own stay?
options: Mainly by the rental income they can generate
Mainly by the owner's family size
Mainly by the HDB resale price index
Mainly by the CPF balance of the buyer
questions.explanation: Income-producing properties are priced largely on rent and yield, which makes them sensitive to business conditions. A residential owner-occupier buys partly for personal use.
questions.common_trap: Assuming all property types are priced on owner-occupier needs.

questions.stem: A factory plans a process that is dangerous or offensive to neighbours, such as handling highly hazardous chemicals. Under the traditional classification, which type of industrial building is this?
options: Light industrial building
General industrial building
Warehouse
Special industrial building
questions.explanation: Special industrial buildings house processes that are dangerous or offensive. Light industrial uses are those that can sit near homes without harming amenity, and warehouses are mainly for storage.
questions.common_trap: Placing hazardous processes under general industrial by default.

questions.stem: Jia Wei lists her five-year-old condo unit for resale. Which source of supply does her listing add to?
options: Supply of vacant sites for building
Supply of existing properties (resale)
Supply of new properties
Supply of State land by the Government
questions.explanation: Resale listings come from the existing stock owned by individuals, known as the secondary market. New launches and land releases are different sources.
questions.common_trap: Counting any new listing as new supply.

questions.stem: Which planning control most directly sets how much floor area can be built on a site, and so the potential new supply from it?
options: The sale price of neighbouring units
Plot ratio, together with the permitted use
The developer's marketing budget
The buyer's age
questions.explanation: Plot ratio sets the allowable gross floor area relative to site area, and the zoning limits use, so both cap potential supply. Prices and marketing do not change what the law allows.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking the planning controls that cap supply.

questions.stem: In a small estate, many buyers are chasing very few listings and sellers are receiving offers above asking. How is this market described?
options: A buyer's market
A stable market
A recession
A seller's market
questions.explanation: When demand exceeds supply, sellers hold the bargaining power and prices tend to rise. A buyer's market is the opposite, with excess supply.
questions.common_trap: Reversing seller's and buyer's market.

questions.stem: The Government announces a higher stamp duty for buyers of a second home. Under which category of macro factors affecting demand does this fall?
options: Political and institutional
Social and demographic
Economic
Micro (property-specific)
questions.explanation: Changes in law and housing policy are political and institutional factors that can shift demand. Demographic factors relate to household structure, and economic ones to income and rates.
questions.common_trap: Classing a policy change as an economic factor because it affects costs.

questions.stem: More Singaporeans are staying single and more households are forming with one or two members. Which type of macro factor is at work, and what is the likely effect?
options: Economic; less demand for smaller homes in general
Political; less demand for homes of any size
Social and demographic; more demand for small homes
Micro; no effect on overall demand
questions.explanation: Household size and structure are social and demographic factors, and smaller households tend to favour smaller units. They are not property-specific micro factors.
questions.common_trap: Treating a society-wide trend as a property-specific micro factor.

questions.stem: Other things equal, what is the usual effect of a rise in mortgage interest rates on demand for homes?
options: Demand tends to rise, as buyers rush to lock in prices today
Demand is unaffected, as homes are a basic necessity of life
Supply is cut immediately, so demand plays no role at all
Demand tends to fall, as monthly repayments become costlier
questions.explanation: Higher rates raise instalments and reduce what buyers can afford, so demand softens. Some buyers may rush in anticipation, but the general effect is a fall.
questions.common_trap: Assuming homes are insensitive to financing costs.

questions.stem: Which set contains only micro factors, meaning ones tied to the individual property?
options: Interest rates, GDP growth and unemployment
Floor level, orientation and view
Population growth, immigration and marriage rates
Stamp duty policy, GLS supply and loan limits
questions.explanation: Floor level, orientation and view are features of the unit itself. The other sets are economic, demographic or policy factors that operate across the whole market.
questions.common_trap: Mixing market-wide conditions with features of a single unit.

questions.stem: Two similar units in the same area are on offer. One is freehold and the other has 40 years left on a 99-year lease. Why is the leasehold unit usually cheaper?
options: Leasehold properties cannot lawfully be sold to Singapore citizens
Leasehold units are never eligible for any kind of bank loan
It has fewer years of use left, and the land reverts to the State at lease end
Freehold units are guaranteed to rise in value over any period
questions.explanation: A shorter remaining lease means fewer years of use and reversion to the State, so buyers pay less and may find financing harder. No guarantee of price growth exists for freehold either.
questions.common_trap: Believing freehold is a guarantee of capital gains.

questions.stem: Developers have launched too many projects, unsold stock is piling up, prices are slipping and banks are tightening credit. Which phase of the property cycle is this?
options: Decline, moving towards the trough
Recovery
Boom (the peak)
Expansion
questions.explanation: Excess supply, weaker prices and tighter lending are signs of a downturn in the cycle. Recovery would show falling vacancy and returning confidence.
questions.common_trap: Confusing a supply glut with a recovery phase.

questions.stem: Why does the property cycle usually lag the broader business cycle?
options: Because property values are not affected by the economy at all
Because property prices are reset by the market only once a year
Supply reacts slowly because development takes years to complete
Because banks lend for property only during recessions
questions.explanation: Land acquisition, approvals and construction create a delay between demand and new supply, so property turns later than the economy. Property is strongly linked to the economy.
questions.common_trap: Assuming property moves independently of the business cycle.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches an agency with the price index it publishes?
options: URA publishes the private home price index, and HDB the HDB resale price index
HDB publishes the private home price index, and URA the HDB resale index
IRAS publishes both the private and the HDB resale indices
CEA publishes both the private and the HDB resale indices
questions.explanation: URA tracks private residential prices and HDB tracks public housing resale prices. Neither IRAS nor CEA compiles these indices.
questions.common_trap: Swapping the roles of URA and HDB.

questions.stem: What is a URA or HDB flash estimate of a quarterly price index?
options: A forecast of next year's prices prepared by the banks
A final audited figure that is never revised afterwards
A figure covering only new project launches by developers
An early preliminary figure using transactions so far, later updated with full data
questions.explanation: Flash estimates give an early read on the quarter from partial data and are later revised once complete statistics are released. They are not forecasts.
questions.common_trap: Treating the flash estimate as the final number.

questions.stem: A client's address has the postal code 238xxx. Using the old postal district system, which district is it in?
options: District 10
District 9
District 11
District 23
questions.explanation: The first two digits (23) are the postal sector and sectors 22 and 23 form District 9, the Orchard area. District 23 is a different thing from sector 23.
questions.common_trap: Reading the sector number 23 as District 23.

questions.stem: Mr Tan's buyer wants a home in District 10. Which postal code starts with the right sector?
options: 228xxx
268xxx
289xxx
408xxx
questions.explanation: Sectors 24 to 27 make up District 10, so a code starting with 26 qualifies. 22 falls in District 9, 28 in District 11 and 40 in District 14.
questions.common_trap: Matching the district number to a code that begins with the same digits.

questions.stem: Which district covers postal codes starting with 81, for the Changi and Loyang area?
options: District 18
District 19
District 16
District 17
questions.explanation: Postal sectors 49, 50 and 81 all fall under District 17. Sector 82 belongs to District 19.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the districts follow the sector numbers in simple order.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur wants a flat in Upper Thomson, and the listing shows a postal code starting with 77. Which district is it?
options: District 26
District 25
District 27
District 28
questions.explanation: Sectors 77 and 78 map to District 26, which covers Upper Thomson and Springleaf. Sectors 75 and 76 belong to District 27.
questions.common_trap: Confusing neighbouring northern districts.

questions.stem: Which statutory board is Singapore's national land use planning authority, preparing the Master Plan and publishing private property price statistics?
options: Urban Redevelopment Authority
Singapore Land Authority
Building and Construction Authority
Housing & Development Board
questions.explanation: URA prepares long-term plans, controls development intensity and publishes the private property price data. SLA handles State land and land registration.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up URA's planning role with SLA's land administration role.

questions.stem: Mr Tan wants to know which agency manages State land, runs the land titles registry and oversees the national land survey system. Which agency is it?
options: Urban Redevelopment Authority
JTC Corporation
Singapore Land Authority
Land Transport Authority
questions.explanation: SLA, under the Ministry of Law, manages State land and buildings and is the land registration authority. URA plans land use but does not register titles.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the planning authority also keeps the land register.

questions.stem: Which agency builds and sells public housing and sets the eligibility rules for flat purchases?
options: Central Provident Fund Board
Monetary Authority of Singapore
Building and Construction Authority
Housing & Development Board
questions.explanation: HDB is the public housing authority under the Ministry of National Development. CPF Board only handles the use of CPF savings for housing.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the CPF Board decides who may buy a flat.

questions.stem: A small manufacturer wants leased factory space in a planned industrial estate with shared facilities. Which agency is the leading developer and manager of such industrial land and buildings?
options: Housing & Development Board
JTC Corporation
Singapore Land Authority
Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
questions.explanation: JTC develops and manages industrial estates and specialised parks. HDB handles public housing, not industrial land.
questions.common_trap: Linking industrial estates to HDB because it also builds estates.

questions.stem: A developer has finished building a condominium block and now needs permission for residents to move in before all works are fully complete. Which agency is responsible for the Temporary Occupation Permit?
options: Urban Redevelopment Authority
Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
Building and Construction Authority
Singapore Land Authority
questions.explanation: BCA oversees building control and issues the TOP and the Certificate of Statutory Completion. URA's role lies in planning permission, which comes earlier.
questions.common_trap: Linking TOP to the planning authority instead of building control.

questions.stem: Which agency plans and manages public and private transport infrastructure such as MRT lines and roads?
options: Land Transport Authority
JTC Corporation
Building and Construction Authority
Urban Redevelopment Authority
questions.explanation: LTA is responsible for transport infrastructure, systems and policies, and its plans affect property values near new stations. URA sets land use, not transport operations.
questions.common_trap: Crediting URA with transport infrastructure planning.

questions.stem: Which agency collects property tax and stamp duties on behalf of the Government?
options: Monetary Authority of Singapore
Central Provident Fund Board
Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
Singapore Land Authority
questions.explanation: IRAS administers, assesses and collects taxes including property tax and stamp duty. MAS regulates financial institutions and sets lending rules.
questions.common_trap: Assuming MAS collects the stamp duties it indirectly influences.

questions.stem: On what basis is annual property tax on a Singapore property calculated?
options: The annual value, which is the estimated gross yearly rent
The price the owner paid when buying the property
The balance of the outstanding mortgage loan owed
The owner's declared annual income for the year
questions.explanation: Property tax is levied on annual value, which reflects the market rental potential and not the purchase price. Loan balance and income do not enter.
questions.common_trap: Using the purchase price as the tax base.

questions.stem: Hui Min is buying an HDB flat and wants to use her CPF Ordinary Account savings and be covered by mortgage reducing insurance if she dies. Which agency administers the CPF housing schemes and the Home Protection Scheme?
options: Housing & Development Board
Monetary Authority of Singapore
Singapore Land Authority
Central Provident Fund Board
questions.explanation: The CPF Board manages the use of CPF for housing and runs the Home Protection Scheme. HDB approves flat purchase but does not manage CPF savings.
questions.common_trap: Thinking HDB runs the mortgage insurance because the flat is its product.

questions.stem: Which of these property cooling measures is set by the Monetary Authority of Singapore?
options: Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty
The Total Debt Servicing Ratio framework
Seller's Stamp Duty
The Government Land Sales programme
questions.explanation: TDSR is a lending rule set by MAS, which regulates banks and other financial institutions. Stamp duties are fiscal measures collected by IRAS, and land sales are managed by the land agencies.
questions.common_trap: Assuming MAS sets the stamp duties used as cooling measures.

questions.stem: Under the TDSR framework (55% of gross monthly income), Hui Min earns S$8,000 per month and already pays S$800 monthly on a car loan. What is the most she can commit to a new monthly mortgage repayment?
questions.explanation: The cap on total debt repayments is 55% of S$8,000, which is S$4,400. Subtracting the S$800 car loan leaves S$3,600 for the mortgage.
questions.common_trap: Forgetting to deduct existing debt from the TDSR limit.

questions.stem: Farhan has a gross monthly income of S$6,000 and plans to take a bank loan for an HDB flat. Under the 30% Mortgage Servicing Ratio, what is the highest monthly mortgage instalment allowed?
questions.explanation: The MSR caps the monthly mortgage repayment at 30% of gross monthly income, so 30% of S$6,000 is S$1,800. 55% of S$6,000 is S$3,300, which is the TDSR cap.
questions.common_trap: Applying the 55% TDSR cap to the mortgage alone.

questions.stem: To which purchases does the Mortgage Servicing Ratio apply?
options: HDB flats and new ECs bought from developers, with bank loans
All private condominiums and landed houses bought with bank loans
Commercial and industrial properties bought by companies
Any residential property bought by a foreigner
questions.explanation: MSR limits the mortgage repayment on public-housing-type purchases, being HDB flats and new ECs, to a share of income. Other private purchases are governed by the TDSR.
questions.common_trap: Assuming MSR applies to every residential purchase.

questions.stem: Jia Wei, a first-time buyer with no housing loan, buys a condo for S$1,000,000 but the bank values it at S$960,000. If the LTV limit is 75%, what is the maximum bank loan?
questions.explanation: The LTV limit applies to the lower of the price and valuation, so 75% of S$960,000 gives S$720,000. Using the S$1,000,000 price would give S$750,000, which overstates the loan.
questions.common_trap: Applying the LTV percentage to the price instead of the lower of price and valuation.

questions.stem: Why does MAS set lower LTV limits for a buyer who already has one or more housing loans?
options: To make first-time buyers pay a higher interest rate on loans
To raise the Government's stamp duty collections each year
To speed up the completion of new projects by developers
To discourage heavily leveraged purchases of more properties
questions.explanation: Lower LTV limits require more cash upfront, which restrains leveraged investment demand. They have no bearing on interest rates or stamp duty receipts.
questions.common_trap: Thinking LTV rules are meant to raise revenue or lower rates.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur, a Singapore citizen, buys her first and only residential property, a private condo. What is her ABSD position?
options: She pays the same ABSD rate as a foreign buyer would
No ABSD is payable, as citizens pay it only from the second property
She pays ABSD only if she uses her CPF to pay
She pays ABSD only if the condo is on a freehold title
questions.explanation: ABSD varies with the buyer's profile and number of residential properties, and a Singapore citizen buying a first property pays none. Financing source and tenure do not matter.
questions.common_trap: Assuming every residential buyer pays some ABSD.

questions.stem: Jia Wei, a Singapore citizen, already owns an HDB flat and signs an option to buy a private condo. How does her existing flat affect her ABSD?
options: It is ignored because HDB flats are never counted for ABSD purposes
It exempts her from ABSD on any future private purchase
It counts as a property already owned, so the condo is an additional one
It doubles the BSD she pays but leaves the ABSD unchanged
questions.explanation: ABSD looks at the residential properties a buyer holds, including HDB flats, so the condo is her second property. She may seek a refund if she sells the flat within the prescribed period.
questions.common_trap: Believing an HDB flat does not count as a property owned.

questions.stem: What is the main policy purpose of ABSD on residential purchases?
options: To dampen demand from investors, foreigners and multiple-home buyers
To raise funds for the construction of new HDB flats
To compensate sellers who sell their homes quickly
To limit the amount that a bank can lend to a borrower
questions.explanation: ABSD adds to the cost of buying more homes or buying as a foreigner or entity, discouraging investment demand. Loan limits are a separate MAS tool.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up ABSD's purpose with a lending restriction.

questions.stem: Raj buys a private condo and resells it 18 months later at a profit. Which cooling measure is aimed at discouraging this kind of quick resale?
options: Mortgage Servicing Ratio
Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty
Seller's Stamp Duty
Land Betterment Charge
questions.explanation: SSD is paid by sellers who dispose of residential property within a set holding period after buying it, to deter short-term flipping. ABSD hits buyers at purchase.
questions.common_trap: Choosing ABSD because it is also a stamp duty cooling measure.

questions.stem: Under the SSD rules for properties bought on or after 4 July 2025, a private home is sold after being held for more than four years. What is the SSD?
options: Nil, as the holding period has ended
The lowest tier of SSD still applies
The highest rate of SSD still applies
SSD applies only if it is sold at a loss to the owner
questions.explanation: SSD applies only during the holding period, which is four years for properties bought on or after 4 July 2025. After that, no SSD is payable.
questions.common_trap: Thinking SSD is still payable after the holding period ends.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a supply-side measure, as opposed to a demand-side cooling measure?
options: Lowering the maximum LTV ratio on mortgage loans
Raising the ABSD rates for second homes
Tightening the TDSR limit for all borrowers
Adding more sites to the Government Land Sales programme
questions.explanation: Releasing more land increases future housing supply. Lowering LTV, raising ABSD and tightening TDSR all work by reducing demand.
questions.common_trap: Treating a tool that eases supply as a demand curb.

questions.stem: Prices of private homes have surged because of strong speculative demand. Which combined effect would the Government most likely intend by raising ABSD and lowering LTV limits?
options: A sharp rise in new housing supply within a few months
Slower price growth and fewer speculative purchases soon after
Higher mortgage interest rates set directly by the Government
A permanent fall in the cost of construction materials
questions.explanation: These tools raise the cost and cash needed to buy, which cools speculative demand. They cannot add supply quickly or change the interest rates banks set.
questions.common_trap: Expecting demand-side tools to increase supply.

questions.stem: A GLS site appears on the Reserve List. When is it offered for tender?
options: Automatically at the start of each half-year period
When a developer applies with a minimum bid price the Government accepts
Only when a statutory board such as HDB asks for the site for flats
Only after all the Confirmed List sites have been sold
questions.explanation: Reserve List sites go to tender only when a developer applies and commits to a minimum bid price that the Government accepts, whereas Confirmed List sites are launched on a set timetable.
questions.common_trap: Assuming Reserve List sites are automatically released.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between the Confirmed List and the Reserve List of the Government Land Sales programme?
options: Confirmed sites are only for HDB flats, and Reserve sites for private housing
Confirmed sites are freehold, and Reserve sites are leasehold
Confirmed sites are chosen by lottery, and Reserve sites by tender
Confirmed sites are launched on schedule, while Reserve sites await developer demand
questions.explanation: Confirmed List sites will be offered during the period, while Reserve List sites are held back until a developer triggers them. The difference lies in timing and trigger, not tenure or buyer type.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the two lists differ by tenure or the type of buyer.

questions.stem: A developer obtains approval to build at a higher plot ratio than the site's previous permitted intensity. What charge may be payable to the State because of the increase in land value?
options: Land Betterment Charge
Mortgage Servicing Ratio
Seller's Stamp Duty
Property tax
questions.explanation: Since 1 August 2022 the Land Betterment Charge, collected by SLA, taxes the increase in land value arising from a chargeable consent such as planning permission, and it replaced the Development Charge. Property tax is an annual charge on annual value.
questions.common_trap: Naming the old Development Charge, or confusing a planning-related levy with an annual property tax.

questions.stem: The Government needs a strip of privately owned land to widen a road, and the owner objects. What legal basis can the State rely on?
options: The Residential Property Act, with no compensation payable
The Estate Agents Act, with a balloting process
The Land Acquisition Act, with compensation to the owner
The Housing Developers Act, with a tender exercise
questions.explanation: The Land Acquisition Act allows compulsory acquisition for public purposes, with compensation payable. An owner's objection does not stop a lawful acquisition.
questions.common_trap: Believing an owner can veto acquisition for a public purpose.

questions.stem: Hui Min bought a new subsidised HDB flat, not a Plus or Prime flat, three years ago and wants to sell it on the open market now. What is the obstacle?
options: There is no restriction on selling HDB flats at any time
She must first offer it back to the HDB at the purchase price
She needs the written consent of her neighbours to sell
She has not yet completed the 5-year Minimum Occupation Period
questions.explanation: MOP restricts selling or renting out the whole flat during an early period so that flats serve housing needs rather than speculation. Flats other than Plus and Prime, such as Standard flats, have a 5-year MOP.
questions.common_trap: Believing resale of an HDB flat is unrestricted at any time.

questions.stem: Farhan owns a Prime-classified HDB flat that is still within its MOP. He plans to work overseas and wants to rent out the whole flat meanwhile. What is the position?
options: He may do so freely, as ownership of the flat gives him full rights
He cannot rent out the whole flat, as Plus and Prime flats bar whole-flat rental
He may do so, provided that the tenant is a foreigner
He may do so, but only for the first two years of the MOP
questions.explanation: Plus and Prime flats have a 10-year MOP and whole-flat renting is not permitted for them. Renting individual rooms may be allowed in some cases.
questions.common_trap: Assuming whole-flat rental is a general ownership right.

questions.stem: Why does HDB impose an income ceiling on buyers of new subsidised flats?
options: To stop buyers from using their CPF savings for the flat
To reduce the number of new flats that HDB builds
To direct subsidised flats to households that need support
To raise the resale prices of existing HDB flats
questions.explanation: Subsidised flats are meant for households of modest means, so a ceiling directs support to them. The ceiling has been raised in recent years, so check the current figure.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the ceiling is for price management and not for targeting subsidies.

questions.stem: A company wants to sell uncompleted residential units in a new development to the public. What must it first have?
options: A housing developer's licence
A letter of consent from HDB
A CEA estate agent licence
An IRAS tax clearance for each buyer
questions.explanation: Sellers of uncompleted private residential units must be licensed under the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act. An estate agent licence is for property agents.
questions.common_trap: Mistaking an estate agent licence for a developer licence.

questions.stem: Madam Lim buys a second condo to rent out and plans to keep it long term for rental yield and capital growth. How is she classified?
options: An end user
A speculator
An investor
A developer
questions.explanation: Someone buying to hold for rent and appreciation is an investor, while a speculator aims at a quick resale profit. An end user buys for own stay.
questions.common_trap: Labelling a long-term landlord a speculator.

questions.stem: Which body licenses and regulates estate agents and salespersons in Singapore?
options: Council for Estate Agencies
Singapore Land Authority
Monetary Authority of Singapore
Urban Redevelopment Authority
questions.explanation: CEA regulates the estate agency industry under the Estate Agents Act. SLA deals with State land and land registration.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the land authority licenses estate agents.

questions.stem: Why is ABSD on housing developers normally remitted in part if the project is completed and sold within the stipulated time?
options: To reward developers that sell most of their units to foreigners
To cut the rents of existing tenants in older buildings
To reduce the CPF savings used to buy new homes
To deter land banking without penalising developers who deliver on time
questions.explanation: The ABSD for developers works as a deterrent against holding sites idle, and is remitted when the units are built and sold within the time limit. It has no link to tenants or CPF.
questions.common_trap: Seeing the remission as a subsidy and not a land-banking deterrent.

questions.stem: A developer wants to demolish an old condo and rebuild with a different use. Which agency grants planning permission for the new development?
options: Land Transport Authority
Urban Redevelopment Authority
Central Provident Fund Board
JTC Corporation
questions.explanation: URA is the planning authority that decides on written permission for development. BCA later reviews the structural and building plans.
questions.common_trap: Going to BCA for planning permission instead of building plan approval.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a proprietary right in land?
options: A right that only the two original contracting parties can enforce against each other or their estates
A right that lasts only for as long as the holder personally lives on the land
A right that is created only when a buyer pays the full purchase price in cash
A right that attaches to the land itself, so it can generally be asserted against later owners
questions.explanation: A proprietary right is tied to the property and so can usually be enforced against whoever later acquires it. A personal right is enforceable only against the particular person who owes the obligation.
questions.common_trap: Assuming every right connected with a property deal follows the land to new owners.

questions.stem: Farhan lets his friend Wei Jie park in his private driveway every night on a verbal arrangement. Farhan then sells the house, and the buyer tells Wei Jie to stop. What is Wei Jie's position?
options: He acquired a proprietary right that automatically binds every later owner of the house
He may stay on because his regular use created a legal easement over the driveway
He held only a personal permission from Farhan, so the buyer is not bound by it
He becomes the buyer's tenant on the same terms from the date of sale
questions.explanation: A bare permission given by one person is a personal right and does not run with the land. Regular use alone does not turn it into an easement or a lease.
questions.common_trap: Believing that long use of someone's land converts a favour into a right that binds new owners.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a personal right rather than a proprietary right?
options: A homeowner's right to keep trespassers off her land
A bank's registered mortgage over a condominium unit
A contractor's claim for unpaid renovation fees against the homeowner
A neighbour's registered right of way over the shared driveway between two houses
questions.explanation: The contractor's claim is a contractual claim against the homeowner personally and does not attach to the land. The other three are rights in or over the land itself.
questions.common_trap: Treating any right that involves a property as automatically a right in the property.

questions.stem: Which set of rights best describes full ownership of land?
options: To occupy it for an agreed period and then hand it back to the person who granted it
To possess it, enjoy it, keep others out, dispose of it in life and pass it on at death
To use it only for the purposes that the State from time to time approves
To receive rent from it but never to sell, mortgage or give it away
questions.explanation: Ownership is the widest bundle of rights over land, including the powers to exclude others and to transfer the land both during life and on death. Lesser interests carry only part of that bundle.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the narrow rights of a tenant or licensee with the wide bundle that makes up ownership.

questions.stem: Hui Min owns a shophouse and grants a registered three-year lease to a florist. During the lease, which statement is correct?
options: Hui Min has given up ownership for three years and keeps only a right to collect rent
Hui Min may walk in at any time because an owner's rights always override a tenant's
The florist's interest is greater than Hui Min's because it carries exclusive possession
Hui Min still owns the building, but the florist's exclusive possession limits her entry
questions.explanation: A lease carves a lesser interest out of the owner's larger estate, and the owner keeps the reversion. During the term the tenant's exclusive possession restricts the owner's entry.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that granting a lease transfers ownership, or that an owner can ignore a tenant's possession.

questions.stem: A tenant is said to hold a 'lesser interest' than the landlord. What does this mean?
options: The tenant's rights are valid only against the landlord personally and never against anyone else
The tenant's rights exist only in equity and have no standing under the law
The tenant's rights over the land are narrower and are limited by the terms and duration of the lease
The tenant has paid less than the market value and so holds a discounted title
questions.explanation: A lesser interest gives only some of the powers of ownership, for a limited time and on set conditions. A registered lease can still bind outsiders, so it is not merely a personal claim.
questions.common_trap: Reading 'lesser' as 'weaker or unprotected' rather than 'smaller in scope and duration'.

questions.stem: Which of these is the BEST example of a lesser interest in land?
options: A registered three-year lease of a shop unit
Freehold ownership of a shophouse
A registered estate in perpetuity over a bungalow plot
A company's fee simple over an industrial lot
questions.explanation: A fixed-term lease gives limited rights for a limited time and sits beneath the landlord's estate. The other options are forms of full ownership.
questions.common_trap: Assuming any interest registered on a title is a form of ownership.

questions.stem: Real estate as a legal concept refers to interests in which kind of property?
options: Any asset that can be mortgaged to a bank, whether or not it is land
Buildings only, because the land beneath belongs to the State
Only property whose ownership has been recorded in the Land Titles Register
Immovable property, meaning land and whatever is permanently part of it
questions.explanation: Real property means land and the things permanently attached to it. Registration and mortgageability do not decide whether property is real or personal.
questions.common_trap: Equating 'real' with 'registered' or 'buildings only'.

questions.stem: In law, what is personal property (also called chattels)?
options: Movable things that are not interests in land, such as furniture and appliances
Land that belongs to one individual instead of a company or a group
Property that the owner is not allowed to sell or transfer to others
Anything the owner uses for private purposes rather than for any business or trade
questions.explanation: Personal property is the movable category set against land, and it is not about who owns it or how it is used. A sofa and a washing machine are typical chattels.
questions.common_trap: Reading 'personal' as 'privately owned' instead of 'movable, not land'.

questions.stem: Why does the law treat dealings in land more formally than dealings in most chattels?
options: Land is owned by the State, so every dealing in it needs a Minister's signature, and the Registrar must also certify each sale
Land is permanent and valuable, so transfers need written, registered documents while chattels pass by delivery
Chattels are never capable of being sold, so only land needs formal documentation rules
Land can only be dealt with through licensed salespersons and developers registered with CEA
questions.explanation: Because land is durable and its title must be traceable, the law requires written and often registered dealings. A chattel can usually change hands by simple delivery.
questions.common_trap: Believing formality arises from State ownership or from agent licensing rather than from the nature of land.

questions.stem: Under Singapore's land registration system, who is recognised as holding the legal interest in registered land?
options: The person who lives on the land and pays the utilities
The person whose name appears on the title as the registered proprietor
The person who paid the full price but has not yet been registered
The person who holds the original sale and purchase agreement
questions.explanation: Registration is what vests the legal estate, so the registered proprietor is the legal owner. A buyer who has paid but is not registered holds at most an equitable interest.
questions.common_trap: Treating payment or occupation as equivalent to being the registered owner.

questions.stem: Mei Ling signs a valid and enforceable agreement to buy a freehold house, but completion is two months away and the seller is still the registered owner. What does Mei Ling generally hold in the meantime?
options: The legal interest, because her signature on the agreement transfers legal title to her at once
No interest in the land, only a right to claim damages if the seller backs out
An equitable interest, since the agreement can be enforced by an order for specific performance
A tenancy of the house until the day of completion
questions.explanation: Where a contract for the sale of land is binding and specifically enforceable, the buyer is treated as holding the beneficial interest before legal title passes. Legal title moves only on registration.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a buyer has either full legal title or nothing until completion.

questions.stem: Mr Lim holds a house as trustee for his two nieces. Who holds which interest?
options: Mr Lim holds the legal interest and the nieces hold the equitable (beneficial) interest
Mr Lim holds both interests, and the nieces hold only a personal claim against him
The nieces hold the legal interest and Mr Lim holds the equitable interest
Both interests are held jointly by Mr Lim and his nieces in equal shares
questions.explanation: A trust splits ownership: the trustee has legal title and manages the property, while the beneficiaries enjoy the equitable interest. The two interests sit with different people.
questions.common_trap: Assuming whoever is named on the title also enjoys all the benefit.

questions.stem: Hock Seng is the only name on the title of a flat. His partner Li Na contributed half of the purchase price. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Li Na has no interest, because only registered names count in law
Li Na may have a beneficial interest even though she is not the registered owner
Li Na is automatically a joint legal owner of the flat from the date of purchase onward
Li Na holds a 99-year lease over half of the flat
questions.explanation: A person who contributes to the price may be treated as a beneficial owner under a resulting or constructive trust. That interest is equitable and does not appear on the register without a caveat.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that the title shows everyone who has a financial stake in the property.

questions.stem: Under the general law, an unregistered equitable interest in land may be defeated by which of the following?
options: Any later buyer, including one who received the land as a gift with notice
The State, which can cancel any equitable interest on request
Nobody, because equitable interests always beat legal interests
A later buyer who obtains the legal interest for value without notice of it
questions.explanation: Equity's classic rule is that a bona fide purchaser of the legal estate for value without notice takes free of equitable interests. A caveat on the register gives notice and so protects the claimant.
questions.common_trap: Believing equitable rights always prevail over legal ones.

questions.stem: Priya holds an unregistered equitable claim over a shophouse. Which step is the usual way to alert the world to her claim on the register?
options: Register a mortgage in her own favour
Lodge a caveat against the title
Ask the seller to change the lot number
Notify the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
questions.explanation: A caveat is the notice that records a claimed interest on the title and warns later dealers. Property tax records and lot numbers have nothing to do with protecting such a claim.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an unregistered claim protects itself automatically.

questions.stem: Raj mortgages his condominium unit to a bank and the mortgage is registered. A year later he sells the unit to Sofia, subject to the mortgage. Why can the bank still enforce its security against the unit?
options: A registered mortgage is a proprietary right that stays attached to the property despite a change of owner
Sofia personally signed a fresh loan agreement with the bank, promising to repay Raj's existing debt
Raj remains the owner on paper until the whole mortgage has been paid off
Banks automatically rank above every owner under the Residential Property Act, whatever the date of registration
questions.explanation: A mortgage gives the lender a right in the property itself, so a change of owner does not remove it. It is the proprietary nature of the right, not a new promise by Sofia, that keeps it alive.
questions.common_trap: Believing a security interest depends on the new owner promising to honour it.

questions.stem: What does the right to 'alienate' land mean for an owner?
options: The right to transfer the land or an interest in it, for example by sale or gift
The right to keep the land empty and unused for as long as the owner likes
The right to stop the State from ever acquiring the land under any law
The right to demand that neighbours stay out of their own gardens
questions.explanation: Alienation is the power to dispose of land or an interest in it, and it is one of the main elements of ownership. It has nothing to do with leaving land vacant or blocking State acquisition.
questions.common_trap: Mistaking 'alienate' for a power to exclude or to resist acquisition.

questions.stem: Jia Wei owns a terrace house. Which of the following is, by its nature, real property rather than personal property?
options: The sofa bought for the living room
A mobile phone left on the dining table
The freehold land under the terrace house
A branded watch kept in the safe
questions.explanation: Land, and the interests that arise from it, are real property. Furniture and other movables are personal property.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking that land itself is the core example of real property.

questions.stem: In law, what does 'land' include besides the surface of the ground?
options: Only the surface, because everything under and over it belongs to the State and cannot be owned privately
The space below and above the surface, so far as reasonably needed for use and enjoyment
Everything from the centre of the earth up to the edge of outer space
The surface and any airspace, but never the buildings standing on it
questions.explanation: Land covers the surface plus subterranean space and airspace so far as reasonably necessary to use and enjoy it, together with things permanently attached. Ownership is not unlimited in depth or height.
questions.common_trap: Assuming ownership runs from the earth's core to the sky.

questions.stem: A State title for a bungalow plot says nothing about depth. Up to what level does the owner's land extend below the surface?
options: 10 metres below the lowest floor of the building
As deep as the owner can physically excavate
All the way down with no limit
30 metres below the Singapore Height Datum
questions.explanation: Under the State Lands Act, where the title states no depth, the land includes subterranean space to -30.000 metres from the Singapore Height Datum. The deeper space stays with the State.
questions.common_trap: Believing that a landowner automatically owns unlimited depth.

questions.stem: Madam Aini owns a landed house. A neighbouring developer plans a sky bridge that would pass about 40 metres above her garden. Which statement about her airspace is most accurate?
options: She owns all the airspace above her lot with no limit on its height
She owns no airspace at all because every bit of it belongs to the State
Her rights reach only as high as reasonably needed to use and enjoy the land
She owns airspace only if it is mentioned in her fire insurance policy
questions.explanation: Land includes airspace only to the extent reasonably needed to use and enjoy the surface. Space far above that level can be dealt with separately.
questions.common_trap: Assuming airspace ownership is unlimited, or that none exists.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an incorporeal hereditament?
options: A bungalow built on freehold land
A mango tree growing in the garden
A boundary wall between two lots
A right of way over a neighbour's land
questions.explanation: Incorporeal hereditaments are intangible rights enjoyed over land, with easements as the standard example. Buildings, trees and walls are tangible and so corporeal.
questions.common_trap: Calling any valuable feature of a property 'incorporeal' even though it is physical.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts corporeal and incorporeal hereditaments?
options: Corporeal hereditaments are rights over land, while incorporeal ones are buildings and other physical structures
Corporeal hereditaments exist only on freehold land, while incorporeal ones exist on leasehold land
Corporeal hereditaments are tangible parts of land, while incorporeal ones are intangible rights over land
Corporeal hereditaments are registered, while incorporeal ones are never registered
questions.explanation: Corporeal means physical, such as soil and buildings. Incorporeal means a non-physical right, such as an easement, even though it may still be recorded on a title.
questions.common_trap: Swapping the two terms or tying them to tenure.

questions.stem: Which pair of tests do courts use to decide whether an item has become a fixture?
options: The cost of the item and the age of the building
The degree of annexation and the purpose of annexation
The name of the buyer and the date of delivery
The size of the item and the colour of the fixing
questions.explanation: A court looks at how firmly the item is attached to the land or building and why it was attached. Price and size do not decide the question.
questions.common_trap: Guessing that value or size decides fixture status.

questions.stem: A heavy bookshelf stands on the floor of a flat, held in place by its own weight only. On the degree of annexation test, how is it initially treated?
options: As a fixture, because its weight makes it permanent
As a fixture, because it came with the flat when it was bought
As neither, because the test applies only to items fixed outdoors
As a chattel, because there is no physical attachment to the building
questions.explanation: An item resting by its own weight is presumed to be a chattel, though the purpose of annexation can displace that presumption. Weight alone does not make a fixture.
questions.common_trap: Thinking heavy things are automatically fixtures.

questions.stem: Mdm Kaur, the owner of her house, screws a set of antique tapestries to the wall so that visitors can admire them. Is each tapestry likely to be a fixture?
options: No, because they were fixed to display them and not to improve the building
Yes, because any item that is fixed with screws becomes part of the land
Yes, because the tapestries are valuable and look permanent on the wall
No, because only items that were installed by a tenant can be fixtures
questions.explanation: The purpose of annexation is to enjoy the object as an object, and the degree of attachment is slight. In that situation the item is treated as a chattel despite the screws.
questions.common_trap: Equating any physical fixing with fixture status.

questions.stem: Farhan has a concrete-lined koi pond built into the garden of his house and then sells the house. The contract does not mention the pond. Who is entitled to the pond?
options: Farhan, because only items listed in the contract pass to the buyer
The buyer, because a pond built permanently into the land forms part of it
Farhan, because water features are always treated as removable fittings
Neither, because ponds belong to the State under the State Lands Act
questions.explanation: A permanent, substantial improvement to the land is a fixture and passes with the land unless excluded. A silent contract does not strip the buyer of fixtures.
questions.common_trap: Believing that anything not written into the sale contract stays with the seller.

questions.stem: A prefabricated chalet sits on concrete pillars in a garden, held in place by its own weight, and was built to serve as a permanent dwelling. Can it still be a fixture?
options: No, because anything resting only by its own weight is always a chattel
No, because only brick buildings are capable of being fixtures
Yes, because an intention of permanence can outweigh the lack of fixing
Yes, but only if it is registered with SLA as a separate lot
questions.explanation: Courts assess the purpose and circumstances as a whole, so a structure meant to stay permanently may be part of the land even without being fixed. Registration is irrelevant to this question.
questions.common_trap: Treating the degree of annexation as the only test.

questions.stem: As a starting rule, who owns a fixture once it is attached to land?
options: The person who bought the fixture, until the end of its warranty
The contractor who installed it, until the invoice is settled
The owner of the land, because the fixture becomes part of the land
The State, because every fixture is classed as State property
questions.explanation: A fixture becomes part of the land and follows its ownership. Rights of suppliers or tenants to remove certain items are exceptions to this rule.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that the person who paid for an item keeps owning it after it is fixed.

questions.stem: Raj sells his condominium unit. The contract is silent about the built-in kitchen cabinets and wall-mounted air-conditioning units. The buyer finds them removed on handover. What is the legal position?
options: The seller should not have removed them, as items that are fixtures pass with the unit
The seller was entitled to remove them, since only listed items pass to the buyer
The seller was entitled to remove the cabinets but not the air-conditioners, since cabinets are movable
The buyer may keep only what he separately pays for after completion
questions.explanation: Fixtures form part of the property being sold, so they pass to the buyer unless the contract excludes them. Removing built-in items that are fixtures is therefore likely a breach, even though they were not listed.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a seller can take anything the contract does not mention.

questions.stem: Which of these household items is most likely a fitting (chattel) rather than a fixture?
options: A built-in wardrobe fixed to the wall
A wall-mounted air-conditioning unit
A freestanding dining table
A bathroom sink plumbed into the pipes
questions.explanation: A freestanding table is movable and not attached to the building, so it is a chattel. The other items are attached and form part of the property.
questions.common_trap: Treating every item that stays in a home as part of the property.

questions.stem: Ethan buys a flat. The seller leaves a free-standing refrigerator that was never mentioned in the contract, and Ethan assumes it comes with the flat. Who owns the refrigerator?
options: The seller, unless the contract provides that it is included in the sale
Ethan, because everything left in a flat on handover goes to the buyer
The management corporation, because it is a common appliance
Ethan, because movable items pass automatically with a strata title
questions.explanation: A fitting is a chattel and does not pass with the land unless the parties agree it does. That is why sale documents list the fittings that are included.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that movables left in the unit are included by default.

questions.stem: Which pairing of terms is correct?
options: Fixtures are treated as part of the land, and fittings are movable personal property
Fixtures are movable personal property, and fittings are treated as part of the land
Fixtures and fittings are both treated as part of the land but differ in price
Fixtures and fittings are both personal property but differ in how they are taxed
questions.explanation: A fixture is a chattel that has become part of the land through attachment. A fitting stays a chattel, even though it may be placed in the building.
questions.common_trap: Reversing the two labels.

questions.stem: Hock Seng, a tenant, bolts a commercial oven to the floor of his bakery unit. When the lease is about to end, may he take the oven away?
options: Yes, as a trade fixture he may remove it, but he must make good any damage
No, because bolting it down made the oven the landlord's property for good
Yes, but only if the landlord pays him the oven's price
No, because tenants may never remove anything fixed to the premises
questions.explanation: Equipment fixed by a tenant for the purpose of his trade is a trade fixture that he may usually remove during the tenancy. He must repair damage caused by the removal.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that anything bolted down automatically belongs to the landlord.

questions.stem: Weng Kiat's fixed-term lease ended and he moved out. Three months later he asks to collect the shelving he had fitted for his shop. What is the likely position?
options: He may collect them at any time, since he paid for them in the first place and the landlord never owned them
He may collect them, but only if the landlord has not yet re-let the unit
He has probably lost the right, as trade fixtures must be removed within the tenancy
The landlord must buy them from him at their depreciated value
questions.explanation: A tenant's right to remove trade fixtures generally has to be exercised during the term, or within a short period while still lawfully in possession. After leaving, the items are treated as belonging to the landlord.
questions.common_trap: Believing the right to remove survives indefinitely after the lease ends.

questions.stem: Under a lease, the landlord installs built-in wardrobes in a flat. The tenant removes them when moving out. How should this be viewed?
options: It is wrongful, because the wardrobes are the landlord's fixtures, not the tenant's
It is proper, because a tenant may remove anything fixed during the tenancy provided he tells the landlord first
It is proper, because built-in wardrobes are always treated as chattels
It is wrongful only if the landlord gave written notice not to remove them
questions.explanation: The tenant's right to remove covers fixtures the tenant installed for trade, and similar tenant-installed items. Items installed by the landlord belong to the landlord as part of the premises.
questions.common_trap: Applying the tenant's removal right to items it never covered.

questions.stem: Mr Tan mortgages his factory to a bank. Heavy machinery has been permanently bolted to the factory floor. Does the mortgage security cover the machinery?
options: No, because a mortgage covers only the bare soil
No, because machinery always remains personal property
Yes, but only if the bank lists each machine in its valuation report and the owner consents in writing
Yes, because fixtures are part of the land and fall within a mortgage of it
questions.explanation: Fixtures are part of the land, so a mortgage of the land generally extends to them. Loose, unattached equipment would not be covered in the same way.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a mortgage covers only the land and not what is attached.

questions.stem: How many survey districts does Singapore have, and how do they divide?
options: Sixty-four: 34 Town Subdivisions and 30 Mukims
Sixty-four: 30 Town Subdivisions and 34 Mukims
Fifty: 20 Town Subdivisions and 30 Mukims
Seventy: 40 Town Subdivisions and 30 Mukims
questions.explanation: SLA divides Singapore into 30 Town Subdivisions (TS) and 34 Mukims (MK). The two sets together make 64 survey districts.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up which of the two types has 30 and which has 34.

questions.stem: Which description of the two types of survey district is correct?
options: Town Subdivisions cover the city area, and Mukims cover the outer parts of Singapore
Town Subdivisions cover the outer parts, and Mukims cover the city area
Town Subdivisions cover leasehold land, and Mukims cover freehold land
Town Subdivisions cover landed property, and Mukims cover strata and high-rise property
questions.explanation: TS districts lie mostly in the central, built-up area and MK districts in the outer region. The split is geographic and has nothing to do with tenure or property type.
questions.common_trap: Linking TS and MK to tenure or property form instead of location.

questions.stem: A title shows 'TS 21 Lot U4567K'. What does it describe?
options: An ordinary land lot of freehold land in Town Subdivision 21
An accessory lot, such as a car park, attached to a unit in that district
An airspace lot above a road in Town Subdivision 21
A strata lot, being a unit in a subdivided building, in Town Subdivision 21
questions.explanation: The prefix U marks a strata lot, and the final letter is a check alphabet. A plain land lot has no prefix, and an accessory lot carries the prefix A.
questions.common_trap: Not recognising U as the strata lot prefix.

questions.stem: A purchaser of a condominium unit also receives a car park lot whose title reads 'MK 17 Lot A1234T'. How is that lot classified?
options: As a strata lot in its own right
As a plain land lot in Mukim 17
As a subterranean lot below the building
As an accessory lot linked to a strata lot
questions.explanation: The prefix A identifies an accessory lot, which is appurtenant to a strata lot. The final T is the check alphabet.
questions.common_trap: Reading the prefix letter as a check alphabet or vice versa.

questions.stem: An agent sees a bungalow title numbered 'MK 18 Lot 4567A' and tells the client it is an accessory lot because of the letter A. What is the correct comment?
options: It is an ordinary land lot, and the trailing A is only a check alphabet
The agent is right, since any A in the lot number marks an accessory lot
It is a strata lot, because the letter A comes after the digits
It is an airspace lot, since the number ends in a letter
questions.explanation: Prefix letters (U or A) come before the number, whereas the final letter is a computer-generated check alphabet. Having no prefix indicates an ordinary land lot.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the check alphabet at the end with the prefix at the front.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the check alphabet at the end of a lot number?
options: To show the property's tenure
To show which survey district the lot lies in
To rank the lot's priority position within the land register of the district
To guard against errors when the number is quoted or typed
questions.explanation: The check alphabet is generated by computer from the rest of the number so that a misquoted number is easily detected. It carries no information about tenure or location.
questions.common_trap: Believing the final letter encodes tenure or district.

questions.stem: SLA reserves a particular block of numbers for airspace lots and for subterranean lots. Which pairing is correct?
options: 80000 series for airspace lots and 70000 series for subterranean lots
10000 series for airspace lots and 20000 series for subterranean lots
Both use the 90000 series with a different prefix
70000 series for airspace lots and 80000 series for subterranean lots
questions.explanation: SLA numbers airspace lots in the 70000 series and subterranean lots in the 80000 series. Ordinary land lots take their numbers from the rest of the sequence.
questions.common_trap: Reversing the two series.

questions.stem: When does SLA allocate a new strata lot number?
options: When a buyer signs the option to purchase for a unit
When a bank registers a mortgage over a unit
When a building is subdivided into strata units with the required approval
When the Urban Redevelopment Authority revises the Master Plan for that area
questions.explanation: Strata lot numbers are allocated on subdivision of a building (or later amalgamation or subdivision of strata lots). Commercial steps such as signing an option do not create lots.
questions.common_trap: Linking lot creation to sales or financing steps.

questions.stem: Two adjacent land lots owned by the same family are approved for amalgamation into a single site. What happens to the lot numbers?
options: Both old lot numbers are kept side by side
The lot with the smaller number is kept and the other is deleted
SLA allocates a new lot number for the combined site
The owner chooses any number he likes
questions.explanation: Amalgamation and subdivision are among the events for which SLA allocates new lot numbers. The history of such changes is recorded so that older lots can be traced.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that old lot numbers simply continue after a merger.

questions.stem: Where can an agent find the official lot number and survey district of a property?
options: On the Master Plan zoning map published by URA
On the property's title, through an official title search with SLA
On the agent's own Commission Statement
On the CEA public register of licensed estate agents and salespersons
questions.explanation: The lot number and survey district form the legal description in the land register, which can be searched through SLA's title system. Zoning maps show use, not legal description.
questions.common_trap: Looking for legal descriptions in planning or licensing records.

questions.stem: What is the role of SLA's Lot Base System?
options: It records the selling prices of all property transactions across Singapore and the names of the buyers
It records the status of each lot, such as provisional or live, as updated by the Chief Surveyor
It lists every caveat that has been lodged against registered titles
It assigns planning zones and plot ratios to each lot in Singapore
questions.explanation: The Lot Base System is where the Chief Surveyor updates a lot's status, for example from provisional to live. Prices, caveats and zoning are held in other records.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the lot status record with transaction, caveat or planning records.

questions.stem: Under the Land Titles Act 1993, which of the following is included in the proprietorship of land, where the context so permits?
options: The right to build to any height regardless of planning controls
Natural rights to air, light, water and support
A guaranteed view of the sea or the skyline
Ownership of unused State land next to the lot
questions.explanation: Section 4(1) provides that, where the context permits, proprietorship of land includes natural rights to air, light, water and support and the right of access to any highway on which the land abuts. It does not guarantee a view, extra height or adjoining State land.
questions.common_trap: Assuming ownership covers only the soil and buildings, or that it carries a right to a view.

questions.stem: Mr Ong sells his bungalow and plans to dig up the mature rain tree in the garden before handover. The contract says nothing about the tree. May he remove it?
options: Yes, because plants are personal property that stay with the seller
No, because a tree growing in the ground forms part of the land that is being sold
Yes, because trees count as fittings
No, because only trees registered with the National Parks Board pass with land
questions.explanation: Vegetation growing on the land is part of it, so it passes to the buyer unless excluded. It is not a loose chattel like a potted plant.
questions.common_trap: Treating growing trees as movable items.

questions.stem: What is the difference between tenure and estate?
options: Tenure is how long the interest lasts, while estate is the way land is held
Tenure applies only to leasehold land, while estate applies only to freehold land
Tenure is the price paid for the land, while estate is the size of the lot
Tenure is the way land is held, while estate is how long the interest lasts
