questions.explanation: Tenure concerns the relationship under which land is held (ultimately from the State), and estate measures the duration of the holder's interest. Price and area do not enter into either idea.
questions.common_trap: Reversing the two terms or treating them as freehold versus leasehold.

questions.stem: A client's title says the land is held under a '99-year lease from 1 January 1990'. Which feature of the title does that wording describe?
options: The tenure only, namely that the land is held by a company and not by an individual
The planning intensity allowed on the land
The duration of the estate, namely a leasehold estate for a fixed term
The size of the lot in square metres
questions.explanation: A stated number of years describes the estate, which is how long the holder's interest will last. It does not describe planning or area.
questions.common_trap: Mixing duration with planning or physical attributes.

questions.stem: Which estate gives the holder an interest with no fixed end date and can pass to heirs?
options: A 99-year lease
A life estate
A periodic tenancy
Fee simple
questions.explanation: A fee simple is the largest estate, lasting indefinitely and inheritable. A life estate ends on death, and leases and tenancies are limited in time.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that a very long lease or a life estate is as large as a fee simple.

questions.stem: Which pair of titles are both treated as freehold in Singapore?
options: Estate in perpetuity and a 999-year lease
Fee simple and a 99-year lease
Fee simple and estate in perpetuity
A life estate and a 999-year lease
questions.explanation: Fee simple and estate in perpetuity both have no fixed expiry date and are classed as freehold. A 999-year lease, however long, is still leasehold.
questions.common_trap: Treating a very long lease as freehold.

questions.stem: Mr Chua holds a house for the duration of his own life, after which it passes to someone else under the grant. What is the nature of his estate?
options: A leasehold estate for a term certain
A fee simple, since he lives in the house
An estate in perpetuity, because the grant gives no stated end year to the interest
A life estate, which is a freehold estate that ends when he dies
questions.explanation: A life estate lasts for a person's lifetime. It counts as freehold because its length is uncertain, but it cannot pass to heirs.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that no stated end date means the estate is inheritable.

questions.stem: A title is described as 'Estate in Perpetuity'. What does this mean in Singapore?
options: A State lease that renews itself automatically every 99 years for the same holder without any fresh premium
A State grant with no end date, treated as freehold and subject to State Lands Act conditions
A tenancy that lasts only until the owner decides to sell the land
A leasehold that the State may cancel at any time without giving any cause
questions.explanation: An estate in perpetuity is a grant by the State that does not expire, and it is classed as freehold. It still carries the covenants and conditions implied by the State Lands Act.
questions.common_trap: Thinking 'perpetuity' means a renewing lease rather than a freehold-type grant.

questions.stem: What is the defining feature of a leasehold estate?
options: It is held for a fixed maximum period, after which the land goes back to the grantor
It is held for an unlimited period, but the holder pays rent every single year
It can be held only by the State itself or by its statutory boards
It lasts until the holder dies and then passes on to the next generation
questions.explanation: A lease has a term certain, and at the end of it the land goes back to the grantor. Yearly rent is not what makes an estate leasehold.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that paying rent, rather than having a fixed term, is what defines a lease.

questions.stem: A condominium sits on land held under a 99-year lease starting on 1 January 2000. How many years of the lease remain on 1 January 2026?
options: 73 years
74 years
75 years
83 years
questions.explanation: Ninety-nine years from 2000 ends in 2099, so 2099 minus 2026 leaves 73 years. A quick subtraction of 26 from 99 gives the same figure.
questions.common_trap: Adding or dropping a year when counting the remaining term.

questions.stem: An agent tells a buyer that a 999-year leasehold condominium is 'basically freehold, so it is the same thing in law'. What is the best response?
options: The agent is right, because any lease above 99 years is freehold by law
It is freehold because the State can no longer take the land back
It is a leasehold estate for a fixed term, even though that term is very long
It is a life estate because nobody alive will see the lease end
questions.explanation: A 999-year lease still has a fixed end date, so in law it remains leasehold. Its practical value may resemble freehold, but the legal category does not change.
questions.common_trap: Merging legal classification with market perception.

questions.stem: In Singapore's land system, how are most titles to land linked back to the State?
options: Titles trace back to a grant or lease from the State, the ultimate holder of land
Titles trace back to the first person who ever built on the land
Titles stand apart from the State once the land has been sold on to a private buyer or developer
Titles trace back to the Urban Redevelopment Authority's Master Plan
questions.explanation: Land is held through a chain that begins with a State grant, and leases leave the State with a reversion. The Master Plan regulates use, not ownership.
questions.common_trap: Confusing ownership origins with planning control.

questions.stem: Li Na owns an industrial plot and grants a company a 30-year lease of the plot. Which statement describes the arrangement correctly?
options: The company holds the freehold, and Li Na keeps only a right to receive rent for the rest of the term
The company holds a leasehold estate, and Li Na keeps the reversion at the end of the term
Li Na has transferred her ownership, so she retains no interest in the plot
The company holds an estate in perpetuity for the first 30 years only
questions.explanation: A private lessor can also grant a lease, which is a leasehold estate for a term. The lessor keeps the reversion and takes the land back when the term expires.
questions.common_trap: Believing that a long lease passes the lessor's whole estate.

questions.stem: Two condominiums in the same area are almost identical, but the freehold unit sells for noticeably more than the 99-year leasehold unit that has 60 years left. Which fact best explains the gap?
options: Leasehold owners are not allowed to sell their units without the State's approval
The leasehold interest shrinks each year and will end on a fixed date, whereas the freehold has no end date
Freehold owners are exempt from paying property tax on their units
Leasehold units cannot be mortgaged to a bank at all
questions.explanation: A fixed-term estate loses length every year and falls to nothing at expiry, so buyers usually pay less for it than for an estate that never ends. Leasehold units can generally be sold, mortgaged and taxed like freehold ones.
questions.common_trap: Attributing the price difference to legal restrictions on dealing rather than to the limited term.

questions.stem: Through which main forms does the State dispose of State land under the State Lands Act framework?
options: Mortgages, liens and charges over the land, granted to approved banks
Easements and restrictive covenants over neighbouring State land
Grants in perpetuity or fee simple, State leases, and temporary licences
Sale and purchase agreements registered with the URA
questions.explanation: State land may be granted as a freehold-type grant, leased for a term, or occupied temporarily under a licence. Mortgages, easements and covenants are dealings by private holders, not forms of State disposal.
questions.common_trap: Mistaking private-law dealings for the State's modes of alienation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is among the covenants the State Lands Act implies in a grant, unless the grant says otherwise?
options: To keep the boundary landmarks in substantial repair
To redevelop the land within five years of the grant
To insure every building on the land with an approved insurer
To lodge the plans of every renovation with the Housing and Development Board
questions.explanation: Implied covenants include paying the rent, maintaining boundary landmarks, not using land for burial without permission, and not dividing the land in parcels. Redevelopment deadlines and insurance are not among them.
questions.common_trap: Believing that State grants carry implied development-timing duties.

questions.stem: Mr Abdul owns land held under a State grant and wants to bury his late father in the garden. What is the position under the implied covenants?
options: He needs the Minister's written permission, as an implied covenant restricts burial
He may bury freely, since private land is not touched by State covenants or by any health regulations
He needs only the written consent of his neighbours on each side
He needs only the consent of his mortgagee, if there is one
questions.explanation: A State grant implies a covenant against using any part of the land for burial without the Minister's written permission. Neighbour or lender consent is not the test.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a landowner may use private land for any purpose.

questions.stem: Madam Goh holds a State grant and leases one half of her large plot to a nursery operator for five years. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a breach, because land under a State grant may never be leased in part
It is allowed only if SLA gives written consent in every single case
It is allowed only if the lease runs for less than one year at most
It is allowed, because leases of up to 7 years are excepted from the covenant
questions.explanation: The implied covenant bars assigning or demising part of the land, but leases not exceeding 7 years are excepted. A five-year lease of half the plot therefore falls within the exception.
questions.common_trap: Believing any partial leasing breaches the covenant regardless of term.

questions.stem: Ravi owns a State-granted plot and sells the eastern half to one buyer and the western half to another by way of separate assignments, without any approval. What is the likely consequence?
options: Nothing, since an owner is free to subdivide by selling off the land in parts
He breaches the implied covenant against dealing in parcels, risking forfeiture
He must only pay the Land Betterment Charge on each of the two parcels
The transfers are valid but the Collector must first buy back each half
questions.explanation: The covenant prohibits assigning the land otherwise than as a whole, and the State may re-enter for breach. Proper subdivision needs the relevant approvals before the parcels are dealt with.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an owner can split a State-granted plot informally.

questions.stem: Unless the grant says otherwise, what royalty does the State reserve on minerals taken from land under the State Lands Act (other than laterite)?
options: 10% of the gross produce
5% of the net profit
25% of the gross produce
50% of the sale price of the land
questions.explanation: The reserved royalty is 10% of the gross produce of mines and minerals, with laterite excluded. It is a continuing reservation by the State and not a one-off charge.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the royalty with a profit share or a land-value charge.

questions.stem: A statutory board needs clay and sand from a State-granted farm plot, not a dwelling site, for a public road project. Mr Yeo owns the plot. What compensation can he expect under the implied conditions?
options: Full market value of all the clay and sand taken from the land
Compensation equal to three times the annual rent of the plot
Compensation only for actual damage to crops, trees or buildings, not for the material
None at all, not even for damage caused to crops or buildings
questions.explanation: The State reserves the right to take earth, clay, gravel, sand and stone for public purposes without compensation except for actual damage to growing crops, roads, paths, fruit trees or buildings. The right does not extend to a dwelling house site, its curtilage and garden.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the State must buy the materials it takes.

questions.stem: Which right is reserved to the Government under the implied conditions of a State grant or lease?
options: A right to veto any sale of the land to a foreign buyer or company without giving reasons
A right to take a share of any profit made on a later resale
Free access for officers to lay and maintain drains, sewers and water pipes
A right to occupy the top floor of any building later erected
questions.explanation: State titles carry reservations that let officers and workmen enter to lay and maintain drainage and utility services. Profit sharing or veto rights are not part of these implied terms.
questions.common_trap: Inventing State reservations that do not exist in the Act.

questions.stem: For which kind of breach does the State Lands Act's implied right of re-entry apply?
options: Breach of an implied covenant, other than those on rent and landmarks
Late payment of the annual rent on the land, and nothing else
Any failure by the holder to renew a tenancy of the land
Failure by the holder to pay the annual property tax on time
questions.explanation: The right to re-enter and forfeit applies to breaches of the implied covenants, with the covenants to pay rent and to keep landmarks excluded. Property tax is a separate matter for IRAS.
questions.common_trap: Assuming non-payment of rent is the main trigger for re-entry.

questions.stem: The Collector lawfully re-enters a State-granted plot after the grantee breaches an implied covenant. What is the usual legal effect?
options: The land passes to the grantee's heirs on exactly the same terms as before the breach
The land is forfeited to and vests in the Government
The State must first pay the grantee the market value of the land
The grant continues, but the grantee must pay a fixed fine to SLA
questions.explanation: Under the State Lands Act, re-entry for breach of an implied covenant forfeits the land to the Government, where it vests. The State does not have to pay the grantee for it.
questions.common_trap: Believing the State must compensate a defaulting grantee.

questions.stem: A temple holds land granted at nominal rent for religious purposes. Without the President's written consent, the committee leases part of the building to a retail chain. What can the State do?
options: Raise the rent by up to 50% under the rent revision rules
Treat the land as forfeited to the Government because the purpose has changed
Require the temple to pay a Differential Premium before the new use starts
Do nothing, so long as the nominal rent is paid on time each year
questions.explanation: Land granted free or at nominal rent for religious or charitable purposes is forfeited if used for another purpose without consent. Paying the rent does not cure the change of use.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that paying rent protects a grant that has been diverted to another use.

questions.stem: Under the State Lands Act, by how much may the rent for a new term exceed the rent of the previous term when the State revises rent at the end of each 30-year term?
options: By no more than 10%
By no more than 25%
By no more than 100%
By no more than 50%
questions.explanation: Rent for the new term may not exceed the previous term's rent by more than 50%, and improvements made by the holder are disregarded. The cap is a statutory protection for holders.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that revised rent can reset to full market rent.

questions.stem: Hui Min buys a plot held under a State grant and later discovers that the grant reserves mineral rights to the State. She says she had no notice of the reservation and is not bound. Is she right?
options: No, an assignee is bound by the reservations and covenants in the State grant, with or without notice
Yes, an innocent buyer takes free of any reservation or covenant that she did not know about
Yes, but only if the seller also did not know about the reservation when he sold the plot
No, but only if the reservation was registered within the past 12 months
questions.explanation: The Act binds the assignee to the exceptions, reservations and covenants in the State title, regardless of notice. The State's reservations are therefore part of what she buys.
questions.common_trap: Carrying over the 'innocent purchaser' idea to State titles.

questions.stem: What happens when a 99-year State lease reaches the end of its term, with no extension?
options: The lessee automatically becomes the freeholder
The land reverts to the State, which holds the reversion
The lessee keeps the land for another 99 years at the same rent
The land passes to the Housing and Development Board
questions.explanation: A lease has a fixed term, and the State's reversionary interest takes effect at its end. Any extension is a matter for the State's discretion and is not automatic.
questions.common_trap: Assuming leasehold land converts to freehold or renews on its own.

questions.stem: An organiser wants to hold a two-week food bazaar on a vacant State site. Which arrangement is most suitable?
options: A grant in perpetuity of the site
A temporary occupation licence from SLA
A 99-year State lease of the site
A restrictive covenant over the site
questions.explanation: A TOL lets a person use State land for a limited period and a defined activity such as an event. A grant or long lease would be out of proportion to a two-week event.
questions.common_trap: Choosing a permanent tenure for a short-term use.

questions.stem: What kind of right does a temporary occupation licence give?
options: A leasehold estate in the land that can be registered on the title by the licensee
A freehold title that is limited to one calendar year only
Permission to use State land for a stated activity and period, with no estate in it
A right to build permanent structures on the land for the licence term with SLA's later consent
questions.explanation: A TOL is a licence, which is a permission to use bare State land for a stated activity and period. It is not an estate or a lease, and it carries reinstatement requirements.
questions.common_trap: Treating a TOL as a short lease or tenancy that gives an interest in land.

questions.stem: What is the maximum period for a non-renewable temporary occupation licence (NRTOL) issued by SLA?
options: 30 days
6 months
3 years
90 days
questions.explanation: SLA issues non-renewable TOLs for no more than 90 days, mainly for short events, while renewable TOLs can run up to three years. The short cap reflects the one-off nature of the use.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the 90-day non-renewable limit with the three-year limit for renewable licences.

questions.stem: Which charge, collected by SLA from 1 August 2022, replaced the Differential Premium and the Development Charge?
options: The Land Betterment Charge
The Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty
The Temporary Development Levy
The Annual Value Premium
questions.explanation: The Land Betterment Charge took effect on 1 August 2022 and replaced the Differential Premium, the Development Charge and the Temporary Development Levy. Stamp duty is a different kind of tax altogether.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that the old charges still operate alongside the LBC.

questions.stem: A developer obtains URA permission to turn an industrial site into a residential development, which greatly increases the land's value. Which agency issues the liability order for the resulting betterment charge?
options: Singapore Land Authority
Urban Redevelopment Authority
Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
Housing and Development Board
questions.explanation: URA grants the planning permission, but SLA follows up with the taxable person by issuing the Liability Order for the Land Betterment Charge. The charge is not issued by the planning authority.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the planning authority also collects the charge.

questions.stem: How is the Land Betterment Charge fundamentally determined?
options: From the price that the owner originally paid when buying the land, adjusted for inflation since then
From the annual value that is used to compute yearly property tax
From the number of units that the developer intends to sell
From the gap between the post-chargeable and pre-chargeable valuations of the land
questions.explanation: The charge is based on the increase in land value caused by the chargeable consent, measured by comparing the value after the approval with the value before it. Purchase price, property tax value and unit count do not enter.
questions.common_trap: Linking the charge to price paid or property tax value.

questions.stem: A site is valued at S$40m on its existing permitted use and at S$52m on the use approved by URA. If the charge is taken as 70% of the increase in value, what is the LBC?
options: S$12m
questions.explanation: The increase is S$52m minus S$40m, which is S$12m, and 70% of that is S$8.4m. Applying the rate to the post-approval value would wrongly give S$36.4m.
questions.common_trap: Applying the rate to the whole new value instead of to the increase.

questions.stem: Which event is most likely to trigger a Land Betterment Charge?
options: Registration of an ordinary transfer of freehold land from seller to buyer, whatever the price paid
Payment of the yearly property tax bill on an investment property
Renewal of a two-year tenancy of a shop unit in a shophouse
Planning permission that raises the land's value, such as allowing a higher intensity
questions.explanation: The charge arises on a chargeable consent such as planning permission or a variation of a restrictive covenant that adds value. Ordinary transfers, tax payments and tenancy renewals do not.
questions.common_trap: Treating any property transaction as a trigger for the charge.

questions.stem: How long does a taxable person have to pay the Land Betterment Charge after SLA issues the liability order?
options: Seven days from the date of the order
One month from the date of the order
Six months from the date of the order
Five years from the date of the order
questions.explanation: SLA's liability order requires payment within one month of its date. Payment in full ends the order.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a long instalment period applies.

questions.stem: Which statute allows the Government to acquire private land compulsorily?
options: The State Lands Act
The Land Titles Act
The Planning Act
The Land Acquisition Act
questions.explanation: The Land Acquisition Act sets out the process and the compensation for compulsory acquisition. The State Lands Act deals with State-owned land, not with taking private land.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the Act on State land with the Act on taking private land.

questions.stem: On which basis may land be acquired under the Land Acquisition Act?
options: The owner has fallen behind on his property tax
The land is needed for a public purpose, such as a new MRT line
The owner is a foreigner holding private residential land
The owner is in a dispute with a neighbour
questions.explanation: Acquisition is allowed where the land is needed for a public purpose, for a work in the public interest, or for residential, commercial or industrial purposes in accordance with the Act. Tax arrears and private disputes are not grounds.
questions.common_trap: Assuming acquisition is a penalty for the owner's conduct.

questions.stem: On what basis is compensation for acquired land assessed?
options: The price that the owner originally paid when he bought the land
The owner's own figure for what the land is worth to him
The annual value that is used to compute property tax
Market value, as at the date fixed by the Land Acquisition Act
questions.explanation: Compensation is based on market value fixed as of the date the Act specifies, and not on what the owner paid or wants. The property tax value is a different figure.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the owner's original price or asking price decides compensation.

questions.stem: Mdm Kaur receives the Collector's award for her acquired shophouse and feels the amount is too low. What can she do?
options: Ask the Collector to cancel the acquisition itself and return the land to her
Refuse to hand over possession until the dispute ends
Appeal to the Appeals Board within 28 days of receiving the award
Apply to URA for a fresh valuation
questions.explanation: An owner who disagrees with the Collector's award may lodge a notice of appeal with the Appeals Board within 28 days of receiving the award. The appeal is about the amount of compensation, not about whether the land may be acquired.
questions.common_trap: Believing an owner can contest the acquisition itself or hold on to the property during an appeal.

questions.stem: Mr Lau owns a house plot whose State title restricts it to one single dwelling. He asks SLA to vary the restrictive covenant so that he can build a small block of flats. The change will raise the land's value. What is likely to result?
options: Nothing is payable, because only URA planning permission attracts the charge
The Differential Premium, since that regime still applies to covenant variations
A Land Betterment Charge may be payable on the increase in value arising from the variation
Stamp duty on the increase in value, collected by IRAS
questions.explanation: Since 1 August 2022, variations of restrictive covenants that add value fall under the Land Betterment Charge, which replaced the Differential Premium. Stamp duty relates to documents and transactions, not to this uplift.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the old Differential Premium still applies to covenant changes.

questions.stem: In land law, what is an encumbrance?
options: The official register entry that shows who owns a parcel of land and for how long it is held
A physical flaw in the land, such as poor drainage or uneven ground, that reduces its value
A third party's claim over land, such as a mortgage or right of way, that limits its use
A restriction on land use that arises only from the Master Plan zoning of the area
questions.explanation: An encumbrance is a right or claim held by someone else over the land (for example a mortgage, easement or restrictive covenant). Zoning is a planning control, not a private claim over the title.
questions.common_trap: Students confuse encumbrances on title with planning rules or physical defects.

questions.stem: Mei Ling signs an option to buy a terrace house. The seller's title shows a registered mortgage to a bank, and the contract says the property is sold free from encumbrances. What must happen by completion?
options: The mortgage must be discharged so the property passes to her without that burden
Mei Ling must take over the mortgage, since a mortgage never needs to be cleared on a sale
The mortgage ends automatically once the option is exercised
The bank keeps its charge, but Mei Ling can ignore it if she pays the full price
questions.explanation: 'Free from encumbrances' means existing burdens such as a mortgage must be cleared (usually from the sale proceeds) before or at completion. A mortgage does not fall away on its own when an option is exercised.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a registered mortgage disappears once the buyer pays the price without it being discharged.

questions.stem: A developer's conditions of sale forbid every buyer of a terrace house from building a fence at the front boundary. This burden on each house is best described as which of the following?
options: A positive easement
A bare licence
A lease of the front garden to the developer
A restrictive (negative) covenant
questions.explanation: The buyer is only prevented from doing something on their own land, which is the nature of a restrictive covenant. An easement would give another landowner a right over the land.
questions.common_trap: Confusing a covenant that restricts building with an easement that gives a right to use.

questions.stem: What is the legal nature of a licence over land?
options: A legal estate that lasts as long as the licensee lives
A personal permission that creates no estate in the land
A right attached to neighbouring land that passes to each new owner
A registered interest that always binds a buyer of the land
questions.explanation: A licence only makes lawful what would otherwise be a trespass; it gives no estate and is personal to the licensee. Rights that attach to land and bind successors are easements, not licences.
questions.common_trap: Treating any permission to use land as a proprietary right that survives a sale.

questions.stem: Madam Teo lets her neighbour's son cut through her garden to the bus stop, without any payment or promise. After a quarrel she tells him to stop. What is the legal position?
options: He has gained an easement because he used the path regularly for several months
She may withdraw it, since a bare licence is revocable and he must stop crossing
She needs a court order first, since permission to cross land can only be ended by the court
He may keep crossing because no money was demanded, so the permission is irrevocable
questions.explanation: A gratuitous permission is a bare licence and can be withdrawn at will. Regular use with permission does not turn into an easement.
questions.common_trap: Believing that long or repeated use of a path with permission creates a lasting right.

questions.stem: Hui Min pays Mr Goh S$20,000 for the right to enter his plot for six months to dig out and carry away the sand deposits. Mr Goh tries to cancel after two months. What kind of right does Hui Min have?
options: A bare licence, which Mr Goh can end whenever he wishes
A freehold estate in the plot for the six months he paid for
A negative easement over the rest of Mr Goh's land
A licence coupled with a grant, which Mr Goh cannot simply cancel
questions.explanation: A permission to enter that is tied to a grant of a right to take something from the land (a profit) goes with that interest and cannot be withdrawn at will. A bare licence has no such grant.
questions.common_trap: Assuming every licence can be revoked at any time, even when it accompanies a granted right.

questions.stem: A training academy hires out a seminar room to Farhan for one Saturday at S$300, and its staff keep access to the room. What does Farhan hold?
options: A contractual licence
A one-day lease of the room
An easement over the academy's building
A tenancy at will
questions.explanation: Farhan's permission rests on a contract, but without exclusive possession it gives no estate in land. A lease needs exclusive possession for a defined term.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that paying for use of space automatically makes the user a tenant.

questions.stem: Which feature most strongly points to a lease rather than a licence?
options: The occupier pays the owner a regular sum each month
The agreement is described by the owner as a licence
The occupier has exclusive possession for a defined term
The occupier may use the premises only for residential purposes
questions.explanation: Exclusive possession for a fixed period is the hallmark of a lease. Payment alone does not make a lease, and the label the parties use does not decide the question.
questions.common_trap: Relying on the document's heading or on payment rather than on exclusive possession.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur signs a document called a 'Licence Agreement' giving Jia Wei a shop unit for two years at S$3,000 a month. Jia Wei holds the only key, and Madam Kaur may not enter without his consent. How would a court likely treat the arrangement?
options: As a licence, because the parties chose that title for the document
As an easement, because Jia Wei is allowed to use the unit
As a lease, since Jia Wei has exclusive possession for a fixed term
As a licence, because rent was paid monthly instead of in a lump sum
questions.explanation: Courts look at the substance of the arrangement, and exclusive possession for a certain term indicates a tenancy. A heading cannot turn a lease into a licence.
questions.common_trap: Believing the parties' label decides whether the arrangement is a lease or a licence.

questions.stem: Mr Tan lets a flat to Jia Wei 'for as long as I do not need it for my own family'. No end date is stated. Does this create a valid lease?
options: No, because the maximum length of the term was not certain at the start
Yes, because any right to occupy a flat for money is a lease
Yes, but only for a year, which the law fills in automatically
No, because a lease cannot be granted to someone who is not related to the landlord
questions.explanation: A lease must have a term whose beginning and maximum duration are certain from the start. An open-ended 'until I need it' arrangement does not meet that test.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking that the length of a lease must be certain at the outset.

questions.stem: Which pair of features are the essential hallmarks of a lease, as opposed to a licence?
options: Exclusive possession and a term that is certain
A written deed and rent paid in advance
Registration at the Singapore Land Authority and a security deposit
Payment of rent and the owner's right to enter at any time
questions.explanation: A tenancy is exclusive possession for a term. Rent is the usual consideration but is not what separates a lease from a licence, and a deed or registration is not the defining feature.
questions.common_trap: Treating rent or a written document as what makes an arrangement a lease.

questions.stem: A company holds a 30-year lease of a shop unit. Who is entitled to the unit when the term ends?
options: The tenant, because a lessee who has paid rent for 30 years becomes the owner
The landlord, who has kept a reversionary interest in the land
The State, because every lease reverts to the State at the end of its term
Whoever lodges a caveat on the title first
questions.explanation: The lessor grants a lease out of a larger interest and keeps the reversion, so the land returns to that lessor when the term ends. Only a State lease reverts to the State.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that long occupation under a lease gives the tenant ownership when it ends.

questions.stem: Mr Gan has a 2-year tenant, Hui Min, with exclusive possession of one unit, and a friend, Raj, who has only been allowed to stay in another unit as a favour. Mr Gan sells the property to Mr Ho, who registers the transfer. Who is more likely to keep a right to stay against Mr Ho?
options: Raj, because a person who has been allowed to stay becomes protected after a sale
Hui Min, because a lease is an interest in land capable of binding a new owner
Both of them equally, because any occupier is protected against a new owner
Neither of them, because every occupation right ends when the land is sold
questions.explanation: A tenancy is a proprietary interest and can bind a purchaser, while a licence is personal and gives no right against a buyer. Under the Land Titles Act, a registered buyer takes subject to the rights of an occupying tenant whose term is 7 years or less, even if the tenancy is not on the register.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a licence binds a purchaser in the same way a tenancy does.

questions.stem: Which description best fits an easement?
options: A right to take the whole of the neighbour's land after using it for a fixed number of years
A promise by one landowner to pay money to another each year for using the land
A permission given to a named person that ends when the permission-giver dies
A right of one landowner to use, or restrict the use of, a neighbouring parcel of land
questions.explanation: An easement is a limited right over another's land that benefits the dominant land. It gives neither ownership nor possession of the servient land.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up an easement with ownership gained through long use of someone's land.

questions.stem: Which set correctly lists the essential conditions for a valid easement?
options: Two plots with different owners, a right benefiting the dominant plot, and a right that can be granted
A dominant and a servient tenement, the same owner, rent payable, and an agreement signed by both owners before a witness
A servient tenement only, a right that benefits a named person, a deed, and 20 years of use
Two adjoining lots, a right to possess part of the servient land, a registered lease, and a caveat
questions.explanation: The four conditions are: dominant and servient land, different owners, the right accommodates the dominant land, and it is capable of forming the subject matter of a grant. Possession or rent does not feature.
questions.common_trap: Forgetting that an easement must benefit land, not just a person, and that the two plots need different owners.

questions.stem: Why can a person who owns no nearby land not claim an easement over a path he has walked across for years?
options: The path is not wide enough to qualify
Easements can only be claimed over State land
There is no dominant tenement that the right benefits
He has not paid the owner a fee for using the path
questions.explanation: An easement must attach to land owned by the claimant (the dominant tenement). A purely personal benefit cannot be an easement.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that repeated personal use alone can create an easement.

questions.stem: Jia Wei owns Lot 7 and the neighbouring Lot 8. He drives across Lot 8 to reach the public road from Lot 7. He asks whether he holds an easement over Lot 8. What is the answer?
options: Yes, because the route is clearly necessary for reaching Lot 7
Yes, but only if he registers the right of way at the Land Registry
No, as an easement needs the two lots to have different owners
No, because a right of way can never be an easement
questions.explanation: Where one person owns both parcels, he simply uses his own land and no easement can exist between them. A right of way is a typical easement when the owners differ.
questions.common_trap: Ignoring the rule that the dominant and servient land must have different owners.

questions.stem: Which of the following rights would qualify as an easement benefiting a house?
options: A right for the house owner to cross the neighbouring lot to reach the public road
A right for the house owner's cousin to fish in the neighbour's pond for pleasure
A right for the house owner to occupy the neighbour's spare room for a month
A right for the house owner to receive a share of the neighbour's rent
questions.explanation: A right of way benefits the dominant land and can be granted over the servient land without taking possession. The other rights are personal, take possession, or are purely financial.
questions.common_trap: Believing that any right to use or occupy a neighbour's property is an easement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a NEGATIVE easement?
options: A right to walk across the neighbour's courtyard
A right to run a water pipe under the neighbour's lot
A right to park a car on the neighbour's driveway
A right to light that stops the neighbour blocking a window
questions.explanation: A negative easement prevents the servient owner from doing something on their own land, such as blocking light. The other three let the dominant owner do something on the servient land, so they are positive.
questions.common_trap: Assuming any right over a neighbour's land is positive, including rights that only restrict the neighbour.

questions.stem: A house owner is allowed to lay and maintain a drain across the back of the neighbouring lot. How is this easement classified?
options: A negative easement, since the neighbour loses use of part of the lot
A positive easement, since the owner acts on the servient land
A restrictive covenant, since it concerns the use of land
A bare licence, since it was agreed between neighbours
questions.explanation: A right to do something on another's land (lay a drain, use a path) is a positive easement. A negative easement only restrains what the servient owner may do.
questions.common_trap: Confusing a right to act on the neighbour's land with a restriction on the neighbour.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between an easement and a licence?
options: An easement can be given orally, while a licence always needs a deed
An easement attaches to land and binds later owners; a licence is personal
An easement gives possession of the neighbour's land, while a licence does not
An easement can only be created by a court, while a licence is created by agreement
questions.explanation: An easement is a proprietary right that benefits the dominant land and burdens the servient land for successors. A licence is only a personal permission and does not bind a buyer.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an easement gives possession, when it only gives a right of use.

questions.stem: Which statement about the nature of an easement is correct?
options: The holder may exclude the neighbour from the land that carries the easement
The holder becomes the registered owner of the strip of land used
The holder acquires the right only for as long as the neighbour lives
The holder may use the neighbour's land in a limited way but cannot possess it
questions.explanation: An easement is an incorporeal right: it allows enjoyment of a limited use but not possession or ownership. The servient owner remains owner and can use the land in a way that does not interfere.
questions.common_trap: Treating an easement as if it transferred part of the servient owner's land.

questions.stem: How is a new right of way normally created over land registered under the Land Titles Act?
options: By a registered instrument of grant noted on both lots' folios
By the dominant owner using the path openly for a long enough time
By a verbal agreement between the two owners in front of two witnesses
By the Controller of Residential Property lodging a caveat
questions.explanation: Easements over registered land are created deliberately by a registered instrument and notified on the folios. Long use alone cannot create one on registered land.
questions.common_trap: Expecting an informal agreement or years of use to be enough on registered land.

questions.stem: Raj has crossed a neighbour's registered lot to reach his gate every day for 25 years, without hiding it and without ever asking permission. The neighbour now blocks the path. Under the Land Titles Act, can Raj rely on the long use to claim an easement?
options: Yes, because 25 years of open use is above the minimum for prescription
Yes, but only if he proves the neighbour knew of the use throughout
No, since easements over registered land cannot arise by long use
No, because prescription covers rights of light and not rights of way
questions.explanation: The Land Titles Act bars acquiring an easement over registered land by long use, prescription or presumed grant, unless the statute itself gives the easement. Raj would need a registered grant.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that decades of open use create a right on registered land.

questions.stem: At common law, long use can support a claim to an easement by prescription. Which kind of use is needed?
options: Use that is occasional, secret and with the owner's written permission
Use that was begun with force but continued for at least ten years
Use that is continuous and open, as of right, without force or permission
Use that was by the owner's friend with the owner's repeated verbal permission
questions.explanation: Prescription needs uninterrupted use that is open and not by force, secrecy or permission. Use that depends on permission is not use 'as of right'.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking that use by permission can never found a prescriptive claim.

questions.stem: Mr Ong buys an inner plot whose only possible access to a road is across the vendor's remaining land. No route is mentioned in the sale documents. Under the common law (apart from the Land Titles Act), on what ground could a court find that an easement exists?
options: Necessity, because the plot would otherwise have no access at all
Prescription, because the vendor must have allowed him to cross for years
Unity of seisin, because both plots once belonged to the vendor
Estoppel, because the vendor sold the plot for a high price
questions.explanation: At common law an easement of necessity may be implied where a grant would leave land landlocked. On land registered under the Land Titles Act, s 97(1) restricts implied easements to those the Act provides.
questions.common_trap: Confusing necessity with prescription, which needs long use.

questions.stem: Jia Wei buys Lot 3 in a landed estate that was subdivided into separate lots sharing sewer and water lines. The main water pipe for Lot 4 runs beneath his lot. Is Lot 4's right to keep the pipe there protected?
options: No, because no easement is valid unless it is written into each lot's transfer
No, because Jia Wei's lot is registered and nothing can burden it
Yes, but only for ten years from the date of subdivision
Yes, as the Act implies service easements between lots in such a development
questions.explanation: The Act implies cross-easements for water, drainage, electricity, gas and similar services among lots in a development. They exist without being written into the transfers.
questions.common_trap: Thinking every easement over registered land must be expressly granted.

questions.stem: Which easements are implied between lots in a strata development under the Land Titles (Strata) Act?
options: Use of the swimming pool, parking lots and the roof terrace by all residents
Support, shelter, and passage of services such as water and electricity
Only rights of way along the common corridors and stairwells
Exclusive use of balconies and the right to alter the building facade
questions.explanation: The Act implies rights of support, shelter and services, plus ancillary rights, among strata lots and the common property. Facilities like parking are not implied easements.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that rights of use of facilities must be implied by statute.

questions.stem: Farhan buys a strata unit. The title shows no entry about easements, but the water pipe serving the unit above runs through his ceiling void. Can the upper owner insist on keeping the pipe there?
options: No, because only easements recorded on the folio can bind a buyer
Yes, since a statutory easement for services needs no entry on the register
No, because the pipe is a trespass unless Farhan consented in writing
Yes, but only if the upper owner lodged a caveat before Farhan bought
questions.explanation: Easements implied by the Land Titles (Strata) Act do not need to be registered or notified to be enforceable. The upper owner's right arises by statute.
questions.common_trap: Treating the register as showing every easement even where the statute implies them.

questions.stem: How can the owners of the dominant and servient land bring an easement to an end by agreement?
options: By the dominant owner moving out of the property for more than six months
By the servient owner renewing the lease of the land to the dominant owner
By lodging a caveat against the dominant land
By an express release, normally made by deed
questions.explanation: An easement may be released expressly by the person entitled to the benefit, usually in a deed. Absence or a caveat does not end it.
questions.common_trap: Believing a right of way ends automatically when the owner stops living there.

questions.stem: Does eight years of non-use of a right of way, by itself, bring the easement to an end?
options: No, since non-use alone does not show intent to abandon the right
Yes, because any easement lapses after five years of non-use
Yes, because a shorter route removes the need for the easement
No, because an easement can only end when the neighbour dies
questions.explanation: Abandonment requires non-use plus evidence that the holder intended to give up the right for good. Mere non-use, even over a long period, does not end the easement by itself.
questions.common_trap: Assuming non-use alone extinguishes an easement.

questions.stem: Does common ownership of two lots in a subdivided development wipe out the implied utility easements between them?
options: Yes, because one person cannot hold an easement over his own land, so they ended permanently
Yes, because they would need to be recreated by registered instrument
No, common ownership does not extinguish them, and they revive when ownership separates
No, but only if the developer lodged a caveat during that time
questions.explanation: The Land Titles Act says common ownership of two lots does not extinguish the implied easements, and they revive when ownership separates. This differs from the general rule on unity of ownership.
questions.common_trap: Applying the general common law rule on unity of ownership to statutory easements.

questions.stem: In land law, what is a covenant?
options: A right to use another person's land for a defined purpose without being allowed to exclude the owner
A registered interest that lets a bank sell land if a loan is not repaid
A promise made in a deed that creates a legal obligation, with the promisor called the covenantor
A court order stopping a person from entering another's land
questions.explanation: A covenant is a binding promise contained in a deed. It is the covenantor who is obliged and the covenantee who benefits.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up covenants with easements or mortgages.

questions.stem: Which of these covenants given by a landowner is a POSITIVE covenant?
options: A promise to repair and maintain the fence between the two properties
A promise not to build a house taller than two storeys on the plot
A promise not to use the premises as a food factory or workshop
A promise not to build any structure on the front garden of the plot
questions.explanation: A positive covenant requires the covenantor to spend money or do something. The other promises only restrain the covenantor, so they are restrictive.
questions.common_trap: Treating any boundary-related promise as restrictive.

questions.stem: Mei Ling buys a plot from Mr Chan and promises in the deed not to build a shop on it. Later she sells to Farhan. Who remains bound to Mr Chan by privity of contract?
options: Farhan, because he now owns the plot
Both Mei Ling and Farhan, equally, in all cases
Neither of them, since a covenant is not enforceable after a sale
Mei Ling, because she was an original party to the covenant
questions.explanation: Privity of contract binds the original parties to what they promised, even after they dispose of the land. A successor is bound only if the covenant runs with the land.
questions.common_trap: Believing that the original covenantor is freed once the land is sold.

questions.stem: On what basis is an assignee of a lease liable to the landlord for rent, although she never signed the original lease?
options: Privity of contract, since she is bound by the original lease
Privity of estate, since she holds the tenant's estate
Prescription, since she paid rent for a long period
Unity of seisin, since she took over the whole premises
questions.explanation: Privity of estate exists between the landlord and the person who holds the tenant's estate, so covenants touching and concerning the land can bind the assignee. She did not sign the original lease.
questions.common_trap: Thinking only the original signatories can ever be liable under a lease.

questions.stem: A buyer of a freehold plot covenants with the seller to contribute to the upkeep of the boundary fence. The buyer later sells to Farhan, who refuses to pay anything. Can the original seller enforce the covenant directly against Farhan?
options: Yes, because covenants relating to land always run with the land to every later owner
Generally not, because a positive covenant does not bind a later freehold owner
Yes, because Farhan is deemed to have signed the original deed with the seller
No, because covenants can only bind the original covenantor's family members
questions.explanation: The burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land to successors, whereas some restrictive covenants do. The seller's claim lies against the original buyer who gave the promise.
questions.common_trap: Assuming positive and restrictive covenants bind successors in the same way.

questions.stem: A restriction on building above two storeys was agreed between two neighbouring lot owners, but nobody had it noted on the land register. A buyer of the burdened lot later builds three storeys. Can the original beneficiary enforce the restriction against the buyer?
options: Yes, because the buyer must have known about the neighbour's promise
Yes, because all restrictions bind buyers once they are 20 years old
No, because restrictions on height are never enforceable
Generally not, as an unnotified restriction does not bind a later owner
questions.explanation: On registered land a restriction must be notified on the folio of the burdened land to bind later owners. Without that, the buyer takes free of it.
questions.common_trap: Believing that a private agreement binds buyers even when it is not on the register.

questions.stem: A restriction was created over land already registered under the Land Titles Act and notified on the folio of the servient lot in March 2004. Nobody has ever extended it. In October 2026, is it still enforceable against the current owner?
options: No, since it lapses 20 years after notification unless extended
Yes, since a restriction lasts as long as the dominant land exists
Yes, since extension is automatic every 10 years
No, since all restrictions end after 10 years
questions.explanation: A restriction notified under the Land Titles Act stops being enforceable 20 years after notification unless extended, and the Registrar cancels the entry. Here 20 years ran out in 2024.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a restrictive covenant on registered land lasts indefinitely.

questions.stem: A notified restriction is about to lapse. By how many years can an extension continue the restriction each time?
options: 5 years, by a request made by the servient owner to the Registrar
20 years, by a request made by the Registrar to the servient owner
10 years, by an instrument from the person entitled to benefit
10 years, by a request made by the servient owner to the Registrar
questions.explanation: A restriction can be extended by an instrument signed by someone entitled to the benefit, each extension adding 10 years. The servient owner has no power to extend a burden on his own land.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the 5-year period for caveats with the 10-year period for restriction extensions.

questions.stem: How can a private restriction on registered land be released without going to court?
options: The servient owner lodges a caveat against the dominant land
The servient owner simply stops complying for ten years
A release signed by the dominant owner and registered interest holders
The Registrar cancels it once the servient owner asks
questions.explanation: A release needs the consent of the persons entitled to the benefit, executed in the approved form. Non-compliance or caveats do not discharge a restriction.
questions.common_trap: Believing the burdened owner can end a covenant alone.

questions.stem: Hui Min owns a burdened lot and wants to build a two-storey extension prohibited by an old restriction. The dominant owner will not release it. On which ground may the High Court vary or discharge the restriction?
options: The change would not materially injure the person who has the benefit of it
The burdened owner has found a cheaper design for the extension than the original plan
The dominant owner is abroad and cannot easily be asked for consent to a release
The restriction was agreed more than five years ago and has not been enforced since
questions.explanation: The court may discharge or vary a restriction where it would impede development approved under planning law or where no material injury is caused to the beneficiary. Cost or absence is not a ground.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that the burdened owner's convenience can justify discharge.

questions.stem: Mr Wong's State title contains a covenant limiting the use of his plot, and he wants it lifted. To whom does he apply, and what may he have to pay?
options: The Urban Redevelopment Authority, which will charge a stamp duty on the lifting
The Housing and Development Board, which will charge a resale levy
The Registrar of Titles, who will lift it for a small registration fee
The Singapore Land Authority, which may charge a Land Betterment Charge if the land's value rises
questions.explanation: Variations of State title covenants are handled by SLA, and for variations granted from 1 August 2022 a Land Betterment Charge may be payable on the increase in land value. URA planning approval is separate, and HDB resale levy and stamp duty are unrelated.
questions.common_trap: Confusing planning permission and covenant removal, which are separate approvals with separate payments.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the Torrens system under the Land Titles Act from the older Registration of Deeds system?
options: Only deeds are recorded, and registration is optional because ownership passes when the deed is signed
The register shows the owner and interests, and registration is needed for an estate or interest to pass
The State refuses to record interests in land unless they are held by Singapore citizens
Each buyer must trace the ownership of the land back to the original grant before buying
questions.explanation: Under the Torrens system, title is registered and registration is mandatory to transfer an estate or interest. The old deeds system just records documents, so a buyer must still investigate the chain of ownership.
questions.common_trap: Treating the two registration systems as the same thing with different names.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of registering a deed under the Registration of Deeds Act?
options: To make the State guarantee the owner's title against all earlier claims
To secure priority over later claimants, without any State guarantee of title
To replace the deed with a certificate of title issued by the Registrar
To make the transfer legally effective, which is otherwise impossible
questions.explanation: Registration of a deed gives priority over competing interests but the deed system does not guarantee title, and registration is not compulsory. Under the common law, interests pass on signing, sealing and delivery of the deed.
questions.common_trap: Assuming deed registration works like Torrens registration with a State guarantee.

questions.stem: Mr Chua signs a transfer of his registered house to Raj and hands over the keys, but the transfer is never lodged for registration. Who holds the legal title on the land register?
options: Raj, because the signed transfer and the keys give him legal ownership
Neither of them, because the land reverts to the State until registration
Raj, but only if he lodges a caveat within 14 days
Mr Chua, since the transfer takes effect only once it is registered
questions.explanation: Under the Land Titles Act an instrument does not pass the legal estate until it is registered. Raj holds at most an unregistered (equitable) interest.
questions.common_trap: Thinking ownership passes when the transfer is signed rather than when it is registered.

questions.stem: What is a certificate of title in Singapore?
options: A copy of the folio in the land register, issued by the Registrar of Titles
A planning approval from URA that confirms the permitted use of the land
A mortgage document issued by the bank holding the property as security
A tenancy summary prepared by the property agent for both parties
questions.explanation: The Registrar of Titles at SLA can issue a certificate of title, which is a copy of the entries in the folio of the land register. It is not a planning or lending document.
questions.common_trap: Mistaking the certificate of title for planning or finance paperwork.

questions.stem: What does a caution on a qualified title tell a buyer?
options: The land is mortgaged to the State until the caution is paid
The owner is a foreign person who needs ministerial approval
That interests existing when the folio was created may still bind the land
The land lease has less than 60 years left
questions.explanation: A caution on a qualified folio warns that earlier interests existing at conversion may still affect the land. The buyer must therefore check older documents.
questions.common_trap: Reading a caution as a debt, foreign ownership flag or lease length warning.

questions.stem: A qualified folio was created in 2015. In 2018 Hui Min bought the land for value and was registered as proprietor. When does the caution lapse for her estate under the five-year rule?
options: Five years after the date on which she was registered as proprietor
On the day her purchase was registered at the Land Registry office
Five years after the last deed cancelled when the folio was created
Ten years after the date on which she was registered as proprietor
questions.explanation: If a purchaser for value is registered after the qualified folio is created, the caution lapses five years from the date of the last deed cancelled on creating the folio, not from the purchase. The ten-year rule may still operate separately.
questions.common_trap: Counting the five years from the purchaser's registration instead of from the cancelled deed.

questions.stem: A qualified folio created in January 2014 has never been sold. What has happened to its caution by now?
options: It lapsed automatically after 10 years, with no application needed
It stays until the owner applies and pays a fee
It remains until the next sale is registered
It lapses only if every previous owner is traced
questions.explanation: Since the 2001 amendments, a caution lapses automatically 10 years after the folio is created (or by the later transitional date), even if there is no sale. The owner need not apply for this.
questions.common_trap: Believing that the owner must apply to have a caution cancelled once the time has passed.

questions.stem: After a qualified folio is created, a bank registers a mortgage over the land. Does this start the five-year period for the caution to lapse?
options: Yes, because the bank has paid value for its interest
Yes, because any registered dealing starts the period
No, because the five-year period only starts when the owner dies
No, as mortgagees and chargees are not treated as purchasers here
questions.explanation: The five-year rule requires a purchaser for valuable consideration registered as proprietor. The Land Titles Act says mortgagees and chargees are not purchasers for it.
questions.common_trap: Assuming any registered dealing counts as a purchase for the caution period.

questions.stem: After a bank registers a mortgage over Madam Kaur's condominium unit to secure a loan, whose name is shown as the owner of the unit on the folio?
options: The bank, which becomes the registered owner until the loan is repaid
Madam Kaur stays as the registered owner; the mortgage is notified
Both names, as joint proprietors
Neither, until the loan is repaid in full
questions.explanation: A registered mortgage is security and does not pass ownership to the lender. The borrower stays as proprietor, and the mortgage appears as a notified interest.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the bank becomes the owner while the loan is outstanding.

questions.stem: What does a CPF charge on a property secure?
options: The management fees owed to the managing agent of the building
The refund to the CPF Board of CPF used, with accrued interest
The price still owing to the developer on a new purchase
The stamp duty payable on the transfer
questions.explanation: CPF monies used for housing must be refunded with accrued interest when the property is sold, and the CPF charge protects that claim. Fees and stamp duty are not secured by it.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the CPF refund with debts owed to other parties.

questions.stem: What may a management corporation do on the title of a unit whose owner has long ignored written demands for contributions?
options: Lodge a caveat that cancels his ownership of the unit after a year
Cancel the strata title plan covering the whole building
Have the folio of his unit closed until he pays the arrears
Lodge a charge against his unit, enforceable like a mortgage
questions.explanation: A management corporation may secure unpaid contributions by registering a charge on the unit, which gives it rights like a mortgagee. It cannot cancel title or the strata plan.
questions.common_trap: Believing a management corporation can take away ownership for unpaid fees.

questions.stem: What is the main function of a caveat on a land register?
options: To warn of a claimed interest and block conflicting dealings
To transfer ownership of the land to whoever lodges it
To prove that the claimant's interest is legally valid
To cancel the registered owner's title to the land
questions.explanation: A caveat warns that someone claims an interest in the land and stops dealings that would defeat it. It does not prove or transfer anything.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that lodging a caveat gives the claimant the rights claimed.

questions.stem: Raj has signed a sale and purchase agreement for a freehold shophouse and paid the deposit. Completion is three months away. How can he protect his interest on the register?
options: By registering a charge in favour of the vendor
By asking the vendor to transfer the certificate of title to him
By lodging a caveat claiming his interest as purchaser
He cannot, since only completed transfers appear on the register
questions.explanation: A purchaser under a binding contract has an unregistered interest that can be protected by a caveat until the transfer is registered. A transfer is registered only on completion.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a buyer has no way to flag an interest before completion.

questions.stem: Mr Sim has bare permission (a licence that would not bind later owners) from Mr Ho to store goods in a warehouse, but has no estate in it. Can Mr Sim lodge a caveat against the warehouse title?
options: Yes, because any permitted occupier may lodge a caveat
Yes, but only after paying a fee to the Registrar
No, since a bare licence gives no interest in the land
No, because only banks can lodge a caveat
questions.explanation: A caveat needs a claim to an interest in the land. A bare licence gives none, although the Act treats a licence that binds the licensor's successors as an interest for caveat purposes.
questions.common_trap: Treating any right to be on land as caveatable.

questions.stem: What is the position under the Housing and Development Act if a licensed moneylender seeks a caveat over an HDB flat as security for a loan?
options: The agreement is void, so the moneylender cannot validly caveat the flat
The caveat is allowed as long as the loan is under S$50,000
The caveat is allowed if HDB gives approval after the loan is made
The caveat is allowed but lapses after one year
questions.explanation: The Housing and Development Act makes an agreement to use a protected HDB flat or its sale proceeds as security for a debt null and void. Such documents cannot create an interest in land or be registered.
questions.common_trap: Believing that a moneylender can take a charge on an HDB flat with a caveat.

questions.stem: Mdm Goh owes a supplier S$12,000 under an unsecured invoice. The supplier wants to lodge a caveat against her house to stop her selling. Can the supplier do so on that ground alone?
options: Yes, because any person owed money by the owner can lodge a caveat
Yes, but only if the debt is more than S$10,000
No, because a caveat can only be lodged by the registered owner
No, as an unsecured debt gives no interest in the land
questions.explanation: A caveat must rest on a claimed interest in the land. An ordinary creditor must first obtain a judgment and take enforcement steps before it has any claim affecting the land.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that being owed money is enough to caveat the debtor's property.

questions.stem: A caveat lodged on 12 August 2023 is neither extended nor withdrawn, and no dealing is lodged. When does it lapse by the passing of time?
options: On 12 August 2026, three years after lodgment
On 12 August 2028, five years after lodgment
On 12 February 2024, six months after lodgment
It never lapses unless the caveator withdraws it
questions.explanation: A caveat lapses five years from the date of lodgment unless extended. A shorter 30-day lapse only follows notice of a prohibited dealing.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a caveat remains on the register until it is actively withdrawn.

questions.stem: A caveator wants to keep a caveat in force beyond its first five years. What may the caveator do?
options: Apply to the Registrar for it to be renewed after it has lapsed
Lodge an extension before the caveat lapses
Ask the registered owner to sign a fresh transfer to the caveator
Do nothing, because caveats renew automatically every five years
questions.explanation: An extension must be lodged before lapse and continues the caveat for a further 5 years. After lapse, a new caveat is the only route and may need leave if it lapsed after notice.
questions.common_trap: Expecting caveats to renew by themselves.

questions.stem: Hui Min has a caveat on a house. The owner contracts to sell the house to Farhan, and the transfer is lodged without Hui Min's consent. What follows from the Registrar?
options: The transfer is registered at once, since the caveat has already served its purpose
The transfer is refused permanently, as a caveat bars all dealings while it exists
Farhan is given 14 days to have the caveat removed himself, failing which it is cancelled
She is notified, and the transfer registers after 30 days unless a court order stops it
questions.explanation: A caveat does not bar dealings forever. The Registrar warns the caveator and registers the dealing after 30 days unless a court extends the time or the dealing falls away.
questions.common_trap: Believing a caveat permanently blocks a transfer.

questions.stem: Mr Ang lodges a caveat on his neighbour's house without any real claim, intending only to cause trouble. The neighbour loses a sale as a result. What is Mr Ang's exposure?
options: He may be liable to pay compensation for the neighbour's pecuniary loss
He faces no consequence, because the Registrar accepted the caveat
He loses only the lodgment fee
He automatically becomes owner of the neighbour's house
questions.explanation: The Land Titles Act makes a person who lodges a caveat wrongfully, vexatiously or without reasonable cause liable for the loss caused. The Registrar does not test the claim's merit.
questions.common_trap: Believing that acceptance by the Registrar means the claim is valid.

questions.stem: When the Registrar accepts a caveat for lodgment, what does that acceptance show about the caveator's claim?
options: That the claimed interest has been checked and found valid
That the court has ordered the caveat to remain for 5 years
Nothing about its merits; the Registrar does not assess the claim
That the registered owner has agreed to the claim
questions.explanation: The Registrar accepts a caveat without deciding whether the claim is justified. Disputes over validity are for the courts.
questions.common_trap: Treating an entry on the register as proof of the claim.

questions.stem: Where is an express easement over registered land recorded?
options: Only on the folio of the dominant land that benefits from it
Only in the Caveat Index kept by the Registrar of Titles
On the servient folio and, unless waived, the dominant folio
Only in the mortgage records held by the lending bank
questions.explanation: An easement is entered on the burdened (servient) land's folio and also notified on the benefited (dominant) land's folio unless the dominant owner waives it. A caveat index entry is a different thing.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an easement is recorded on only one folio.

questions.stem: A lease of registered land becomes registrable once its term is longer than what?
options: More than 7 years
More than 1 year
More than 3 years
More than 12 years
questions.explanation: A lease of registered land with a term exceeding 7 years is registered as a lease. Tenancies of 7 years or less are governed by the general law.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the 7-year registration threshold with other time limits in tenancy law.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur lives in a landed house under a 3-year tenancy, which is not shown on the title. Mr Ho later buys and registers the house. Is Madam Kaur's tenancy still binding on Mr Ho?
options: No, because anything not shown on the folio can never bind a buyer
No, because a tenancy ends automatically when ownership changes hands
Yes, but only if she had lodged a caveat before the sale happened
Yes, since a tenancy of 7 years or less is an exception to indefeasibility
questions.explanation: A purchaser takes subject to the rights of a person in occupation under a tenancy of 7 years or less, even if unregistered. This is one of the statutory exceptions to indefeasibility.
questions.common_trap: Assuming every unregistered interest is wiped out by a registered purchase.

questions.stem: Can a court enforcement order against a proprietor's land be shown on the folio of that land?
options: It cannot be shown on the folio because only private dealings are recorded
The order can be entered on the folio as it may affect the interest
It automatically transfers the house to the court
It only affects the house if the owner is a company
questions.explanation: An enforcement order, or a court order empowering someone other than the owner to sell registered land, does not affect the land until its particulars are entered in the land register. It does not transfer ownership to the court.
questions.common_trap: Believing the register records only voluntary transactions.

questions.stem: In the land register, who is the owner of an apartment in a strata development called?
options: A managing proprietor
A subsidiary proprietor
A registered chargee
A freehold trustee
questions.explanation: The owner of a strata lot is a subsidiary proprietor, who also has a share in the common property. The registered chargee is a lender, not an owner.
questions.common_trap: Using terms for lenders or managers instead of the term for the lot owner.

questions.stem: Two friends buy a house as tenants in common. What does the title show about the manner of holding?
options: That they hold as joint tenants and that either may sell the whole house
That they hold as mortgagors and the bank owns half
Nothing, since the manner of holding is not shown
That they hold as tenants in common and what each person's share is
questions.explanation: The register shows whether co-owners hold as joint tenants or tenants in common, and for tenants in common their respective shares. Joint tenants do not have separate shares.
questions.common_trap: Believing the register never records how co-owners hold.

questions.stem: A condominium unit's title states a leasehold estate of 99 years from 1 March 1995. About how long is left on the lease in October 2026?
options: About 67 years
About 72 years
About 88 years
About 99 years
questions.explanation: The lease ends on 1 March 2094. From October 2026 that is about 67 and a half years remaining.
questions.common_trap: Forgetting that the 99 years are counted from the lease start date, not from today.

questions.stem: For a landed house, what does the area shown on the title refer to?
options: The built-up area of the house only
The gross floor area allowed by URA
The land area, not the built-up area of the house
The land area together with the area of nearby roads
questions.explanation: The title records the area of the land lot (usually in square metres). It does not show floor area of the building.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up land area with built area.

questions.stem: A title shows a strata title plan number and a share value for the unit. What kind of property does this suggest?
options: A detached bungalow on its own plot of freehold land
A vacant State land lot being let on a short-term basis
A unit in a strata development such as a condominium
A detached factory standing on a lot of industrial land
questions.explanation: A strata title plan number and share value point to a strata lot, which is part of a subdivided building. A bungalow is on an ordinary land lot.
questions.common_trap: Not recognising strata features as a sign of a subdivided building.

questions.stem: Mr Gan secretly agreed with a neighbour years ago to let the neighbour build a garage on a strip of his land, but nothing was registered or caveated. Farhan then buys from Mr Gan, without fraud, and registers as proprietor. What is the position?
options: Farhan takes free of the unregistered claim, subject to statutory exceptions
Farhan is bound because he ought to have known about the garage
Farhan is bound because all private agreements run with the land
Farhan must pay compensation to Mr Gan for the garage
questions.explanation: A registered proprietor holds the land free of unregistered interests, other than the exceptions stated in the Act, and knowing about an unprotected interest is not fraud. The neighbour should have lodged a caveat.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that unregistered agreements always bind a later owner.

questions.stem: Which of the following can defeat a registered proprietor's title despite indefeasibility?
options: A change in the Master Plan zoning that applies to the land
A neighbour who has a verbal agreement about access to the lot
A fall in the market price of the property after registration
Fraud or forgery involving the proprietor or the proprietor's agent
questions.explanation: The Land Titles Act preserves the right to defeat a title obtained through fraud or forgery involving the proprietor. Zoning and price changes do not affect title.
questions.common_trap: Believing that registration makes title unchallengeable even where fraud occurred.

questions.stem: Mr Tan signs Mortgage A to Bank X on 1 March, and it is registered on 10 March. He signs Mortgage B to Bank Y on 5 March, and it is registered on 6 March. Which bank ranks first?
options: Bank X, because its mortgage was signed first
Bank Y, because priority follows registration, not signing date
Bank X, because it is the larger lender
Neither, because both rank equally
questions.explanation: Interests on the register rank by when they were registered, not by the dates of the instruments. Bank Y registered first.
questions.common_trap: Ranking mortgages by signing date instead of registration date.

questions.stem: A property sells for S$1,200,000. The first-registered mortgage has S$650,000 outstanding and the second-registered mortgage has S$400,000 outstanding. Ignoring costs, how much is left for the owner?
