questions.explanation: The first mortgagee is paid S$650,000, leaving S$550,000. The second takes S$400,000, so the owner gets S$150,000.
questions.common_trap: Only deducting one mortgage when two are registered.

questions.stem: Two people, neither with a registered interest, each claim to have bought the same unregistered interest in a lot. One has lodged a caveat; the other has not. Which statement is correct?
options: The earlier agreement always wins, regardless of any caveat
Both rank equally until a transfer is registered
The claim with the larger deposit wins
The caveated claim ranks ahead of the unprotected claim
questions.explanation: Under the Land Titles Act, a caveat protecting an unregistered interest gives it priority over unprotected unregistered interests that existed when it was entered. So a caveat can change the ranking.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the order of the original agreements always decides priority.

questions.stem: A property portal shows a condo unit with the line "Asking price S$1.28 million". In contract law, this listing is best described as:
options: a firm offer that any buyer can accept simply by replying that they agree
a unilateral offer that binds the seller to sell for the period of the listing
a counter-offer made in response to earlier enquiries from buyers
an invitation to treat, which invites interested buyers to make offers
questions.explanation: An advertised price is an invitation to treat. The buyer's response is the offer, and the seller is free to accept it or not.
questions.common_trap: Students treat any stated price as an offer that can be accepted to create a contract.

questions.stem: A landlord posts "Room for rent, S$850 per month" on a rental platform. Hui Min messages "I accept, please reserve it for me." The landlord replies that the room has gone to someone else. Has a tenancy contract been formed?
options: No, because the post was an invitation to treat and the message was an offer
Yes, because Hui Min accepted the advertised rent before anyone else could
Yes, but it is only a periodic tenancy, since no fixed term was stated in the post
No, because a tenancy cannot be created without a written agreement signed first
questions.explanation: The post invited offers; Hui Min's message was an offer that the landlord was free to decline, so nothing was formed. A written agreement is good practice but is not the reason here.
questions.common_trap: Believing that an advertisement can be accepted like an offer.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a legal offer?
options: Any statement of the price at which a person might be willing to consider selling a unit
A proposal that becomes binding only after the offeror later confirms it a second time
A clear statement of readiness to be bound on stated terms once the other party accepts
A request for information about the terms on which the other party might be willing to deal
questions.explanation: An offer shows a clear intention to be bound on acceptance. Statements of price, enquiries and general invitations do not meet that test.
questions.common_trap: Confusing an offer with a mere statement of price or an enquiry.

questions.stem: Mr Tan offers in writing to sell his shop unit for S$2.4 million. Raj replies, "I accept, but at S$2.3 million." What is the legal effect of Raj's reply?
options: It is an acceptance with a minor variation, so a contract is formed at S$2.4 million
It is a counter-offer that ends Mr Tan's original offer
It is an acceptance, so a contract is formed at S$2.3 million
It is an invitation to treat that leaves Mr Tan's original offer open
questions.explanation: Acceptance must match the offer without change. A changed price is a counter-offer, which rejects and ends the original offer.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the word "accept" in a reply makes it an acceptance even when terms are changed.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur offers her unit to Farhan for S$1.9 million. Farhan counters at S$1.8 million, and she refuses. The next day Farhan says, "Fine, I accept your S$1.9 million." Madam Kaur says no. Is there a contract?
options: Yes, because her original offer was still open and he accepted it within time
Yes, because Farhan changed his mind before Madam Kaur withdrew her offer
No, because an acceptance that is given on the following day is always too late
No, because the counter-offer ended her offer, leaving nothing for him to accept
questions.explanation: A counter-offer rejects the original offer, and a rejected offer cannot be revived by later acceptance. Farhan's new statement is a fresh offer that she may decline.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the first offer stays open in the background during negotiations.

questions.stem: Mr Lim offers his flat at S$1.1 million. Sunita, a prospective buyer, writes back, "Would you be open to S$1.05 million?" Mr Lim does not respond. Two days later Sunita writes, "I'll take it at S$1.1 million." What is the position?
options: No contract is formed, because her question was a counter-offer that rejected the offer
A contract is formed, because her question was only an enquiry and did not end the offer
No contract is formed, because Mr Lim never replied to the question she asked
A contract is formed only if Mr Lim confirms the acceptance in writing
questions.explanation: Asking whether a seller would take a lower price is an enquiry, not a rejection, so the original offer remains open. Her later unqualified acceptance forms the contract.
questions.common_trap: Treating any negotiating question as a counter-offer.

questions.stem: A seller sends a buyer an offer and adds, "If I do not hear from you by Friday, I will take it that you accept." The buyer says nothing. What is the legal result?
options: No contract arises, because silence cannot be imposed as a way of accepting
A contract arises on Friday, because the buyer had notice of the deadline
A contract arises, because the seller set the terms of acceptance as the offeror
No contract arises only if the buyer actually tells the seller he rejects it
questions.explanation: An offeror cannot make the offeree's silence amount to acceptance. The buyer has no duty to reply.
questions.common_trap: Believing the offeror can decide that silence counts as acceptance.

questions.stem: Jia Wei posts a signed acceptance of Mr Tan's written offer to sell on Monday. On Tuesday Mr Tan posts a letter withdrawing the offer. Jia Wei's letter reaches him on Wednesday and his withdrawal reaches her on Thursday. When was the contract formed?
options: On Wednesday, because acceptance takes effect only when the offeror receives it
On Thursday, because the later communication overrides the earlier one
On Monday, because under the postal rule acceptance takes effect when it is posted
Never, because Mr Tan's withdrawal was posted before his acceptance arrived
questions.explanation: Where post is a proper way to reply, acceptance is complete on posting. A posted withdrawal only takes effect on receipt, which was too late.
questions.common_trap: Applying the receipt rule to a posted acceptance, or the posting rule to a withdrawal.

questions.stem: Mei Ling accepts an offer by phone. The call is clear and instantaneous. At what point is her acceptance effective?
options: When the offeror hears it, as the postal rule does not cover instant communication
When she finishes speaking, in the same way as with any acceptance sent through the post
When she later confirms the telephone call by sending a signed letter to the offeror
When the offeror repeats the terms back to her at the end of the same telephone call
questions.explanation: For instant means of communication, acceptance takes effect on receipt. The postal rule is limited to communications that are delayed, such as letters.
questions.common_trap: Treating every form of acceptance like a posted letter.

questions.stem: Mr Wong offers his flat to Ravi at S$1.5 million and leaves the offer open for a week. On day three, Ravi's agent tells Ravi, truthfully, that Mr Wong has just agreed to sell to another buyer. Ravi then tries to accept. Is there a contract?
options: Yes, because only Mr Wong himself is able to validly withdraw an offer he has made
Yes, because an offer that is left open for a stated period can never be revoked early
No, because Ravi learned from a reliable source that the offer was effectively withdrawn
No, because the sale to a second buyer automatically cancels every other open offer
questions.explanation: A withdrawal need not be communicated by the offeror; reliable news from another source is enough. A promise to keep an offer open is not binding unless it is supported by consideration.
questions.common_trap: Believing a withdrawal counts only if the offeror personally tells the offeree.

questions.stem: Buyer Farhan pays an option fee of S$12,000 for a 14-day option to buy a flat at S$1.2 million. On day five, the seller gets a higher offer and says he is withdrawing the option. What is the legal position?
options: The seller may withdraw so long as he refunds the S$12,000 option fee to Farhan
The seller cannot withdraw during the option period, because the fee made the offer irrevocable
The seller may withdraw at any time up to the moment that Farhan signs the sale agreement
The seller may withdraw because an offer to sell land is always open to revocation
questions.explanation: The option fee is consideration for keeping the offer open, so the seller is bound during the option period. A bare promise to keep an offer open would be revocable.
questions.common_trap: Treating an option like an ordinary offer that the seller can retract.

questions.stem: In a typical option to purchase, which statement correctly describes the buyer's position during the option period?
options: An existing duty to buy, with the option fee being a first instalment towards the price
A duty to buy that arises once the seller signs the document within the option period
A right to walk away at any time and ask for the option fee to be returned in full
A right to buy that the buyer need not use, with the fee lost if the right lapses
questions.explanation: An option is a one-sided arrangement: the seller is bound while the buyer decides. If the buyer lets it lapse, the option fee is forfeited because it paid for that right.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the option fee is a refundable booking amount.

questions.stem: For a private property sold under an option to purchase, when does a binding contract of sale normally come into existence?
options: When the seller signs the option document and then hands it over to the buyer
When the buyer pays the option fee, even if the option is never exercised afterwards
When the buyer validly exercises the option in time and in the way the option requires
When the buyer completes the purchase and the title is transferred to the buyer
questions.explanation: The grant of the option is the seller's standing offer; exercising it in time and in the stipulated manner is the acceptance that forms the sale contract.
questions.common_trap: Placing contract formation at completion or at payment of the option fee.

questions.stem: Under a typical resale option for private property, the buyer pays 1% as option fee and 4% on exercising. The agreed price is S$1.6 million. How much does the buyer pay in total if the option is exercised, and how much of that is paid on exercise?
options: Total S$80,000; S$80,000 on exercise
Total S$64,000; S$48,000 on exercise
Total S$96,000; S$80,000 on exercise
Total S$80,000; S$64,000 on exercise
questions.explanation: 1% of S$1.6 million is S$16,000 and 4% is S$64,000, adding to 5% or S$80,000. The option fee was already paid earlier. These percentages are market practice and can be negotiated.
questions.common_trap: Forgetting that the option fee is part of the total, not an extra amount.

questions.stem: In property contract law, the "3Ps" that must be settled for there to be a valid offer and acceptance are:
options: Parties, Property and Price
Promise, Payment and Possession
Purchaser, Possession and Period
Parties, Purpose and Performance
questions.explanation: The 3Ps are the essential terms of a property deal: who the parties are, which property it is, and the price. Singapore courts also look for any other essential provisions, and if a core term is missing or uncertain there may be no binding contract.
questions.common_trap: Guessing another set of P words that sounds plausible.

questions.stem: Mr Chew and Hui Min sign a note: "Mr Chew will sell his Tampines flat to Hui Min. Price to be agreed later." Mr Chew later refuses to proceed. Can Hui Min enforce the note?
options: Yes, because the parties and the property are both clearly identified in the note
No, because the price was left open, so an essential term is still uncertain
Yes, because the court will simply insert whatever price Hui Min later proposes
No, because every contract for the sale of land must be made in the form of a deed
questions.explanation: A contract needs the parties, the property and the price to be certain or fixable. Where the price is simply left for future agreement, there is no binding bargain.
questions.common_trap: Assuming two out of three essential terms is enough.

questions.stem: A prospective tenant signs a letter of intent saying he "intends to lease the shop unit for two years at S$6,000 a month, subject to a formal tenancy agreement being signed". The landlord then rents to someone else. What is the likely position?
options: The letter is a binding tenancy already, because parties, property and rent are all stated
The landlord must pay damages, since the letter works as a binding option on the unit
The landlord is bound for 14 days, as every letter of intent works as an option period
The letter is not binding, as it says a formal tenancy agreement is still to be signed
questions.explanation: A document that expresses intention and is expressly subject to a formal agreement shows that the parties do not yet intend to be bound. The 3Ps being present does not alter that.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the 3Ps alone make a letter of intent binding.

questions.stem: Over dinner, Mrs Goh says to her son Jun Hao, "When I retire, the Bedok flat is yours." Years later she sells the flat to someone else. Can Jun Hao sue for breach of contract?
options: Yes, because both the property and the people concerned were clearly identified
Yes, because a promise to give land to a family member is enforceable on its own
Probably not, because family promises are presumed not to carry legal intention
No, because a gift of land is valid only where money is paid in return for it
questions.explanation: In family and social settings the courts presume no intention to be legally bound, and the dinner remark lacks the marks of a binding deal. Certain terms alone are not enough.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking the presumption against legal intent in domestic arrangements.

questions.stem: Which statement about intention to create legal relations is correct?
options: Business deals carry that intention only when they have been put into written form
Business deals are presumed to carry that intention, though it can be rebutted
That intention is always presumed to exist, whatever the setting of the agreement
That intention is not needed at all once the contract has some consideration
questions.explanation: Business deals are presumed to be intended as binding unless the parties clearly say otherwise. Intention is a separate requirement from consideration.
questions.common_trap: Treating intention as the same thing as consideration.

questions.stem: Which statement about consideration is correct?
options: It must have some value in law, but the court does not weigh whether it is a fair price
It must always be equal in value to the promise it supports
It must always be money paid before the contract is made
It must be shown in a written document signed by both parties
questions.explanation: Consideration must be sufficient, meaning real value in the eyes of the law, but need not be adequate. A bad bargain is still a bargain.
questions.common_trap: Confusing sufficiency of consideration with adequacy.

questions.stem: After a flat sale completes, the seller says to the salesperson Sunita, "You worked so hard, I will pay you S$3,000 extra." The seller later refuses to pay. Can Sunita enforce the promise?
options: Yes, because the seller made the promise freely and also put it in writing afterwards
Yes, because work done at the seller's request always supports a later promise to pay
No, because a salesperson may never receive more than the agreed commission amount
No, because her work was already done, so the promise rests on past consideration
questions.explanation: Consideration must be given in exchange for the promise, not before and independently of it. The completed work cannot support a new promise made afterwards.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that a promise of thanks for work already done is enforceable.

questions.stem: Mr Ong signs a properly executed deed promising to give his nephew S$40,000 towards a flat. The nephew gives nothing in return. Mr Ong later changes his mind. What is the position?
options: The promise is unenforceable, because the nephew gave no consideration
The promise is enforceable, because a deed does not need consideration
The promise is enforceable only if the nephew has paid a nominal sum
The promise is unenforceable until it is registered with the Land Registry
questions.explanation: A promise made by deed is binding without consideration because the formality itself supplies the support. Registration is unrelated to enforceability here.
questions.common_trap: Assuming every enforceable promise needs consideration.

questions.stem: Nur Aisyah is 19 and signs an option to buy a condo unit. Unlike a contract for necessaries, such a purchase generally:
options: binds her fully, because a person of 19 is old enough to open a bank account
binds her fully, as long as her parents did not object when she signed it
cannot be enforced against her, as a purchase of this kind is not for necessaries
is void from the very start, so that even she cannot choose to carry it on
questions.explanation: Since 1 March 2009 a person aged 18 or above generally has full contractual capacity, but contracts to buy or sell land are carved out of that rule, so a 19-year-old is still treated as a minor here. A minor's contract that is not for necessaries is generally not enforceable against the minor, although the minor can usually choose to carry on with it.
questions.common_trap: Applying the general age-18 rule to a land purchase, which is excluded from it.

questions.stem: Which purchase by a 16-year-old school student is most likely to be treated as a contract for necessaries?
options: Basic clothing and food she genuinely needs, bought at a reasonable price
A designer handbag bought on instalment as a treat for her birthday celebration
A second-hand sports car bought through a dealer's financing plan for the year
A condominium unit bought through an option as an investment for the future
questions.explanation: Under the Sale of Goods Act, necessaries are goods suitable to the minor's condition in life and actual requirements at the time of sale and delivery, and a minor must pay a reasonable price for them. A handbag treat, a car or a condo does not meet that test.
questions.common_trap: Treating anything the minor wants as a necessary.

questions.stem: Mr Ng, who has advanced dementia, signs an option to sell his flat well below market value. The buyer's agent knew about his condition. Which is the best description of the contract?
options: It is fully valid, because Mr Ng signed the document with his own hand in the end
It is voidable at Mr Ng's option, as the other side knew he lacked capacity
It is void, so that no one can ever choose to affirm or enforce it later
It is valid, but only the price term can be challenged on his behalf later
questions.explanation: A contract made with someone who lacks mental capacity can be set aside by that person where the other party knew of the incapacity. It remains valid until avoided.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a signature always makes a contract binding.

questions.stem: ABC Pte Ltd wishes to sign a tenancy agreement for its new office. Who can properly sign for it?
options: A director, or another person authorised by the board or the constitution
Any employee who happens to work at the office that the company is renting
The shareholders of the company, each of them signing in his own personal name
Only the external auditor, who must witness every contract the company makes
questions.explanation: A company is an artificial person that can act only through authorised individuals, such as its directors or persons they authorise. Staff or shareholders as such have no automatic authority.
questions.common_trap: Thinking shareholders or ordinary staff can sign for a company.

questions.stem: To save stamp duty, a buyer and seller write a lower price on the sale document and agree to settle the difference in cash. The seller later refuses to hand over the flat, so the buyer wants to sue on the document. How will the court likely treat the matter?
options: As a fully valid contract, because both parties signed it knowing what it said
As a valid contract, once the buyer pays the stamp duty that was left out
As a voidable contract, which only the seller would be entitled to set aside
As a contract tainted by illegality, which the court will not help to enforce
questions.explanation: A contract made to defeat tax or duty has an unlawful purpose. The court generally will not lend its aid to enforce it.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that a contract signed by both sides is enforceable whatever its purpose.

questions.stem: Mr Chua is not a registered salesperson but still brings a buyer to a seller and, after the sale, sues the seller for the agreed commission. What is the likely result?
options: He can recover, because the seller received the benefit of the work that he did
He can recover, if the seller told him orally that he was free to go ahead
He cannot recover, because the work was an offence and the commission is not recoverable
He can recover half, since the seller received only part of what was promised
questions.explanation: The Estate Agents Act bars recovery of fees for estate agency work done in breach of the licensing and registration rules. The contract is tainted by that illegality.
questions.common_trap: Believing the seller must pay for work from which he benefited.

questions.stem: A contract that is voidable is best described as one that:
options: has no legal effect from the start, whatever the parties want
is valid but cannot be sued on for want of written evidence
is valid until the innocent party chooses to set it aside
is valid until a court rules on whether it should continue
questions.explanation: A voidable contract binds both sides unless and until the party entitled to do so rescinds it. Typical causes are misrepresentation, duress and undue influence.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up voidable with void.

questions.stem: Which of these contracts is void rather than voidable?
options: A contract signed after the seller was misled about the flat's size
A contract signed because of a threat made against the buyer
A contract signed because of improper pressure from a trusted adviser
An agreement to commit a crime in return for payment
questions.explanation: A void contract has no legal effect from the beginning, as with agreements with an unlawful object. Contracts affected by misrepresentation, duress or undue influence are valid until set aside.
questions.common_trap: Treating every defective contract as void.

questions.stem: Mr Koh orally agrees to sell his shophouse to Sunita for S$3 million. Nothing is signed and no money has changed hands. When Mr Koh backs out, Sunita sues. Under the Civil Law Act, what is the position?
options: She succeeds, because oral contracts for land are enforceable just like written ones
She cannot succeed, as there is no signed written evidence of a land contract
She succeeds, because writing is needed only for land contracts priced above S$1 million
She cannot succeed, because an oral land contract is void from the very start
questions.explanation: A contract for the sale of immovable property cannot be sued on unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be sued or his authorised agent. The contract itself is not void, but it is unenforceable in court.
questions.common_trap: Saying the unwritten contract is void rather than unenforceable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an implied term of a contract?
options: A term the law or business sense reads in although the parties never wrote it
A term that the parties clearly stated in the signed written agreement
A term that one party told the other, which the other then put in writing
A term that the parties chose to add after the contract was already finished
questions.explanation: Implied terms arise by statute, custom or the need to make the contract work as intended. Express terms are those the parties actually state.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an implied term is one that the parties agreed to orally.

questions.stem: What is the main difference in remedy between breach of a condition and breach of a warranty?
options: A condition's breach gives damages only, while a warranty's breach lets the innocent party end the contract and claim damages
A condition's breach lets the innocent party end the contract and claim damages, while a warranty's breach gives damages only
A breach of either kind lets the innocent party end the contract, though only a warranty also carries a damages claim
A breach of either kind gives damages only, with the difference being the amount that can be recovered in the end
questions.explanation: A condition goes to the root of the contract, so its breach justifies termination. A warranty is a minor term, so its breach gives damages but the contract continues.
questions.common_trap: Reversing the effect of conditions and warranties.

questions.stem: A term is neither clearly a condition nor a warranty. The innocent party's right to terminate for its breach will depend on:
options: whether the term appeared early in the contract rather than towards the end
whether the party who broke the term acted deliberately or by simple mistake
how serious the effect of the breach is on what the innocent party expected
whether the term is written in short wording or stretched over several lines
questions.explanation: For an innominate term, the court looks at how much of the benefit of the contract the breach removed. A serious loss of benefit permits termination; a minor one gives only damages.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the label or the wrongdoer's motive decides the remedy.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur signs a tenancy agreement without reading it. One clause says the landlord is not liable for loss of the tenant's belongings from the flat. Later her items are stolen. How will the court treat the clause?
options: As ineffective, because she did not read the clause before she signed it
As ineffective, because a landlord is never allowed to exclude any liability
As effective only if it was also explained to her orally before she signed
As part of the contract because she signed it, subject to any statutory limits
questions.explanation: A person who signs a contract is generally bound by its terms even without reading them. The law, including the Unfair Contract Terms Act where it applies, can still limit some exclusion clauses.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that not reading a document avoids a term in it.

questions.stem: How does an indemnity clause differ from an exemption clause?
options: An indemnity clause makes one party compensate for stated losses, while an exemption clause limits the party's own liability
An indemnity clause limits or excludes the party's own liability, while an exemption clause makes one party compensate for stated losses
An indemnity clause binds both parties to the same extent, while an exemption clause binds only the party who signed it
An indemnity clause is found only in contracts for land, while an exemption clause may appear in every other contract
questions.explanation: An exemption clause cuts back the liability the party would otherwise have. An indemnity clause shifts the risk of a specified loss onto the party who gave it.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the two roles in loss allocation.

questions.stem: Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act, what is the position if a business tries to exclude, by contract term or notice, its liability for death or personal injury caused by its own negligence?
options: It can do so, if the customer has signed a form that agrees to the exclusion
It cannot do so at all, whatever the contract or notice may say
It can do so, so long as the exclusion can be shown to be reasonable
It can do so, if a clear notice to that effect is displayed at the premises
questions.explanation: The Act prevents any exclusion of liability for death or personal injury from negligence. Reasonableness is the test only for other kinds of loss.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a signature or notice can remove liability for personal injury.

questions.stem: A property firm's standard terms say it is not liable for any financial loss caused by its negligent advice. A client suffers S$20,000 in losses from careless advice. Who must show that the clause is reasonable?
options: The firm, because it is the party relying on the clause
The client, because she is the party who wants to avoid the clause
Neither side, because the court decides without evidence from either party
The Council for Estate Agencies, because it regulates estate agents
questions.explanation: For other loss from negligence, such a clause counts only so far as it is reasonable, and the burden of proving reasonableness is on the party relying on it.
questions.common_trap: Placing the burden on the person challenging the clause.

questions.stem: A salesperson tells a buyer, "This is the most beautiful unit in the whole condo." The buyer later feels it is average. Is this likely to be an actionable misrepresentation?
options: Yes, because any inaccurate statement made before the contract is actionable at law
Yes, because the buyer relied on the salesperson's words in deciding to buy it
No, because it is an opinion or sales puff, not a statement of fact
No, because only a statement that is made in writing can be a misrepresentation
questions.explanation: A misrepresentation must be a false statement of fact. Vague praise or opinion is not capable of being proved true or false in that way.
questions.common_trap: Treating exaggerated sales talk as a statement of fact.

questions.stem: A fraudulent misrepresentation is one made:
options: only when the maker intends to cause the other party a financial loss by it
carelessly, without taking reasonable steps to check the facts before stating them
innocently, while genuinely and honestly believing that the statement was true
knowing it is false, without belief in its truth, or recklessly careless as to whether it is true
questions.explanation: Fraud requires dishonesty: knowledge of falsity, no belief in the statement, or reckless indifference. Mere carelessness is negligence, and honest error is innocent misrepresentation.
questions.common_trap: Confusing carelessness with fraud.

questions.stem: Under the Misrepresentation Act, a person who made a non-fraudulent false statement that induced a contract can avoid liability in damages by proving that:
options: they did not gain anything for themselves out of the contract that was made
they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, that the facts were true
the other party could have checked the facts independently before contracting
the statement was made by word of mouth and was not recorded in any document
questions.explanation: The Act presumes the maker is liable as if fraud had been committed unless he proves reasonable grounds for his honest belief. The burden is on him.
questions.common_trap: Believing the buyer must prove the maker was careless.

questions.stem: A court finds that a buyer is entitled to rescind for an innocent misrepresentation, but the defect is small and rescission would be harsh. What may the court do under the Misrepresentation Act?
options: Declare the contract subsisting and award damages in place of rescission
Order specific performance of the contract and add a sum as punitive damages
Treat the contract as void and order the full price to be paid back with interest
Rewrite the price down to the figure that the court itself considers to be fair
questions.explanation: Where it is equitable, the court may keep the contract alive and award damages in place of rescission. It has no power to rewrite the price.
questions.common_trap: Thinking rescission is the only remedy for a misrepresentation.

questions.stem: Five months after buying a flat, Hui Min learns the seller lied about the unit's floor area. She keeps living there, pays the mortgage for another 10 months, and then tries to rescind. What is the likely outcome?
options: Rescission is still open, because no time limit at all applies to the right to rescind
Rescission is still open, because she continues to live in the unit that she bought
Rescission is probably lost, as she affirmed the contract after learning the truth
Rescission is lost only if the seller finds out that she knew about the false statement
questions.explanation: A buyer who knows of the misrepresentation and carries on as before may be treated as having affirmed. Delay also counts against rescission.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the right to rescind never runs out.

questions.stem: Mr Ibrahim knows of old damp patches on a ceiling and is not asked about them. What is the usual position on his duty to tell a buyer who inspects the flat?
options: He must always disclose every physical defect of the flat that he happens to know of
He has no duties of any kind, so he may even paint over a patch in order to hide it
He need only disclose the defect if the buyer pays him an additional fee to do so
He has no duty to volunteer physical defects, but must not lie or actively hide them
questions.explanation: Under caveat emptor the buyer must inspect for physical condition. A seller who stays silent is not liable merely for that, but active concealment or false answers amount to misrepresentation.
questions.common_trap: Stating caveat emptor allows even active concealment of a defect.

questions.stem: In March, a seller truthfully tells a buyer that the unit has an unblocked view. In April, before the option is signed, the seller learns that a tower has been approved right in front. The seller says nothing and the buyer signs. What is the likely position?
options: The buyer may be able to set the contract aside, as a once-true statement became false and was not corrected
The buyer has no remedy, because the statement was perfectly true on the day it was made
The buyer has no remedy, because sellers are never required to update earlier statements
The buyer may claim only a refund of the option fee and nothing else from the seller
questions.explanation: A representation is treated as continuing until the contract is made. If the seller knows it has become false, silence can amount to a misrepresentation.
questions.common_trap: Judging the statement only at the time it was first made.

questions.stem: A seller of landed property knows the title is subject to a restrictive covenant that is not shown on the register and that the buyer cannot discover from a physical inspection. What is the seller's duty under the traditional rule?
options: Disclose nothing at all, because caveat emptor applies equally to defects in title
Disclose it only if the buyer's lawyer asks about it in writing before the sale
Disclose the defect in title, as latent defects in title must be revealed
Disclose it only if the covenant has been enforced against an owner in the past
questions.explanation: Caveat emptor mainly covers physical condition. A seller must disclose latent defects in title that the buyer could not discover by reasonable inspection.
questions.common_trap: Applying caveat emptor to defects in title.

questions.stem: Both buyer and seller agree on a sale of a unit, each believing it to be in good condition. Unknown to both, the unit was totally destroyed by fire the night before. What is the likely effect?
options: The contract is valid, since both parties shared the very same mistaken belief
The contract is voidable at the seller's option alone, and the buyer is bound
The contract is valid, though the buyer may claim a reduction in the price paid
The contract is void for common mistake, as the subject matter no longer existed
questions.explanation: If the subject matter has ceased to exist and both parties wrongly assume it exists, the contract is void for common mistake. Shared error does not preserve it.
questions.common_trap: Believing a mistake that both parties share cannot affect validity.

questions.stem: A listing shows a flat at S$318,000 rather than the intended S$1,318,000. A buyer who knows the market realises it is a typing error but still accepts at once. What is the likely result?
options: The buyer can enforce it, because the listing counted as a firm offer to the public
The seller can avoid it, as the buyer knew of the mistaken price
The seller can avoid it only after paying damages for his own typing error
The buyer can enforce it, because the seller alone is responsible for the listing
questions.explanation: A party who knows the other made a fundamental error about a term cannot hold him to it. The contract is not enforceable against the mistaken seller.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the party who made the error must always bear its consequences.

questions.stem: Mr Lee signs an option to sell his flat after a man tells him that he and his family will be harmed if he does not sign. Mr Lee later wishes to undo the deal. What is the position?
options: Void from the start, so that nobody is ever able to affirm it later on
Valid and binding, because he physically signed the document with his own hand
Voidable at Mr Lee's option, as duress made his consent ineffective
Enforceable, unless he repays the price within 14 days of having signed it
questions.explanation: Illegitimate pressure that overbears a person's will makes the contract voidable. He may choose to set it aside or to affirm it.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a contract signed under threat is automatically void.

questions.stem: What most clearly distinguishes undue influence from duress?
options: Undue influence relies on abuse of a relationship of trust, not on threats
Undue influence needs a threat of physical violence, whereas duress does not need one
Undue influence makes the contract void, whereas duress makes it merely voidable
Undue influence can be raised only by elderly persons against their own relatives
questions.explanation: In undue influence, one party takes unfair advantage of trust, so the victim's consent is not free. Duress is pressure by threat. Both make the contract voidable.
questions.common_trap: Thinking undue influence needs an express threat.

questions.stem: Before completion, a seller and buyer both still have obligations under their sale contract. They sign a short document releasing each other from all duties. Is the release effective?
options: No, because a contract can be ended only by performance or a court order
No, because the release needs a payment of money from one side to the other
Yes, but only if the release is registered with the Land Registry
Yes, because each side's release of the other's obligations is consideration for his own
questions.explanation: Where both sides still have unperformed duties, an agreement to release each other is supported by mutual promises. No money or registration is needed.
questions.common_trap: Believing a contract cannot be ended by mutual agreement.

questions.stem: After exercising an option to buy a unit, Raj's bank refuses to grant him the loan he expected. He tells the seller that the contract is frustrated. Is he right?
options: Yes, because he cannot perform and so is excused
No, because inability to fund the purchase does not frustrate the contract
Yes, because the bank's refusal was beyond his control
No, but he may claim back the option fee since he was not at fault
questions.explanation: Frustration applies to events that make performance impossible or radically different, not personal financial difficulty. Raj remains bound and risks forfeiting sums paid if he fails to complete.
questions.common_trap: Equating a financing failure with frustration.

questions.stem: A seller delivers the keys three days after the agreed completion date, causing the buyer only minor inconvenience, and time was not made essential. What can the buyer usually do?
options: Claim damages for the delay, but not end the contract over such a minor breach
End the contract at once, since every breach allows the innocent party to terminate
Keep the contract alive but make the seller refund the whole price that was paid
Do nothing at all, because late performance is never a breach of a contract
questions.explanation: Only a breach that goes to the root of the contract, such as breach of a condition or a serious breach of an innominate term, justifies termination. A minor breach gives damages.
questions.common_trap: Believing any breach allows the other party to end the contract.

questions.stem: Three weeks before completion, the seller writes that he will not sell the flat at the agreed price. The buyer is ready to complete. What may the buyer do?
options: Wait only, since no claim can be made before the date for completion
Sue only for the return of the deposit, since damages are not allowed
Treat the contract as ended and sue immediately, or wait until the completion date
Do nothing, since a refusal letter has no legal effect
questions.explanation: A clear refusal to perform before the due date is an anticipatory breach. The innocent party can accept it and claim now, or keep the contract alive.
questions.common_trap: Believing a claim can arise only on the day performance falls due.

questions.stem: A tenant leaves a unit six months into a 12-month lease without justification. The landlord accepts the breach and ends the lease, then claims damages for the remaining months, but makes no attempt to advertise the unit and leaves it empty. What can the landlord likely recover?
options: The full unpaid rent, because a tenant who breaks a lease is liable for all of it
Nothing at all, because a landlord is never allowed to claim for an empty period
Double the unpaid rent, since the tenant acted wrongfully by leaving early
Only the loss that could not reasonably have been avoided, given his duty to mitigate
questions.explanation: The innocent party must take reasonable steps to limit his loss and cannot recover loss that he could have avoided. Damages compensate loss; they do not punish.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the innocent party may sit back and claim everything.

questions.stem: A seller of a landed house refuses to complete although the buyer is ready and willing. Why might the court order specific performance instead of damages?
options: Because the court must always order performance of land contracts
Because each piece of land is unique, so money damages may not be adequate
Because the buyer pays an extra fee to ask for the order
Because damages for land contracts are barred by law
questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable and discretionary remedy. It is often available for land because no sum of money can replace the particular property.
questions.common_trap: Thinking specific performance is automatic.

questions.stem: A seller who has granted a valid option to Mei Ling is about to sell the same unit to another buyer during the option period. What kind of order might Mei Ling seek to stop him?
options: A writ of possession over the unit that is the subject of the option
A decree of rescission to cancel the option she holds from the seller
An injunction restraining the seller from selling to anyone else
An order for liquidated damages to be paid by the seller to her
questions.explanation: An injunction is a court order to refrain from doing something. It can protect a buyer's contractual right while the option remains valid.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up injunction with rescission or possession.

questions.stem: A buyer pays an option fee but lets the option lapse. The seller keeps the fee. Why is the forfeiture not a penalty?
options: Because every sum paid under a property contract is non-refundable
Because the court never examines clauses about fees in option documents
Because the buyer broke the contract by failing to exercise it
Because the fee was the agreed price for holding the offer open, not a sum payable for a breach
questions.explanation: Failing to exercise an option is not a breach, since the buyer had a choice. The fee was payment for the seller's commitment, and the seller has earned it.
questions.common_trap: Seeing the lapse of an option as a breach by the buyer.

questions.stem: A buyer who has paid a deposit of 5% of the price to the seller refuses to complete the purchase without any legal excuse. What can the seller usually do with the deposit?
options: Return it at once, since the contract was never completed by either side
Keep it as reasonable earnest money, as the buyer defaulted
Keep it only after proving that his actual loss equals the whole deposit
Hand it to the buyer's lawyer to hold until a court decides who is entitled
questions.explanation: A deposit that is reasonable as earnest money can be forfeited when the buyer defaults without excuse. A sum too large to be a true deposit cannot be forfeited at all.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a deposit must be refunded after default.

questions.stem: A one-year tenancy at S$2,500 a month says that if the tenant breaches any term, however small, he must pay S$100,000. Is the clause likely to be enforced as it stands?
options: No, as it is far out of proportion to likely loss and is a penalty
Yes, because the parties agreed the sum freely at the time of signing the tenancy
Yes, because a tenant must pay whatever sum the written contract demands of him
No, because a tenancy agreement is not allowed to contain any damages clause
questions.explanation: A genuine pre-estimate of loss is enforceable as liquidated damages, but a sum extravagantly out of proportion is a penalty and not enforced. The agreed sum is not conclusive.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the court always enforces the sum the parties wrote down.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an agency relationship?
options: One person agrees to give advice to another and charges a fee for giving that advice to the other person
One person, the agent, is authorised to act for another and can bind the other in dealings with third parties
One person agrees to buy goods from another and resells them to third parties in his own name
One person lets another occupy his property and receives rent from that occupier each month
questions.explanation: The core of agency is authority to bind the principal in dealings with others. Giving advice or buying and reselling in one's own name does not make a person an agent.
questions.common_trap: Equating any helper or adviser with an agent.

questions.stem: For two years, Mr Ong has let his friend Jia Wei collect rent from his tenants and sign receipts in his name. There is no written agreement. A tenant now disputes Jia Wei's authority to give a receipt. How was her agency most likely created?
options: It was never created, because every agency must be set out in a signed written document
By ratification, because Mr Ong must approve each separate receipt after it is signed
By implication, from Mr Ong's conduct in letting her act for him this way
By necessity, because the tenants had no one else to whom they could pay the rent
questions.explanation: Agency can arise from conduct that shows the principal is content for the person to act on his behalf. A writing is not needed for most agencies.
questions.common_trap: Believing that agency always needs a written appointment.

questions.stem: Without being told to, a salesperson signs a letter accepting a tenant's offer on a landlord's behalf. The landlord, once he learns of this and knowing all the terms, signs the tenancy agreement and takes the deposit. What is the legal effect?
options: The landlord is not bound at all, because the salesperson had no authority at the time
The landlord is bound only from the later date on which he signed the agreement
The salesperson alone is bound, and the landlord remains free to withdraw as he wishes
The landlord has ratified it, binding himself as if it had been authorised from the start
questions.explanation: Ratification, if made with full knowledge, adopts an unauthorised act and relates back to the date it was done. It makes the principal liable on the contract.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an unauthorised act can never become binding on the principal.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes agency of necessity?
options: An agent acts in a true emergency to protect the principal's property when instructions cannot be obtained
An agent acts without any instructions because he feels it would be of some help to the principal
An agent is appointed by the court after the principal has been declared bankrupt by it
An agent is bound to act because the written contract with the principal says that he must
questions.explanation: Necessity arises only in an emergency where communication with the principal is impossible and the agent acts in good faith in the principal's interest. It is narrow and rare.
questions.common_trap: Treating any helpful act as agency of necessity.

questions.stem: A property agent wants to act for a homeowner who wishes to sell a residential property. What does the Estate Agents regime require for the written agreement?
options: A verbal agreement, provided the owner is a repeat client of the agent concerned
A form prepared by the agency itself, provided that the commission is clearly stated
A deed signed in the presence of a lawyer in each and every case without exception
Use of the CEA prescribed form of estate agency agreement for that kind of deal
questions.explanation: For residential sales, purchases and leases, estate agents must use the prescribed forms, with parties adding extra terms only in the way the form allows.
questions.common_trap: Believing the agent can use its own format for the agency agreement.

questions.stem: Mr Tan signs an exclusive estate agency agreement for the sale of his flat. During the validity period he finds a buyer himself, without the agent's involvement, and signs a sale contract. Is commission payable to the agent?
options: No, because commission is due only where the agent personally introduced the buyer
Yes, because under an exclusive agreement, commission is due on a sale to anyone in the period
No, because an owner always keeps the right to sell directly under any form of agency
Yes, but only half of the agreed commission, whoever the buyer turns out to be
questions.explanation: Under the prescribed exclusive form, commission is payable on a sale contract made with any buyer during the validity period, whether or not the agent introduced that buyer. An owner who finds his own buyer still owes commission.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the owner's own sale never triggers commission.

questions.stem: Sunita holds a non-exclusive estate agency agreement for a seller's unit, and so does another agent, Raj. A buyer introduced by Raj signs the sale contract. Is Sunita entitled to commission?
options: No, as under a non-exclusive appointment only the agent who introduced the buyer is paid
Yes, as she was appointed first and the two agents split the commission equally
Yes, as the seller owes the full commission to every agent whom he has appointed
No, as a seller is not allowed to appoint more than one agent for a single unit
questions.explanation: A non-exclusive agent earns commission only where the buyer was introduced through that agent's efforts. The seller can appoint other agents and sell himself.
questions.common_trap: Thinking every non-exclusive agent is paid whenever the property sells.

questions.stem: What is the maximum initial validity of CEA's prescribed exclusive agreement for selling a home, and how can it be renewed?
options: Up to 6 calendar months, and renewed automatically unless the owner objects in time
Up to 12 calendar months, and renewed by an oral request made before the end date
Up to 3 calendar months, renewable on the same prescribed form for up to 3 months each time
Up to 3 calendar months, and extended once only for a further period of 3 months
questions.explanation: The prescribed exclusive form caps the validity period at 3 calendar months. It can be renewed or extended only on the same prescribed form, and each renewal term is also capped at 3 calendar months.
questions.common_trap: Thinking exclusive agreements can run for six months or renew automatically.

questions.stem: Under a CEA exclusive agreement to sell, the owner ticks "Yes" for the post-expiry commission clause. The agreement ends on 30 April. On 15 June the owner signs a sale contract with a buyer the agent introduced in March. Is commission payable?
options: No, as the agreement had already come to an end on the 30th of April
Yes, as the buyer was introduced during the period and the sale is within 3 months after it
No, as the sale contract was signed over a month after the agreement expired
Yes, but only if the agent first renews the agreement before the sale is signed
questions.explanation: The form lets the parties agree that commission still applies if the property is sold within 3 months after expiry to a buyer introduced during the validity period.
questions.common_trap: Assuming all commission rights end on the expiry date.

questions.stem: A client signs a CEA estate agency agreement through salesperson Hui Min. With whom does the client have the contract?
options: The estate agent, because the salesperson signs on the agent's behalf
Hui Min personally, because she was the person who dealt with the client directly
The CEA, because it is the body that issues the prescribed forms to the industry
Both Hui Min and the estate agent, who share all obligations in equal parts
questions.explanation: The estate agency agreement is made between the client and the estate agent. The salesperson is the agent's representative, who signs for it and fills in her details.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the client contracts with the salesperson personally.

questions.stem: Salesperson Raj, working for Agency A, takes a client to court for unpaid commission under the agreement. Under the Estate Agents Act, what is the likely position?
options: He can sue in his own name, since he did all of the work that was done for the client
He can sue in his own name, if the client wrote his name on the form
He can sue in his own name, but only for half of the agreed amount of commission
He cannot sue in his own name, as the right to recover sums lies with the estate agent
questions.explanation: The Act gives a right of action for agreed estate agency sums to the licensed estate agent, not to the individual salesperson who did the work.
questions.common_trap: Believing the salesperson can claim commission directly.

questions.stem: Under the Estate Agents Act, how many estate agents may a salesperson be registered with or act for at any one time?
options: Up to two, if both consent in writing
As many as the salesperson chooses
Only one
Up to three, if they are in different businesses
questions.explanation: A salesperson may not be registered to act for more than one estate agent at a time, and may not act for more than one in practice. The salesperson works within one estate agent.
questions.common_trap: Thinking salespersons can freely work for several agencies at once.

questions.stem: Salesperson Farhan is engaged by a seller to sell her flat. A buyer then asks Farhan to act for him in buying the same flat. Under CEA rules, what is the position?
options: Farhan can act for both sides, if the buyer and the seller each agree to it in writing
Farhan cannot act for both sides in one transaction, as dual representation is prohibited
Farhan can act for both sides, if he takes commission from only one of the two parties
Farhan can act for both sides, if the property involved is not an HDB flat
questions.explanation: Dual representation of buyer and seller, or landlord and tenant, in the same transaction is prohibited for all property types because it creates a clear conflict of loyalty. Consent does not cure it.
questions.common_trap: Believing consent of both parties allows an agent to act for both.

questions.stem: Salesperson Mei Ling is asked to sell Mr Wong's flat. She tells Mr Wong the market is weak, then arranges for her cousin to buy at a low price, and sells the unit on at a profit. She never discloses the link. What is the principal's main legal complaint?
options: She breached the duty of confidentiality only, since she did not reveal the price
She breached the duty to follow instructions only, as she did not keep to his price
She breached nothing at all, because Mr Wong did accept the price at the time
She breached her fiduciary duty by placing her own interest first and not disclosing it
questions.explanation: A fiduciary must avoid conflicts between duty and interest and disclose any interest. Mr Wong's acceptance of the price does not help where the material facts were hidden.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a conflict is acceptable if the principal signed off without knowing the facts.

questions.stem: Without telling his client, a salesperson accepts S$2,000 from a renovation company that he recommended to the client. What may the client do?
options: Do nothing further, because the client himself has not lost any money in the matter
Claim only the cost of the renovation work that the salesperson had recommended
Demand that the S$2,000 be handed over and treat the agent as in breach of duty
Treat it as a private matter, since the renovation work itself was done properly
questions.explanation: An agent may not make a secret profit from his position. The principal can recover it, and may have other remedies such as dismissal and loss of commission.
questions.common_trap: Believing a profit is acceptable if the principal suffers no loss.

questions.stem: A seller's agent receives two offers for a unit, S$1.45 million and S$1.40 million. The agent thinks neither is good enough and passes on neither. Has the agent acted properly?
options: No, because the agent must pass on all offers promptly for the seller to decide
Yes, because the agent may filter out offers which he considers to be too low
Yes, because the agent need only pass on the single highest offer that he receives
No, because the agent ought to have accepted the higher offer by himself
questions.explanation: Deciding whether to accept is the principal's right. The agent's duty is to forward every offer promptly and not filter them.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the agent can screen offers on the principal's behalf.

questions.stem: A seller tells his agent privately that he must sell fast because of money troubles. The agent mentions this to a buyer to "help close the deal". The buyer then offers a much lower price. Which duty did the agent breach?
options: The duty to keep the principal's confidences and act in his interest
The duty to share all information that he holds with the buyer as well
The duty to follow the reasonable instructions given by the buyer to him
The duty to act in the interests of both the buyer and seller equally
questions.explanation: Information entrusted by the principal must not be used or revealed against him. The agent acts for the seller, not for the buyer.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an agent must be neutral between buyer and seller.

questions.stem: What standard of care applies to a salesperson in doing estate agency work for a client?
options: The care that a person would take of his own property in his daily life
The care and skill that a competent salesperson would reasonably show in the work
The best care that could possibly be given, so any failure is a breach
Care only up to the extent that the commission paid to the agent justifies
questions.explanation: An agent who holds himself out as having expertise must show reasonable competence in that field. It is an objective standard, not perfection.
questions.common_trap: Applying an everyday lay standard or a perfection standard.

questions.stem: Salesperson Raj is engaged to negotiate a sale and is busy, so he asks a friend with no CEA registration to meet the buyers and discuss price on his behalf. The seller was not told. Why is this a problem?
options: An agent may hand any of his duties to a friend, provided he is himself present
An agent may delegate only to a person who will earn a lower commission than he does
An agent must do the duties himself and cannot delegate them without authority
An agent may delegate his duties, but he cannot delegate the right to commission
questions.explanation: Agency is personal: the principal chose this agent, who cannot hand over his core duties to another without consent. Unregistered persons also cannot carry out estate agency work.
questions.common_trap: Believing an agent can freely hand work to an assistant.

questions.stem: Agency is a relationship of utmost good faith. In practice this means the agent must:
options: tell the principal only those facts about which the principal specifically asks
tell the principal only those facts that happen to be favourable to the principal
pass on material facts to the buyer and the seller in exactly the same measure
act honestly in the principal's interest and disclose every material fact known to him
questions.explanation: A relationship of utmost good faith requires full and honest disclosure by the person in the trusted position, without waiting to be asked.
questions.common_trap: Treating good faith as only a duty to answer questions truthfully.

questions.stem: A seller engages an agent to market her unit and state an expected price, and the agreement says the expected price is for advertising only. The agent signs an option to sell at that price with a buyer. Does he have actual authority to do so?
options: No, because his role is to market and pass on offers, not to make or accept them
Yes, because he was the one who stated the expected price on the seller's behalf
Yes, because agents are always free to sign options on behalf of their sellers
No, though only because the price he agreed to was not high enough for her
questions.explanation: Actual authority comes from what the principal has agreed to. The CEA forms say the expected price is for listing only and gives no authority to accept offers.
questions.common_trap: Assuming appointment as agent includes power to commit the seller.

questions.stem: A seller tells buyers, "Raj handles everything for me, including signing papers." In private she tells Raj never to sign anything. Raj signs an option with buyers who knew nothing of the instruction. Is the seller bound?
options: No, because her private instruction limited the real powers that Raj possessed
Yes, because the seller held Raj out as authorised and the buyers relied on that
No, because only the seller herself is allowed to sign an option over her unit
Yes, but only if the buyers also paid an additional fee to the seller or agent
questions.explanation: Apparent authority arises from the principal's own representation. A secret limit on the agent's actual authority does not bind a third party who relied without notice.
questions.common_trap: Thinking secret instructions override what third parties were led to believe.

questions.stem: A buyer wishes to rely on an agent's apparent authority. Which fact is essential?
options: That the agent himself told the buyer that he had authority to sign the option
That the agent was a registered salesperson who had a clean disciplinary record
That the buyer first asked to see a document that proves the agent's authority
That the principal, not merely the agent, made the representation about authority
questions.explanation: Apparent authority needs a representation by the principal (by words or conduct), which the third party relies on. An agent cannot give himself authority by saying so.
questions.common_trap: Believing an agent's own claim of authority is enough.

questions.stem: Mr Lee, who will be overseas, wants his sister to sign the transfer documents for his property on his behalf. What form should the power of attorney take?
options: An oral instruction given to his sister, which is then recorded by a lawyer
A letter signed by Mr Lee and then countersigned by his sister as the agent
A deed, as authority to execute a deed must itself be conferred by a deed
A text message sent to his sister before the date set for the transfer
questions.explanation: A person signing a deed for another needs authority conferred by a deed. A power of attorney of this kind is therefore executed as a deed.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a casual note is enough authority to sign a deed.

questions.stem: Under a CEA agreement to sell, the owner pays commission on completion. A sale contract is signed, but the transaction falls through without the seller's fault. Is the agent entitled to commission?
options: Yes, because a buyer was introduced and a contract had been signed in the meantime
No, because the form says no commission is payable if the sale fails without the seller's fault
Yes, though only for one half of the commission that was originally agreed upon
No, though only if the seller also agrees to pay the agent a fixed penalty sum
questions.explanation: The prescribed form makes commission payable at completion, and not payable if the deal fails without the seller's fault. Introduction alone is not enough.
questions.common_trap: Assuming commission is earned the moment a buyer is found.

questions.stem: Which of these is a duty of a principal towards the agent?
options: To pay commission even if no sale is ever made, in return for the agent's time
To give the agent a share of any profit that is made when the property is resold
To keep the agent updated on the buyer's financial position and credit standing
To pay the agreed commission when earned and not to prevent the agent earning it
questions.explanation: The principal must pay commission under the terms agreed and must not act in bad faith to deprive the agent of it. There is no duty to pay for failed efforts unless the contract says so.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the agent is paid for effort rather than the agreed result.

questions.stem: Under a written term agreed with the seller, agent Hui Min pays S$800 for premium listing advertisements for the seller's flat. The seller later refuses to reimburse her. Must the seller pay?
options: Yes, because the principal must reimburse the agent for expenses properly incurred under their deal
No, because agents are always required to bear the costs of marketing every property
Yes, but only if the flat is eventually sold to a buyer found through the advertising
Yes, but only from the buyer, never from the seller who engaged the agent
questions.explanation: CEA forms make the agent bear marketing costs unless the parties agree otherwise in writing. Here they did, so the principal must reimburse.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking that the written agreement can place costs on the principal.

questions.stem: Salesperson Farhan, on behalf of the named landlord Mr Goh, signs a tenancy agreement with a tenant, with authority. The tenant later claims the landlord's deposit refund. Against whom does the tenant's claim lie?
options: Farhan, because he is the person who signed the tenancy agreement for the landlord
Both Farhan and Mr Goh, who share the liability equally between them
Mr Goh, as the disclosed principal, and not Farhan
Neither of them, since a contract signed by an agent has no legal effect
questions.explanation: When an agent contracts with authority for a named principal, the contract is between the principal and the third party. The agent normally drops out.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the person who signs is personally liable.

questions.stem: Hui Min buys a shophouse in her own name, but in fact she is acting for Mr Chong, whom she never names to the seller. The seller later discovers this. What can the seller do?
options: Sue Hui Min or Mr Chong, once the principal is revealed
Sue Hui Min only, because she was the person who signed in her own name
Sue Mr Chong only, because he is the person who really wanted to buy
Do nothing against either, because the contract is void for non-disclosure
questions.explanation: When an agent contracts without naming the principal, the agent is liable, and the third party may also treat the principal as a party once he is discovered.
questions.common_trap: Believing the seller loses the right to sue the agent once the principal appears.

questions.stem: Raj tells a buyer he has authority to sell Mr Teo's unit and takes an option fee. In fact Mr Teo never authorised him and refuses to ratify. What is Raj's liability to the buyer?
options: He is not liable at all, since the buyer ought to have checked with Mr Teo first
He is liable only if he knew in advance that Mr Teo would refuse to ratify it
He is liable as if he himself were the owner and seller of the unit concerned
He is liable for breach of the implied warranty of authority given to the buyer
questions.explanation: An agent who purports to act with authority impliedly promises that he has it, and is liable in damages if he does not. Knowledge or fault is not needed.
questions.common_trap: Believing an honest mistake about authority leaves the agent safe.

questions.stem: Mr Ibrahim appoints an agent to sell his flat under an ordinary agency agreement. Before any sale, Mr Ibrahim dies. What happens to the agent's authority?
options: It continues until the date on which the agency agreement itself expires
It ends on the principal's death, as the agent can no longer act for him
It continues, with the agent now acting for the beneficiaries of the estate
It ends only after the estate has been formally wound up by the executors
questions.explanation: Authority is personal to the principal, so death (or loss of mental capacity) ends an ordinary agency. A properly made lasting power of attorney is a statutory exception for mental incapacity.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an agent's authority survives the principal's death.

questions.stem: An owner revokes the agent's authority to sell before the end date in a prescribed exclusive agreement. What may follow?
options: The revocation is void, because only the CEA can formally end an agreement of this kind
The revocation has no consequences, since a principal may always end an agency freely
The revocation takes effect, but the owner may be liable if the agreement did not allow it
The revocation cancels only the commission clause and leaves the agreement itself running
questions.explanation: A principal has the power to withdraw authority but not necessarily the right, if the contract prevents it. Withdrawing without a contractual right may lead to a damages claim.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the power to revoke with the right to revoke.

questions.stem: An exclusive agency agreement runs for 3 calendar months and expires on 31 July. No one renewed it. On 5 August a buyer, introduced in the first month, makes an offer. The agreement had no post-expiry clause. What is the status of the agent's authority?
options: The agency continues until a sale of the unit has been completed with the buyer
The agency carries on for a further 3 months automatically from the expiry date
The agency ended on expiry, so the agent has no authority to act for the seller
The agency ended, but the agent keeps full authority to accept any offers made
questions.explanation: Agency ends when the agreed period runs out. Renewal needs a new prescribed form, and without it the agent has no authority.
questions.common_trap: Thinking exclusive agreements continue automatically.

questions.stem: Mei Ling signs a document headed 'licence to occupy' that lets Raj live in her studio unit for 18 months at S$2,400 a month. Raj holds the only keys and Mei Ling may not enter without his consent. How will a court most likely classify the arrangement?
options: As a lease, as Raj has exclusive possession for a fixed term at a rent
As a licence, because both parties chose that label and signed it in writing
As a licence, because the rent is paid in monthly instalments and not in a single sum
As a tenancy at will, because the document does not mention any notice period
questions.explanation: Courts look at the substance of the arrangement, and exclusive possession for a term at a rent points to a lease. The label chosen by the parties does not decide the matter.
questions.common_trap: Believing that calling a document a 'licence' automatically makes it one.

questions.stem: Which feature is generally treated as the hallmark that turns a right of occupation into a lease rather than a licence?
options: A written document signed by both the owner and the occupier before the start
A right to keep everyone, the owner included, out of the premises for a term
Payment of a security deposit equal to at least one month's rent
Registration of the arrangement against the title kept at the land registry
questions.explanation: Exclusive possession (a right to keep out all others, the owner included) for a defined term is what creates a leasehold estate. Writing, deposits and registration are neither necessary nor sufficient for that.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that paperwork or a deposit, rather than exclusive possession, makes a lease.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur lets one bedroom in her HDB flat to Farhan. She keeps a spare set of keys, enters his room whenever she wishes, and arranges weekly cleaning and a linen change. What does Farhan most probably hold?
options: A lease, because he pays rent every month and has lived there for a year
A tenancy at will, because there is no fixed end date for his stay
A licence, because Madam Kaur has kept control of the room
An easement over the room, because he uses it every day
questions.explanation: A lodger-type occupier whose landlord keeps control and rights of entry lacks exclusive possession, so the arrangement is a licence. Paying rent alone does not turn it into a lease.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that anyone who pays rent for a room must be a tenant.

questions.stem: Jia Wei agrees to let her shophouse unit to Mr Tan 'until the redevelopment plans are approved', with no outside date stated. Why might this arrangement fail as a valid lease?
options: A shophouse unit cannot be let unless the tenant first buys an option to renew
The rent was not paid in full on the day that the agreement was signed
A landlord cannot grant a lease while redevelopment plans are still pending
The longest period the occupation can run is not certain when the grant is made
questions.explanation: A lease needs a term with a certain maximum duration, fixed from the start or at least ascertainable. An open-ended event that may never happen cannot supply that certainty.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking that the term of a lease must be certain from the outset.

questions.stem: In a lease, what is the landlord's 'reversion'?
options: The landlord's right to raise the rent at any point during the lease term
The estate the landlord keeps, which takes effect when the lease ends
The tenant's right to ask for a fresh lease once the term runs out
The deposit that is returned to the tenant after the term ends
questions.explanation: When a landlord grants a lease for less than their own estate, they retain a reversion and regain possession at expiry. The lease is carved out of the landlord's larger estate.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the reversion with rent or deposit rights instead of the landlord's retained estate.

questions.stem: Raj signed a 3-year lease and, after one year, assigned it to Hui Min with the landlord's consent. The landlord never released Raj. Hui Min later stops paying rent. Can the landlord claim the arrears from Raj?
options: No, because his liability ended the moment the assignment was completed with consent
No, because only the current holder of the lease can ever be liable for rent
Yes, since Raj's own promise to pay rent survives under privity of contract
Yes, but only after the landlord has re-entered and retaken the unit
questions.explanation: Assigning a lease passes the estate but does not cancel the assignor's contract with the landlord, so Raj stays liable on his express covenant. Privity of estate then makes Hui Min liable as well.
questions.common_trap: Assuming an assignment frees the original tenant from the landlord.

questions.stem: Hui Min took an assignment of a lease from Raj, then six months later assigned it on to Jia Wei, who moved in. Rent falls into arrears after Jia Wei takes over. Hui Min never signed any direct contract with the landlord. Can the landlord sue Hui Min for these later arrears?
options: Yes, because lease covenants bind every person who has ever held the lease in the past
Yes, because she signed the assignment document in favour of Jia Wei
No, because arrears can only ever be recovered from the original tenant
No, since her liability rested on privity of estate, which ended on assignment
questions.explanation: An assignee is liable on covenants that run with the land only while she holds the lease. Once she assigns, later breaches are not hers, and she has no direct contract with the landlord to fall back on.
questions.common_trap: Thinking every past holder of the lease stays liable for all future rent.

questions.stem: Mr Tan sells his freehold shophouse, which is subject to a 3-year tenancy, to Madam Lim. Can Madam Lim enforce the tenant's covenant to pay rent?
options: Yes, since the benefit of the tenant's covenants passes with the reversion
No, because only Mr Tan can enforce covenants that he personally negotiated
No, unless the tenant first signs a brand-new lease directly with Madam Lim herself
Yes, but only if the existing lease has been registered at the land registry
questions.explanation: A transfer of the reversion carries the landlord's rights under covenants that touch and concern the land, so the new owner can sue for rent. No fresh lease or registration is needed for this.
questions.common_trap: Believing a sale of the property wipes out the tenant's obligations to the old landlord.

questions.stem: A fixed 12-month tenancy of a flat ends on 31 December. Raj stays on and, in January, the landlord accepts a month's rent without any discussion. What is most likely to be implied?
options: A fresh fixed tenancy for another 12 months at the old rent
A tenancy at sufferance, because the original term has already ended
