A periodic monthly tenancy on the old terms that fit a periodic letting
A bare licence, because the lease was not renewed in writing
questions.explanation: A tenant who holds over with the landlord's knowledge and pays rent that the landlord accepts is usually taken to hold a periodic tenancy, with the period set by how rent is paid. It is not a new fixed term.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a holding-over tenant automatically gets a new fixed term.

questions.stem: While Farhan and the landlord negotiate a lease, the landlord lets Farhan move into a flat. No term and no rent are agreed, and either side may end the arrangement whenever it likes. This is best described as which kind of tenancy?
options: A periodic tenancy
A tenancy at sufferance
A fixed-term lease of 12 months
A tenancy at will
questions.explanation: A tenancy at will exists where the occupier is in possession with the owner's consent on terms that either side can end at any time. It differs from a periodic tenancy, which needs a recurring period and notice to end.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up tenancy at will with periodic tenancy.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a tenancy at sufferance?
options: A former tenant who stays on after the term without the landlord's consent
A tenant who occupies with the landlord's consent and with no fixed end date at all
A tenant who pays rent weekly under an informal arrangement
A tenant who has sublet the whole premises to someone else
questions.explanation: At sufferance, the tenant's original right has expired and the landlord has not agreed to anything new; the tenant is merely tolerated. Where the landlord consents or accepts rent, a different tenancy arises.
questions.common_trap: Treating any overstay as a periodic tenancy even when the landlord has not consented.

questions.stem: Unless the parties agreed otherwise, what notice does the common law usually require to end a monthly periodic tenancy?
options: At least seven days, whichever day of the month is chosen
At least one month, expiring at the end of a monthly period
At least three months, to match the usual quarterly rent review
None, since periodic tenancies end whenever the landlord asks
questions.explanation: A notice to quit generally has to be at least as long as one period of the tenancy and end on the last day of a period. A contract can set a different notice.
questions.common_trap: Thinking periodic tenancies can be ended on a few days' notice.

questions.stem: Hui Min lets a shop unit to Raj for 5 years at the market rent, using a signed ordinary agreement that is not executed as a deed. Is the lease void at law for want of a deed?
options: Yes, because every lease longer than 3 years must be made by deed
Yes, because every lease of commercial premises must be made by deed
No, because payment of stamp duty cures the lack of a deed
No, as a lease of up to 7 years at a rack rent needs no deed
questions.explanation: In Singapore a conveyance of land must be by deed to pass a legal estate, but a lease not exceeding 7 years at a rack rent (a full market rent) is excepted. The 3-year line belongs to English law, not Singapore law.
questions.common_trap: Importing the English 3-year rule into Singapore.

questions.stem: A 10-year lease of a unit at a full market rent is signed by both parties but is not executed as a deed. What is its likely effect?
options: It is void at law but is enforceable in equity as an agreement for a lease
It is completely void, so the tenant has no rights over the unit in law or in equity
It becomes a valid legal lease as soon as the first month's rent has been paid
It is converted into a tenancy at sufferance for the whole period
questions.explanation: Under the rule in Walsh v Lonsdale, equity treats a specifically enforceable agreement for a lease as if the lease had been granted. The tenant gets an equitable lease, though not a legal estate.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that a defective lease gives the tenant nothing at all.

questions.stem: Under the Land Titles Act, which of these leases of registered land can be lodged for registration in the approved form of lease?
options: A tenancy for exactly 7 years with certain start and end dates
An 8-year lease with certain dates and exclusive possession
A monthly periodic tenancy that has now run for 9 years
A 10-year licence to use a space without exclusive possession
questions.explanation: Only a lease for a term exceeding 7 years, with certain dates and exclusive possession, can be registered as a lease. Exactly 7 years is not enough, and a periodic tenancy or licence lacks the required certainty or possession.
questions.common_trap: Forgetting that the term must exceed 7 years, so exactly 7 years does not qualify.

questions.stem: Raj and Mei Ling sign a 2-year tenancy at S$3,000 a month. Assume the contractual rent is the dutiable rent and the lease is subject to the standard rate of 0.4% of total rent for leases of up to 4 years. How much stamp duty is payable?
questions.explanation: Total rent is S$3,000 x 24 = S$72,000, and 0.4% of S$72,000 is S$288. S$144 would be duty on only one year of rent.
questions.common_trap: Calculating duty on one year's rent instead of the whole lease period.

questions.stem: A tenancy agreement is signed in Singapore. Within how many days of signing should it be stamped to avoid late-stamping penalties?
options: 14 days
7 days
30 days
60 days
questions.explanation: Documents signed in Singapore must be stamped within 14 days of signing; the 30-day period applies to documents signed overseas, counted from receipt in Singapore.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the 14-day local deadline with the 30-day overseas one.

questions.stem: What best distinguishes an assignment of a lease from a sublease?
options: An assignment leaves the tenant with a reversion; a sublease transfers the whole remaining term
An assignment transfers the whole remaining term; a sublease leaves the tenant a reversion
An assignment needs the landlord's agreement, whereas a sublease never can be restricted
An assignment ends the head lease, whereas a sublease leaves the head lease running
questions.explanation: If the tenant parts with everything left of the term, it is an assignment; if even a day is kept back, it is a sublease and the tenant becomes the subtenant's landlord. The head lease continues in both cases.
questions.common_trap: Reversing the two or thinking an assignment terminates the head lease.

questions.stem: Hui Min wants to leave her 2-year tenancy early and be fully released from liability. The landlord is willing to accept Jia Wei as the new tenant. Which step would release Hui Min?
options: A plain assignment of the lease to Jia Wei, with Hui Min staying on the contract
A sublease of the whole unit to Jia Wei for the remaining months
A novation signed by the landlord, Hui Min and Jia Wei, replacing Hui Min with Jia Wei
Hui Min handing the keys to Jia Wei without any paperwork
questions.explanation: Novation substitutes a new contract (and a new tenant) with the consent of all three parties, so the original tenant is discharged. Assignment and subletting leave her liable to the landlord.
questions.common_trap: Treating assignment as if it released the outgoing tenant.

questions.stem: A tenancy agreement bars assignment without the landlord's written consent. Raj assigns his tenancy to Farhan without asking. What is the usual legal position?
options: The assignment is automatically void against everybody, including Farhan and the landlord
No breach arises because the clause covers sublets only and does not reach assignments
The landlord may claim only nominal damages and can never forfeit the lease for this
It binds Raj and Farhan, but Raj is in breach and the landlord may have remedies
questions.explanation: A breach of a covenant against assignment does not stop the assignment taking effect between the parties, but it exposes the tenant to damages and possibly forfeiture if the lease allows re-entry.
questions.common_trap: Believing a prohibited assignment is automatically void.

questions.stem: A lease gives the tenant an option to renew, exercisable by written notice delivered at least 3 months before expiry. Raj sends a notice only 6 weeks before expiry. What is the probable result?
options: The option is still valid because courts read renewal deadlines flexibly
The option has lapsed, as options must be exercised strictly
The option is still valid if the landlord cannot show any actual prejudice
The lease renews, but only on a monthly periodic basis
questions.explanation: Options to renew are construed strictly and the stipulated conditions, especially timing, must be met exactly. Late exercise generally defeats the option.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that substantial compliance with an option's timing is enough.

questions.stem: Which renewal wording is most likely to give an enforceable right to a new term?
options: Rent to be such sum as the parties may later agree between themselves
Rent to be reasonable, as the landlord sees fit when the time comes
Rent to be the market rent, set by an independent valuer if need be
Rent to be negotiated in good faith before the renewal date
questions.explanation: A renewal clause must be certain, and a mechanism that fixes the rent (market rent with a valuer to decide) supplies certainty. A bare agreement to agree is usually too uncertain to enforce.
questions.common_trap: Believing that an 'agree later' rent clause is a binding renewal right.

questions.stem: Raj leaves a unit 8 months before the lease ends and posts the keys to the landlord, Madam Lim. She writes back that she is keeping the keys only for safekeeping and still expects the rent. Has the lease been surrendered?
options: Yes, because handing back possession ends the lease by itself
Yes, because Raj no longer lives in the unit and has handed over the keys
Yes, provided Raj also pays one further month's rent as compensation
No, because surrender needs the landlord's acceptance and her reply shows none
questions.explanation: Surrender must be accepted by the landlord, expressly or by conduct inconsistent with the lease continuing. Keeping keys for safekeeping while demanding rent is not acceptance.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that a tenant can end a lease alone by returning the keys.

questions.stem: Mei Ling rents a freehold unit from Mr Tan under a 3-year tenancy. In year two she buys the unit from him while the lease is still running. What happens to her leasehold interest?
options: It merges into the freehold and ends, as both are held by one person
It continues as a separate estate until the original three-year term expires
It turns into a periodic tenancy under which Mei Ling pays herself rent
It lasts until Mei Ling gives herself a formal notice to quit
questions.explanation: Merger occurs when the lease and the immediate reversion come together in one owner, because a person cannot be both landlord and tenant of the same land. The lease is extinguished.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a lease survives once the tenant becomes the owner.

questions.stem: A lease has a proviso allowing re-entry for breach. Landlord Jia Wei learns that her tenant has sublet without consent. Knowing this, she accepts the next month's rent in full without reserving any rights. What is the likely effect?
options: Nothing changes, because accepting rent never affects a right to forfeit
The unauthorised sublease becomes valid against the landlord for all time
The landlord may be taken to have waived forfeiture for that breach
The lease is converted into a tenancy at will from the date of payment
questions.explanation: Accepting rent that falls due after a known breach affirms the lease and waives the right to forfeit for that breach. Landlords who want to preserve the right should reserve it in writing or refuse the rent.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a landlord can bank rent and still forfeit for a known breach.

questions.stem: A landlord sues to forfeit a lease for unpaid rent. Before the time for the tenant to acknowledge service runs out, the tenant pays all arrears and the landlord's costs. What happens under Singapore's statute on relief for non-payment of rent?
options: The landlord may still take possession because the re-entry right has arisen
The lease ends, but the tenant is granted a fresh fixed term by the court
The tenant must still give up possession within four weeks of paying
The action ceases and the tenant keeps the lease on its existing terms
questions.explanation: Under the Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, payment of arrears and costs within the stated time stops the forfeiture action, and the tenant continues under the same lease. The position differs if the landlord also relies on other breaches.
questions.common_trap: Believing that once the landlord has sued for forfeiture the tenant cannot save the lease.

questions.stem: Mr Tan changes the door locks of a flat while his tenant Mei Ling is overseas, because the rent is late. Which obligation implied in the lease has he most clearly breached?
options: The landlord's covenant for the tenant's quiet enjoyment
The tenant's covenant not to commit waste
The tenant's covenant to yield up the premises at expiry
The landlord's covenant for further assurance
questions.explanation: The covenant for quiet enjoyment protects the tenant's possession from substantial interference by the landlord. Locking the tenant out is a classic breach, and a late-rent landlord must use lawful remedies instead.
questions.common_trap: Treating lock-out as a legitimate self-help remedy for late rent.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur lets a ground-floor unit to Raj for use as a restaurant, then seals the only duct that could serve the kitchen exhaust, which makes running a restaurant impossible. Which implied principle is most obviously in issue?
options: The tenant must pay the rent on the due dates
The landlord must not derogate from the grant
The tenant must permit the landlord to inspect
The landlord must insure the building at her cost
questions.explanation: A landlord who grants premises for a stated purpose cannot then act so as to defeat that purpose, which is the principle of non-derogation from grant. It is closely linked with quiet enjoyment.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the landlord's duty not to undermine the grant with the tenant's duties.

questions.stem: Jia Wei, a tenant, hacks out the built-in wardrobes and the kitchen counter and sells the materials. In landlord and tenant law, this is best described as which of the following?
options: Permissive waste, a failure to carry out needed repairs
Fair wear and tear arising from ordinary use of the unit
A breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment by the tenant
Voluntary waste, a deliberate act damaging the property
questions.explanation: Voluntary (or active) waste is a positive act that damages or alters the premises, and a tenant must not commit it. Permissive waste is neglect, and quiet enjoyment is a landlord's covenant.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up voluntary waste (acts) with permissive waste (omissions).

questions.stem: A tenancy agreement for an unfurnished flat says nothing about repairs, and the water heater fails after four months through ordinary ageing. What is the general common law position?
options: No general duty on the landlord to repair is implied, so the express terms govern
The landlord must repair at his own cost because the tenant is paying monthly rent
The tenant must replace it under the implied duty to use the premises as agreed
The tenant may stop paying rent until the landlord has repaired the heater
questions.explanation: Common law does not generally imply a landlord's repair obligation into an ordinary letting, which is why Singapore tenancy agreements spell out who repairs what. A tenant cannot withhold rent on its own.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that the law automatically makes the landlord responsible for all repairs.

questions.stem: Hui Min's tenancy agreement has no diplomatic clause and no break clause. Four months into a 24-month term, her employer posts her overseas. Can she end the tenancy on her own?
options: Yes, a job posting overseas ends any tenancy by law after two months' notice
No, she stays bound unless the landlord agrees or the lease allows it
Yes, she may leave if she gives up one month's security deposit
Yes, the Estate Agents Act gives employees an early termination right
questions.explanation: A diplomatic clause is a negotiated contract term, not a statutory right. Without it or a break clause, the tenant remains bound for the full term unless the landlord agrees to release her.
questions.common_trap: Treating the diplomatic clause as a legal right that every tenant has.

questions.stem: At the end of a 2-year tenancy, Madam Kaur finds the paint slightly faded and the carpet thinned from ordinary use. The agreement says the unit must be returned in good condition, fair wear and tear excepted. May she deduct the repainting and carpet costs from the deposit?
options: Yes, because any difference from the move-in condition can be charged
Yes, but only half of the cost, since the damage is said to be shared
No, because the clause excepts deterioration from normal use
Yes, provided the tenant had renewed the tenancy at least once before
questions.explanation: A restoration clause that excepts fair wear and tear does not make the tenant answerable for gradual deterioration from ordinary use. Deductions are for damage beyond that.
questions.common_trap: Reading a restoration covenant as a duty to return the unit as good as new.

questions.stem: A 24-month tenancy lets either party end it after month 12 by giving two months' written notice. After 14 months Raj messages the landlord that he 'might move out soon'. What decides whether the tenancy has ended?
options: Whether he strictly complied with the clause's notice requirements
Whether the landlord has already found a replacement tenant for the unit
Whether Raj has paid at least one full month's rent in advance
Whether two months have passed since his first message was sent
questions.explanation: A break clause is exercised strictly in line with its wording, including form, timing and clarity of notice. An informal hint is unlikely to count as valid notice.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a casual message is enough to trigger a break clause.

questions.stem: Farhan owns a private condominium unit and an HDB flat. He wants to let each out to a tenant for 2 months. Under current rules, which statement is correct?
options: Both are allowed, since only periods of under one month are treated as short-term lets
Neither is allowed: the minimum is 3 months for private homes and 6 for HDB flats
The condominium is allowed at 2 months, but the HDB flat needs at least 6 months
The HDB flat is allowed at 2 months, but the condominium needs at least 3 months
questions.explanation: URA requires private residential lets to run for at least three consecutive months, and HDB requires at least six months for a whole flat or a bedroom. A two-month tenancy fails both.
questions.common_trap: Applying a single minimum period to both HDB and private homes.

questions.stem: Madam Kaur's tenant is three months behind. She enters while he is out and takes his television to hold against the arrears. Is this a lawful distress?
options: Yes, because landlords have a common law right to seize goods for rent at once
Yes, as long as she leaves a receipt listing the item that she took
No, distress must follow the Distress Act, via a writ the sheriff executes
Yes, because the arrears already exceed one month's rent in total
questions.explanation: In Singapore a landlord may distrain only in the way the Distress Act provides, which means applying to court for a writ that the sheriff carries out. Taking goods herself is unlawful self-help.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a landlord can seize tenant's goods personally for unpaid rent.

questions.stem: Under the Distress Act, which of a tenant's belongings is protected from seizure?
options: A television that is switched off when the sheriff arrives
A sofa set that the tenant bought outright with cash last year
Jewellery that the tenant keeps in a drawer in the flat
The necessary clothing and bedding of the tenant's family
questions.explanation: The Act exempts items such as the necessary clothing and bedding of the tenant and family, along with goods in use at the time and certain tools. Ordinary furniture and valuables can generally be seized.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that all household furniture is protected from distress.

questions.stem: For which of these can a landlord use distress under the Distress Act?
options: Damage to the walls and floors that goes well beyond fair wear and tear
Unpaid rent, for up to 12 completed months before the application
Breach of a covenant not to sublet any part of the unit without consent
The agent's commission that the landlord has already paid out to the agent
questions.explanation: Distress is a remedy for rent arrears only, limited under the Act to rent for a period not exceeding 12 completed months before the application. Other breaches call for damages or other remedies.
questions.common_trap: Thinking distress can recover any money owed by the tenant.

questions.stem: A tenant keeps running a noisy karaoke business from a flat, contrary to a covenant to use the unit only as a home. Which remedy is most apt to stop the continuing breach?
options: Distress, which lets the sheriff seize the tenant's goods for the breach
An action for arrears, which recovers rent that has fallen due
An injunction, which orders the tenant to stop breaching the use covenant
Surrender, which the landlord may impose by writing to the tenant
questions.explanation: Injunctions are the equitable remedy for restraining a continuing breach of covenant, and damages or forfeiture may also be available. Distress and arrears relate to unpaid rent, and surrender requires agreement.
questions.common_trap: Using rent-focused remedies for non-rent breaches.

questions.stem: The tenancy agreement for Raj's flat contains no clause allowing inspection. Even so, the landlord starts entering every week to check on the unit without asking. What is the legal position?
options: He may enter freely, since the owner always keeps an implied right of access
He may enter once a month, as the law implies a monthly right of inspection
He may enter at any time if he gives a one-day notice by message
He has no general right to enter without an express right or consent
questions.explanation: A tenant with exclusive possession can keep the landlord out, so a right of entry must be reserved by the lease or agreed by the tenant. Many tenancy agreements therefore include a clause allowing entry on reasonable notice.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that landlords have an automatic right to inspect their own property.

questions.stem: Which list sets out what a claimant must establish to succeed in negligence?
options: A contract with the defendant, breach of it, loss suffered, and a written demand for payment
A duty of care, breach of that duty, damage caused by the breach, and damage not too remote
An intention to cause harm, a wrongful act, loss suffered, and refusal of an apology
A statutory duty, a careless act, a loss suffered, and a profit made by the defendant
questions.explanation: Negligence requires duty, breach, causation of damage and damage that is not too remote. No contract, intention or defendant's profit is needed.
questions.common_trap: Thinking negligence needs a contract or an intention to harm.

questions.stem: In Spandeck v DSTA, the Court of Appeal set out a single framework for finding a duty of care. What is its correct order?
options: Policy considerations first, then proximity, then foreseeability of harm
Assumption of responsibility, then reliance, then a check that no contract exists
Foreseeability as a threshold, then proximity, then policy considerations
Foreseeability of the exact type of damage, then proximity, then a check on remoteness
questions.explanation: The test begins with a low threshold of factual foreseeability, then asks whether the parties are legally proximate, and finally whether policy negates the duty. Foreseeability of the type of loss is a remoteness question, not the threshold.
questions.common_trap: Muddling duty-stage foreseeability with remoteness of damage.

questions.stem: A buyer sues a conveyancing lawyer for pure economic loss caused by careless advice. Which approach do Singapore courts use to decide whether a duty exists?
options: The Caparo three-part test, because the loss is financial and not physical
The Hedley Byrne rule alone, since Spandeck covers only physical injury
A presumption of duty whenever the loss suffered is purely financial
The single Spandeck test, which covers all negligence claims
questions.explanation: Spandeck laid down one framework for every kind of negligence claim, expressly including pure economic loss and negligent misstatement, in place of separate tests such as Caparo. Hedley Byrne reliance and assumption of responsibility are considered within the proximity stage.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a separate test (Caparo or Hedley Byrne) applies to economic loss.

questions.stem: Salesperson Hui Min tells a prospective buyer, Raj, 'I personally checked with URA, and this unit can be converted to office use', intending him to rely on it. Raj pays the option fee. Which factor most strongly supports a duty of care?
options: Hui Min took responsibility for the claim and Raj reasonably relied on it
Hui Min is paid commission by the seller on completion of the sale
Raj is a first-time buyer who has not previously met the seller
Hui Min's agency has many other salespersons working for it
questions.explanation: Voluntary assumption of responsibility together with reasonable reliance is a central marker of legal proximity under Spandeck. The commission source or the size of the agency does not create a duty.
questions.common_trap: Looking for proximity in commercial links rather than in assumed responsibility and reliance.

questions.stem: At the policy stage of the Spandeck test, how are factors such as a carefully drawn contractual framework between the parties used?
options: They decide whether the harm was foreseeable at the time of the act
They replace the need for any proximity between the parties
They may negate or limit a duty that proximity supports
They fix the amount of damages once liability is established
questions.explanation: Policy is the last stage and can cut back or cancel a prima facie duty found at the proximity stage. It does not decide foreseeability, proximity or quantum.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the role of policy with foreseeability or quantum.

questions.stem: Mr Tan sues his agent for negligently misstating a unit's floor area. The court assesses his loss at S$120,000 but finds him 25% to blame for not checking the title plan he was given. What damages is he awarded?
questions.explanation: Contributory negligence reduces damages by the claimant's share of responsibility, so S$120,000 less 25% is S$90,000. S$95,000 wrongly subtracts a flat S$25,000 and S$30,000 is the deduction itself.
questions.common_trap: Subtracting the percentage as a flat amount instead of applying it to the total.

questions.stem: Two weeks after getting her licence, salesperson Jia Wei gives a client wrong advice on a stamp duty point that a competent salesperson would have checked. She argues she is brand new. How will the court judge her conduct?
options: Against a reasonably competent salesperson, not a novice
Against a lower standard suited to a first-year salesperson
Against what she personally knew, which was very little at the time
Against the conduct of the estate agent's director, not her own
questions.explanation: The standard of care is objective and set by the reasonably competent practitioner in that role. A novice who takes on the work must meet it.
questions.common_trap: Believing beginners are held to a lower standard of care.

questions.stem: Salesperson Farhan advertises a unit as 1,000 sq ft after repeating the seller's figure without checking the title, which shows 850 sq ft. Raj relies on the figure and pays a premium price. Which claim is most apt against Farhan?
options: Trespass to land, because the inflated figure interfered with Raj's property rights
Negligent misstatement, as he carelessly gave information that Raj relied on
Private nuisance, because the inflated figure disturbed Raj's quiet enjoyment of land
Breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment owed by landlords to tenants
questions.explanation: A careless statement that causes foreseeable financial loss to someone who relies on it, within a relationship of assumed responsibility, is negligent misstatement. The other torts concern land interference.
questions.common_trap: Reaching for land-based torts when the wrong is a careless statement.

questions.stem: For liability in negligent misstatement causing pure economic loss, which pairing is central?
options: Physical contact between the parties and a resulting injury to the recipient
A written contract between the parties and payment of valuable consideration
A fiduciary relationship between the parties and a profit made by the speaker
Assumption of responsibility by the speaker and reasonable reliance by the recipient
questions.explanation: Hedley Byrne liability rests on a special relationship in which the speaker assumes responsibility and the recipient reasonably relies. A contract is not needed for the tort.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a contract between the parties is needed to sue for a careless statement.

questions.stem: Mei Ling buys a unit after the seller's agent wrongly says there is no pending acquisition notice. Her contract is with the seller only. Against whom does section 2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act give her a damages claim?
options: The seller, because the agent's statement is treated as the seller's
The agent only, since the agent personally made the statement to her
The seller and the agent together, as joint contracting parties
Neither, since only a fraudulent misrepresentation gives damages
questions.explanation: Section 2(1) operates against a party to the contract, and statements made by an agent for the seller are treated as the seller's. The agent is not a party, so the claim against the agent lies in negligent misstatement.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the agent is a party to the sale contract.

questions.stem: How does a claim under section 2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act differ from a tort claim for negligent misstatement on who must prove carelessness?
options: Under section 2(1) the claimant must prove carelessness; in tort the defendant must then disprove it
Under section 2(1) the representor must show reasonable grounds; in tort the claimant proves carelessness
In both claims the claimant must prove that the defendant acted fraudulently with intent
In both claims the defendant must prove that the claimant had acted with reasonable care
questions.explanation: Section 2(1) shifts the burden: the representor is liable unless they prove they believed, on reasonable grounds, that the facts were true up to the contract. In the tort, the claimant carries the burden of proving breach.
questions.common_trap: Overlooking the statutory shift in the burden of proof.

questions.stem: An estate agency's standard form says it 'accepts no liability for any loss, however caused, including its own negligence'. A seller suffers financial loss from careless advice. Under UCTA, how is this clause treated?
options: It is void in every case, because negligence liability can never be excluded
It is fully effective, because the seller signed the agreement in advance
It is effective only if it is reasonable, which the agency must prove
It is effective if the wording is printed in bold type and initialled
questions.explanation: UCTA bars exclusion of negligence liability for death or personal injury, but for other loss the term must be reasonable, with the burden on the party relying on it. Signature alone does not save it.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a signed exclusion clause is automatically valid.

questions.stem: Salesperson Jia Wei, acting within her work for Prime Realty Pte Ltd, carelessly tells a client the wrong CPF rule, and the client loses a S$5,000 option fee. Who may be liable to the client?
options: Both Jia Wei personally and Prime Realty vicariously
Only Jia Wei, since a salesperson is always independent of her agency
Only Prime Realty, since a salesperson cannot be sued personally
Neither, since CEA disciplinary action replaces any civil claim
questions.explanation: A person who commits a tort is personally liable, and the agency can also be vicariously liable where the act falls within the work it assigned. Civil claims are separate from CEA discipline.
questions.common_trap: Assuming only the agency, or only the salesperson, can be held responsible.

questions.stem: An estate agency's key executive officer (KEO) personally assures a couple that 'we have fully vetted this overseas project', without making any checks. The couple rely on this and lose their deposit. Is the KEO exposed personally, or only the company?
options: Only the company, since a director's statements are always the company's
He is exposed personally too, if he assumed responsibility and they relied
Only the company, since a director owes duties to the shareholders alone
Neither, since a KEO is protected from civil claims under the Estate Agents Act
questions.explanation: An individual who makes a careless statement, assumes responsibility for it and is relied on can be personally liable even though he acts for the company. Speaking for a company does not shield him from a Hedley Byrne claim.
questions.common_trap: Believing that acting for a company shields an individual from personal liability.

questions.stem: In a negligent misstatement claim, what does the measure of damages aim to do?
options: Put the claimant where they would be had the statement turned out to be true
Strip the agent of any commission that was earned on the transaction
Restore the claimant to the position before the careless statement
Punish the defendant by awarding more than the proven loss
questions.explanation: Tort damages are compensatory and look back to the position before the wrong, whereas contract damages look forward to the promised position. They are not punitive.
questions.common_trap: Applying the contract measure (as if the statement were true) to a tort claim.

questions.stem: Raj proves that Farhan carelessly gave the wrong floor area. However, the evidence shows Raj would have bought at the same price even if told the true area, because he wanted the location. What is the result?
options: It succeeds, because proof of breach alone entitles him to damages
It succeeds for nominal damages only, as a sign of the wrong done
It succeeds, but the damages are halved because of his own lack of care
The claim fails, since his loss was not caused by his reliance on the statement
questions.explanation: Causation is a separate element, and the usual 'but for' test asks whether the loss would have happened anyway. If Raj would have bought regardless, the statement did not cause the loss.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that careless conduct alone is enough without proof it caused the loss.

questions.stem: Under the Wagon Mound principle, for what damage is a negligent defendant liable?
options: Any direct damage, however unforeseeable its kind
Damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable
Only damage that the defendant actually intended
Damage that is below a fixed monetary ceiling
questions.explanation: Remoteness limits recovery to damage of a type that a reasonable person would have foreseen. Directness alone does not make damage recoverable.
questions.common_trap: Treating directness of consequences as the test of remoteness.

questions.stem: After learning of an agent's misstatement, Mr Tan could have resold the unit within weeks at a small loss. He instead left it empty for two years while prices fell further. What principle limits his claim?
options: The defence of voluntary assumption of risk
The rule that the statement was too remote to count
The duty to take reasonable steps to mitigate loss
The rule that only the agent's commission can be recovered
questions.explanation: A claimant cannot recover for loss that reasonable steps would have avoided. Mr Tan's extra loss from waiting is attributable to him.
questions.common_trap: Believing that a claimant may let losses grow and still recover them in full.

questions.stem: A salesperson tells a foreign buyer that he can buy a landed house freely, without checking the Residential Property Act position. Approval is refused and the buyer forfeits his option fee. What does her failure to check most directly show?
options: Remoteness of the loss from her statement to the buyer
Contributory negligence on the part of the foreign buyer
A defence of voluntary assumption of risk by the buyer
Breach of the standard expected of a reasonably competent salesperson
questions.explanation: A competent salesperson would verify a well-known eligibility restriction before advising, so not doing so falls below the standard of care. The forfeited fee is the damage that may follow from that breach.
questions.common_trap: Labelling a failure to check as a defence or a remoteness issue.

questions.stem: What is the general limitation period for a negligence claim for financial loss that involves no personal injury?
options: Six years from the damage, with a later-knowledge extension for latent damage
Two years from the date of the careless statement, with no extension at all
Twelve years from the date of the careless statement in every single case
Three years from completion of the sale, with no extension for late knowledge
questions.explanation: The Limitation Act sets six years from the date of damage for ordinary negligence claims, with an alternative three years from knowledge for latent damage, subject to a long-stop of 15 years.
questions.common_trap: Applying the personal injury three-year period to all negligence claims.

questions.stem: Mr Tan's contractor walks across neighbour Madam Kaur's lawn without permission to fetch a ladder, causing no damage. What is the position on Madam Kaur's claim in trespass?
options: It fails, since she suffered no damage to her lawn at all
It fails, unless she also proves the contractor was negligent
It can succeed, as trespass is actionable without proof of damage
It fails, since trespass applies only to buildings and not lawns
questions.explanation: Trespass is a direct, unauthorised entry onto land and is actionable per se. Damage affects only the amount of compensation, not liability.
questions.common_trap: Thinking damage must be proved before trespass to land is actionable.

questions.stem: A neighbour in a condominium runs noisy renovation works until 2 am every night for months, preventing Hui Min from sleeping. Which tort is most apt?
options: Trespass to land, a direct and unauthorised entry onto her unit by the neighbour
Negligent misstatement, a careless statement by the neighbour relied on by her
Breach of the covenant for quiet enjoyment owed by a landlord to a tenant
Private nuisance, an unreasonable interference with her enjoyment of land
questions.explanation: Nuisance covers indirect but unreasonable interference with a person's use and enjoyment of land, such as persistent noise. Trespass needs direct entry, and the covenant for quiet enjoyment arises only between landlord and tenant.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up nuisance (indirect interference) with trespass (direct interference).

questions.stem: Under the Land Titles Act, what turns a borrower's security over registered land into a legal mortgage?
options: The borrower's signature on the bank's loan facility letter and acceptance of its terms
Registration of the mortgage instrument in the approved form with the Registrar of Titles
The borrower handing the lender the original title documents for safekeeping until repayment
Payment of stamp duty on the loan agreement within the prescribed time period
questions.explanation: A legal mortgage of registered land comes into existence on registration of the approved-form instrument. A signed loan letter is only a contract, and depositing documents can at best support an equitable mortgage.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a signed loan agreement or a deposit of documents is enough to create a legal mortgage.

questions.stem: A borrower signs a written agreement to deposit her title documents with a lender as security for a loan, but no mortgage is registered. How is the lender's security best described?
options: A legal mortgage, because the lender physically holds the documents of title
A first-ranking legal charge, because it is the earliest dealing affecting the property
No security at all, because only a registered instrument can give a lender any rights
An equitable mortgage, since security was intended but formalities were incomplete
questions.explanation: An agreement to give security, backed by a deposit of title documents, creates an equitable mortgage that equity will enforce. It is not a legal mortgage until registered, and it is exposed to later registered interests.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that unless the mortgage is registered the lender has no rights whatsoever.

questions.stem: In March, Farhan signs a written agreement to mortgage his shophouse to Bank X, but nothing is registered and no caveat is lodged. In May, Bank Y lends him money and registers a mortgage over the shophouse. Assuming no fraud, which bank ranks first?
options: Bank Y, as registration beats an earlier unregistered equitable interest
Bank X, because its agreement with Farhan was made earlier in time
Neither, so both banks share the sale proceeds in proportion to their loans
Whichever bank advanced the larger amount of money to Farhan
questions.explanation: Under the Torrens system a registered interest generally defeats an unregistered one, absent fraud. Bank X could have protected itself by lodging a caveat.
questions.common_trap: Applying the old 'first in time' rule and ignoring the effect of registration.

questions.stem: Two banks hold registered mortgages over Madam Kaur's condominium unit. Bank A's mortgage was signed on 1 June and registered on 20 June. Bank B's was signed on 5 June and registered on 10 June. Which statement is correct?
options: Bank A ranks ahead of Bank B because its mortgage was signed first
The two banks rank equally because both mortgages were signed in the same month
Bank B ranks ahead of Bank A because priority follows the order of registration
Bank A ranks ahead because the bank with the larger loan always takes priority
questions.explanation: Registered mortgages rank by the date and time of registration, not the date of signing. Bank B registered first, so it ranks first.
questions.common_trap: Counting priority from the date the mortgage was signed rather than registered.

questions.stem: After a borrower misses the contractual date for repayment, which right does she still hold until the property is sold or foreclosed?
options: The right to keep the property free of the debt once the repayment date has passed
The right to veto the lender's choice of purchaser in a mortgagee sale
The equity of redemption, which lets her get the property back by paying what is owed
The right to compel the lender to extend the loan tenure on the same terms
questions.explanation: The mortgagor keeps an equitable right to redeem by paying principal, interest and costs, even after the legal date has passed. It ends only on sale or foreclosure.
questions.common_trap: Believing that missing the repayment date automatically ends the borrower's claim to the property.

questions.stem: Before a mortgagee of registered land enters into possession after the borrower defaults, what minimum notice must it give under the Land Titles Act?
options: Seven days
One month
Fourteen days
Three months
questions.explanation: The statutory power to enter into possession and take the rents cannot be exercised until one month's notice has been given. A shorter or longer period is not what the Act sets.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the notice for taking possession with other statutory notice periods.

questions.stem: Which mortgagee remedy needs a court order and, once registered, vests the mortgagor's whole interest in the lender, ending the equity of redemption?
options: Foreclosure
Suing on the borrower's personal covenant to repay
Entering into possession and collecting the rents
Selling the property under the power of sale
questions.explanation: Foreclosure is by court order and, once entered on the folio, frees the mortgagee's estate from the equity of redemption. A sale or entry into possession needs no foreclosure order.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a mortgagee sale also needs a court order or ends the equity of redemption in the same way.

questions.stem: Raj defaults, and the bank sells his flat. After costs, the net sale proceeds are S$900,000 but he owed S$1,100,000. Can the bank still claim the S$200,000 balance?
options: No, because a sale by the bank extinguishes the whole debt
Yes, but only if it first obtains a court order for foreclosure
No, unless the CPF Board consents to the claim being made
Yes, it can sue Raj on his personal covenant for the balance
questions.explanation: The personal covenant is a separate promise to repay and survives the sale. The bank can sue for the shortfall, and the sale does not wipe the debt.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that selling the security settles the debt even when the proceeds fall short.

questions.stem: A mortgagee sells a property for S$1,000,000. Sale expenses are S$20,000. The first mortgage debt is S$700,000 and the second mortgage debt is S$250,000. How much is left for the mortgagor?
questions.explanation: Proceeds are applied to the costs of sale first, then the first mortgage, then later mortgages in order of priority, and any balance goes to the owner: 1,000,000 - 20,000 - 700,000 - 250,000 = 30,000. Forgetting the sale expenses gives S$50,000.
questions.common_trap: Leaving out the sale expenses, or skipping the second mortgage, when working out the balance.

questions.stem: Madam Lee mortgages her condominium unit to a bank and the mortgage is registered. Whose name remains on the land register as the proprietor of the unit?
options: The bank's, because registering a mortgage transfers legal ownership to the lender
Madam Lee's, as a registered mortgage gives security without transferring title
Both names, as the bank and Madam Lee become co-owners on the land register
The Singapore Land Authority's, which holds the unit as custodian until repayment
questions.explanation: A mortgage of registered land does not operate as a transfer of the land and has effect as security only (Land Titles Act s 68(3)). The borrower remains the registered owner.
questions.common_trap: Carrying over the idea that a mortgage hands legal title to the lender.

questions.stem: Which benchmark has replaced SIBOR and SOR as the key reference rate for floating-rate Singapore dollar home loans?
options: The interest rate paid on CPF Ordinary Account balances
A revised SIBOR published by the banks' association
The concessionary rate that HDB charges on its housing loans
Compounded SORA, an overnight transaction-based rate
questions.explanation: SOR ceased after 30 June 2023 and SIBOR after 31 December 2024, with MAS steering the SGD market to a SORA-centred landscape, so floating packages are now priced off SORA. The HDB and CPF rates are set by policy, not by a market benchmark.
questions.common_trap: Still treating SIBOR as the benchmark for new floating-rate loans.

questions.stem: Mei Ling's bank package charges 2.0% fixed for the first two years, then 3-month compounded SORA plus 0.75%. What happens to her instalments from the third year?
options: They can rise or fall as SORA moves, because the loan becomes floating
They stay at the 2.0% level for the rest of the loan tenure
They are frozen at the average rate of the first two years
They change only if the HDB revises its concessionary loan rate
questions.explanation: A fixed-then-floating package reverts to a rate that follows the benchmark when the fixed period ends. The initial fixed rate does not carry on.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a promotional fixed rate lasts for the whole loan.

questions.stem: A flat is sold and the net proceeds are S$600,000. The outstanding housing loan is S$420,000 and the CPF refund due (principal plus accrued interest) is S$300,000. Ignoring sale expenses, how much of the proceeds goes towards the CPF refund?
questions.explanation: In a negative sale the outstanding housing loan is repaid first (S$420,000), leaving S$180,000 for the CPF refund. A pro-rata split (S$250,000) or paying CPF first (S$300,000) does not follow the order.
questions.common_trap: Splitting the proceeds in proportion, or paying the CPF refund before the bank loan.

questions.stem: A bank sells a defaulting borrower's unit for S$700,000 after one week, with no advertising, though valuers put the market value near S$1,000,000. What is the borrower's best argument?
options: The sale is void because a mortgagee sale always needs a court order
The bank was obliged to get the borrower's approval of the price first
The bank breached its duty to take reasonable care to obtain a proper price
The bank was bound to wait for the market to reach its peak
questions.explanation: A mortgagee who decides to sell must take reasonable care to obtain a proper (true market) price, so a rushed, unadvertised sale far below valuation points to breach. The bank does not need the borrower's approval of the price or a court order to sell.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a mortgagee has no duty at all, or may sell only with court or borrower approval.

questions.stem: A loan agreement says that if the borrower fails to repay on the due date, the mortgaged house automatically becomes the lender's property. How is this clause treated?
options: It is enforceable because the borrower freely agreed to it when signing
It is enforceable only if the debt is less than the property value
It is a clog on the equity of redemption and cannot be enforced
It is valid once the borrower fails to repay within one further month
questions.explanation: The law does not allow a term that takes away the borrower's right to redeem. The lender must instead sell, or seek foreclosure through the court.
questions.common_trap: Believing the parties' freedom of contract can override the right to redeem.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a lifetime gift of land from a bequest in a will?
options: A gift takes effect in the donor's lifetime, but a will only on death
A gift needs the donee to pay a fair price, but a bequest is free
A completed gift can be revoked at will, but a will can never be changed
A gift needs court approval, but a will needs no formalities at all
questions.explanation: A gift is a transfer made while the donor is alive and without payment. A will, in contrast, is ambulatory and only speaks from death.
questions.common_trap: Treating a gift as a sale, or thinking it works like a will.

questions.stem: What must happen to complete a gift of registered land from a father to his daughter?
options: He must announce the gift to the family in front of two witnesses
He must send her a letter that states his intention to give her the land
He must hand over the keys and let her move in to the property at once
A deed of gift must be executed and the transfer registered in her name
questions.explanation: A gift of land is made by deed, and legal title passes when the transfer is registered. An oral announcement or letter of intention leaves the gift incomplete, and equity will not usually complete it.
questions.common_trap: Thinking an oral promise or a letter of intention is enough to pass land.

questions.stem: Mr Tan transfers his condominium unit to his son by registered deed of gift. After a quarrel, he asks to take it back. Can he do so simply because he has changed his mind?
options: Yes, if he asks within twelve months of the registration of the transfer
No, a completed gift is irrevocable unless fraud or undue influence exists
Yes, since the son gave nothing in return for the unit
Yes, if he gives the Singapore Land Authority a notice of revocation
questions.explanation: Once a gift is validly completed, the donor cannot undo it just by changing his mind. The lack of payment does not make it revocable.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a gift can be reclaimed because nothing was paid for it.

questions.stem: A mother transfers her private flat to her daughter as a gift. On what value is stamp duty computed?
options: Nil, as no money changes hands in a gift
The price the mother originally paid for the flat
The market value of the flat, since no consideration is paid
A nominal sum of S$1 stated in the deed of gift
questions.explanation: Where there is no consideration, stamp duty is computed on the property's market value. ABSD may also apply depending on the donee.
questions.common_trap: Believing a gift of property carries no stamp duty.

questions.stem: Which statement about estate duty and lifetime gifts of property is correct today?
options: Gifts made within five years before death are pulled back into the estate for duty
Estate duty applies only to gifts of landed property above a set value
Estate duty applies to gifts made to anyone who is not a family member
Estate duty was abolished for deaths from 15 February 2008, so none is payable
questions.explanation: IRAS states estate duty has been removed for deaths on or after 15 February 2008. Lifetime gifts are therefore not pulled back into the estate for duty.
questions.common_trap: Relying on an old rule that no longer applies.

questions.stem: Under the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018, within how long before the bankruptcy application can a gift (transaction at an undervalue) by an individual be challenged?
options: Three years
One year
Two years
Five years
questions.explanation: For individual bankruptcy the relevant time for an undervalue transaction is three years before the bankruptcy application, and the transferor must have been insolvent then or become so. The five-year period belonged to the repealed Bankruptcy Act.
questions.common_trap: Remembering the old five-year period of the repealed Bankruptcy Act.

questions.stem: Hui Min, who was already unable to pay her debts, gifts her rental unit to her brother. Eighteen months later she is made bankrupt. What can the Official Assignee do?
options: Nothing, since a completed gift cannot be reached by her creditors
Cancel the transfer at the land registry without a court order
Apply to court to set the gift aside as a transaction at an undervalue
Claim an equal sum from the brother's own separate savings
questions.explanation: A gift made while the donor was insolvent, within the relevant time before bankruptcy, can be set aside by the court so the property is available to creditors. The Official Assignee must apply to court and cannot simply cancel the transfer.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a completed gift is always safe from the donor's creditors.

questions.stem: Madam Lee texts her nephew: 'My condo will be yours when I pass on.' She has no will. What is the legal effect of the message as a gift?
options: It is a valid gift, because it was made in writing and received
None as a gift, because a gift taking effect on death needs a valid will
It becomes a valid gift once the nephew replies to accept it
It is valid as a trust of the condo created for the nephew
questions.explanation: A transfer that is meant to operate only on death must comply with the Wills Act formalities. A text message of intention is neither a completed lifetime gift nor a valid will.
questions.common_trap: Treating an informal statement of future intention as a binding gift.

questions.stem: In a trust of land, who holds the legal title and who holds the equitable interest?
options: The beneficiary holds the legal title and the trustee holds the equitable interest
The settlor keeps both the legal title and the equitable interest
The trustee holds the legal title and the beneficiary holds the equitable interest
The Registrar holds the legal title and the trustee holds the equitable interest
questions.explanation: The trustee is the registered owner and manages the land, while the beneficiary has the right to benefit from it in equity. The roles are not interchangeable.
questions.common_trap: Swapping the legal and equitable ownership between trustee and beneficiary.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a core duty of a trustee of land?
options: To act for the beneficiaries and not profit personally from the trust
To maximise the settlor's returns even where the trust deed says otherwise
To follow every instruction of a beneficiary, even if it breaches the trust deed
To keep the existence of the trust secret from all of the beneficiaries
questions.explanation: A trustee is a fiduciary who must follow the trust terms and avoid conflict or personal gain from the trust. Acting against the deed on a beneficiary's request would itself be a breach.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a trustee can do whatever one beneficiary asks, regardless of the terms.

questions.stem: How does the Singapore land register treat the particulars of a trust over registered land?
options: The full trust deed is entered on the folio so that buyers can read it
The trustee is shown as proprietor, but the trust terms are not entered
The beneficiaries are entered as joint proprietors beside the trustee
No proprietor is entered on the folio until the trust comes to an end
questions.explanation: A person dealing with the registered proprietor is not affected by notice of any trust (Land Titles Act s 47), and a trustee appears as proprietor, possibly with a fiduciary description (s 113). Beneficiaries can protect themselves by lodging a caveat (s 115).
questions.common_trap: Expecting the register to display the beneficiaries or the trust terms.

questions.stem: Jia Wei pays the full price of a condominium unit, but the title is put in her friend Farhan's name, and no gift to him was intended. What is Farhan's position?
options: He is the full owner, because the register shows his name alone
He holds it on a constructive trust for the developer who sold the unit
He owns half, because friends are presumed to share equally
He holds the unit on a resulting trust for Jia Wei, who paid for it
questions.explanation: Where one person pays for property placed in another's name without intending a gift, the law presumes a resulting trust back to the payer. The register shows legal title, not who owns it beneficially.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the person named on title is the beneficial owner no matter who paid.

questions.stem: A company director secretly uses company money to buy a shophouse in his own name. What is the legal position of the shophouse?
options: It belongs to him outright, as the title is in his sole name
It is held on a resulting trust for the bank that financed his dealings
He holds it on a constructive trust for the company whose money paid for it
It belongs to the directors in equal shares as co-owners of the company
questions.explanation: Property bought with misappropriated fiduciary funds is held on a constructive trust for the victim. The law imposes it to stop the wrongdoer keeping the benefit.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that title in the wrongdoer's name makes him the true owner.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a constructive trust?
options: A trust created when the owner signs a trust deed naming a trustee
A trust the law imposes to stop someone unjustly profiting from property
A trust arising where one person pays for property put in another's name
A trust that only a court can create after the owner has died
questions.explanation: Constructive trusts are imposed by law, for example where a fiduciary profits from a breach. The second option describes a resulting trust.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up constructive trusts with resulting trusts.

questions.stem: Which of these trusts of land can arise without any signed writing?
options: An express trust that the owner declares only in a conversation
An express trust that the owner records in an unsigned note
An express trust that rests on the owner's bare promise to settle the land later
A resulting trust arising because someone else paid the purchase money
questions.explanation: An express declaration of trust of land must be manifested and proved by signed writing under the Civil Law Act. Resulting, implied and constructive trusts are exempt from that rule.
questions.common_trap: Thinking every trust of land needs signed writing.

questions.stem: Madam Goh is trustee of a rental shophouse. A developer privately pays her S$50,000 as a 'thank you' for recommending that the trust sell to it. What must she do with the S$50,000?
options: Keep it, because the trust still received a fair price on the sale
Account for it to the trust, as she may not profit from the trust
Keep half of it and pay the other half over to the trust beneficiaries
Keep it, if she first discloses the payment to the developer's own lawyer
questions.explanation: A trustee must not make a personal gain from the trust, and any such gain is held for the trust however fair the sale. The fairness of the price does not change this.
questions.common_trap: Believing a fair outcome for the trust excuses a trustee's personal gain.

questions.stem: Mr Rahman, trustee of a shophouse held for his late brother's children, offers to buy it himself at the full independent valuation. Without any consent or court approval, what is the position?
options: The beneficiaries can set the purchase aside even if the price is fair
The purchase is safe because he paid the full independent valuation
The purchase is void only if the price is less than the valuation
The purchase is safe because trustees may always buy from the trust
questions.explanation: The self-dealing rule makes a trustee's purchase of trust property voidable at the beneficiaries' option however fair the price. It is safe only with authority in the deed, the court's approval, or informed consent of all beneficiaries.
questions.common_trap: Treating a fair price as a defence to a trustee's own purchase.

questions.stem: Which statement about a trustee's power to invest under the Trustees Act is correct now?
options: A trustee may invest only in a fixed statutory list of authorised securities
A trustee may invest freely, with no duty of care and no need to diversify
The authorised list is gone; a trustee may invest broadly but with reasonable care
A trustee may invest only in Singapore land and in bank fixed deposits
questions.explanation: A trustee now has a general power of investment under the Trustees Act, subject to a statutory duty of care, suitability and diversification, and taking advice. The fixed list of authorised investments no longer applies.
questions.common_trap: Relying on the old 'authorised investments only' rule.

questions.stem: Hui Min has exercised an option to buy a house, and completion is eight weeks away. What interest does she have in the house before completion?
options: No interest at all until completion and the registration of the transfer
An equitable interest, as the seller holds the legal title on trust
The legal title, because she has validly exercised the option
A right to the rent only, until the transfer is registered
questions.explanation: Once there is a binding contract that equity would enforce, the buyer holds the equitable interest and the seller is trustee of the legal title pending completion. The legal title passes only on registration.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the buyer has nothing until completion.

questions.stem: In his will, Mr Wee leaves his flat to his brother to hold for Wee's daughter until she turns 25. How is this trust classified?
options: A testamentary express trust, created by the will and effective on death
A resulting trust, because the flat returns to the estate until she is 25
A constructive trust, because the law imposes it on the brother
An inter vivos trust, because it is created during Mr Wee's lifetime
questions.explanation: A trust set up in a will is an express trust that arises on death. It is neither imposed by law nor created while the settlor is alive.
questions.common_trap: Confusing a trust created by will with a trust created by operation of law.

questions.stem: How does testate succession differ from intestate succession?
options: Testate succession applies only to land, whereas intestate applies to money
Testate succession needs a court to divide the estate, but intestate does not
Testate succession applies only to Muslims, whereas intestate applies to non-Muslims
Testate follows a valid will, whereas intestate follows the statutory rules
questions.explanation: A person dies testate if he leaves a valid will and intestate if he does not (or the will fails). The rules of distribution then differ.
questions.common_trap: Thinking testate and intestate refer to the type of asset or religion.

questions.stem: Which grant of representation is issued to the executor named in a valid will?
options: Grant of probate
Letters of administration
Certificate of inheritance
Notice of death
questions.explanation: Probate confirms the executor's authority under the will. Letters of administration are for estates with no valid will or no willing executor.
questions.common_trap: Confusing probate with letters of administration.

questions.stem: Mr Pillai dies without a will. His widow wants to sell the condominium unit registered in his sole name. What must she first obtain?
options: A grant of probate showing that she was named executor in the will
Letters of administration from the court appointing her to deal with the estate
A certificate of inheritance issued by the Syariah Court
A notice of death lodged with the Singapore Land Authority
questions.explanation: With no will there is no executor, so the court must appoint an administrator through a grant of letters of administration. Probate needs a will.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a spouse can deal with a deceased's sole-name property without a grant.

questions.stem: A non-Muslim dies intestate, leaving a spouse and three children and an estate of S$1,200,000. How much does each child receive?
questions.explanation: Under the Intestate Succession Act the spouse takes one-half and the children share the other half equally. Half of S$1,200,000 is S$600,000, so each of three children receives S$200,000.
questions.common_trap: Dividing the estate equally among spouse and children as if they were equal heirs.

questions.stem: A non-Muslim dies intestate leaving a wife and both parents, but no children, and an estate of S$800,000. How much does the wife receive?
questions.explanation: With no children the spouse takes one-half and the parents share the other half, so the wife receives S$400,000. The parents take S$200,000 each.
questions.common_trap: Giving the spouse the whole estate or a two-thirds share.

questions.stem: A single non-Muslim dies intestate. His parents died earlier and he had no spouse or children, but he leaves a brother and a sister. Who inherits his estate?
options: The brother and sister, who share the estate equally
The Government, because siblings are not intestacy heirs
The brother alone, since the eldest male sibling takes first
The sister alone, since she lived with him at the time
questions.explanation: Siblings inherit equally under the Intestate Succession Act when there is no spouse, child or parent. Gender and age do not matter.
questions.common_trap: Thinking siblings have no claim, or that seniority decides.

questions.stem: Mr Teo, a non-Muslim, dies intestate leaving his wife and a brother. He had no children and his parents died earlier. How is the estate divided?
options: The wife takes half and the brother takes half
The wife takes two-thirds and the brother takes one-third
The brother takes the whole estate as the nearest blood relative
The wife takes the whole estate and the brother receives nothing
questions.explanation: If there is a spouse but no children or parents, the spouse takes the entire estate. Siblings inherit only when there is no spouse, child or parent.
questions.common_trap: Believing siblings share with the spouse.

questions.stem: How is the estate of a Muslim who dies without a will shared among the heirs?
options: Under the Intestate Succession Act, as it applies to every resident
Equally among all relatives who attend the funeral rites
Under Muslim law (faraid), not the Intestate Succession Act
Under the Wills Act default rules, with the widow taking half
questions.explanation: The Intestate Succession Act applies to non-Muslims. A Muslim's estate is distributed under Muslim law (faraid), which fixes a share for each qualifying heir.
questions.common_trap: Applying the Intestate Succession Act to Muslim estates.

questions.stem: Without the heirs' agreement, what is the most a Muslim can leave by will to a person who is not a faraid heir?
options: One-half of the net estate
One-third of the net estate
Two-thirds of the net estate
The whole of the net estate
questions.explanation: A Muslim's will is limited to one-third of the net estate (after debts and expenses). A bequest beyond that, or to a faraid heir, is effective only if the other heirs agree after death.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a Muslim has the same freedom of testation as a non-Muslim.

questions.stem: Which body issues the certificate that names the heirs of a deceased Muslim and the shares each is entitled to under Muslim law?
options: The Syariah Court
The Public Trustee's Office
The Singapore Land Authority
The CPF Board
questions.explanation: The Syariah Court issues the Faraid (Inheritance) Certificate identifying the heirs and their shares. The Public Trustee, SLA and CPF Board are not the source of this certificate.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the Land Authority or the CPF Board determines the Muslim heirs.

questions.stem: Madam Goh's will gives her condominium unit to her nephew Jia Wei. Jia Wei is also one of the two witnesses who signed the will. What is the effect?
options: The whole will is void because a beneficiary witnessed it
The gift is valid because he signed in front of Madam Goh
The gift is valid if the other witness is an independent person
The will stands, but the gift to Jia Wei fails because he witnessed it
questions.explanation: A will witnessed by a beneficiary remains valid, but a gift to a witness (or his spouse) is void. The solution is to use independent witnesses.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a beneficiary-witness invalidates the entire will, or that a second independent witness saves the gift.

questions.stem: In 2020, Raj, a bachelor, made a will leaving everything to his brother. In 2024 he marries and makes no new will. What is the effect of his marriage on the will?
options: The will stays fully valid, because marriage never affects a will
The marriage revokes the will, unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage
The will stays valid but the new wife takes half of the gift
The will is revoked only after Raj registers the marriage with the Registrar of Titles
questions.explanation: Under the Wills Act a will is revoked by the testator's later marriage, except where it was made in contemplation of that marriage. The 2024 marriage therefore revokes the 2020 will.
questions.common_trap: Believing marriage does not affect an earlier will.

questions.stem: Which statement about a life estate is correct?
options: It lasts for exactly 99 years and then reverts to the State
It passes to the holder's heirs under the holder's will when the holder dies
It gives the holder the right to sell the land outright and keep the full value
It lasts for the holder's lifetime and cannot be left on to the holder's heirs by will
questions.explanation: A life estate ends on the holder's death, so there is nothing left to pass by will. What follows depends on whether a remainder or reversion exists.
questions.common_trap: Treating a life estate like a freehold that the holder can leave to heirs.

questions.stem: Mr Lim transfers his bungalow 'to my wife for her life, and then to my son'. After the wife dies, what happens to the bungalow?
options: It passes to the son, who holds the remainder, and nothing returns to Mr Lim
It returns to Mr Lim's estate, as the original owner of the bungalow
It passes to the wife's heirs under the terms of her will
It becomes State land because the life estate has ended
questions.explanation: The son's interest is a remainder: it follows the life estate and takes effect on the wife's death. Because the whole interest was given away, no reversion is left with the grantor.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the land always reverts to the original owner after a life estate.

questions.stem: An owner grants a life estate to his cousin and says nothing about who takes the land afterwards. To whom does the land go when the cousin dies?
options: To the cousin's heirs, as part of the cousin's own estate
To the Singapore Land Authority, which holds ownerless land
Back to the grantor or his estate, by way of reversion
To the cousin's spouse, who takes the remainder automatically
questions.explanation: What the grantor did not give away stays with him as a reversion. It takes effect on the cousin's death and passes to the grantor or his estate.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a life estate holder's heirs inherit when the grantor is silent.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a remainder and a reversion?
options: A remainder is held by the grantor, whereas a reversion goes to a stranger
A remainder is held by a third party, whereas a reversion stays with the grantor
A remainder needs registration, but a reversion arises only on death
A remainder lasts a lifetime, but a reversion lasts for fifty years
questions.explanation: Both are future interests that follow a smaller estate. A remainder is given to someone other than the grantor, while a reversion is what the grantor keeps.
questions.common_trap: Reversing which of the two belongs to the grantor.

questions.stem: When a 99-year HDB lease expires, in whom does the land's reversionary interest lie?
options: The lessor, that is the State or HDB, which takes the land back
The last registered owner, who becomes the freehold owner
The owner's heirs, who take it under the Intestate Succession Act
The Urban Redevelopment Authority, which holds all expired leases
questions.explanation: A lease is a limited estate, and the reversion is held by the lessor. When the term ends, the land goes back to the lessor, unless the lease is extended.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the owner turns freehold when the lease runs out.

questions.stem: Madam Chua holds a life estate in a house, with the remainder to her niece. She sells the house to Farhan. How long can Farhan's interest last?
options: Forever, because Madam Chua sold the entire house to him
For fifty years, counted from the date of the sale to him
Until the niece reaches the age of 21 and claims the house
Only until Madam Chua dies, when the niece takes the house
questions.explanation: A life tenant can transfer only what she has, which is an interest lasting for her life. The remainder is unaffected, so Farhan's interest ends at her death.
questions.common_trap: Believing a life tenant can sell the whole land and defeat the remainderman.

questions.stem: A life tenant of a bungalow decides to demolish the house permanently to build a larger one. What may the person entitled to the remainder do?
options: Nothing, since the life tenant is entitled to treat the land as her own
Seek an injunction or damages, as the life tenant must not commit waste
Take over the bungalow immediately and cancel the life estate
Only wait until the life tenant dies before bringing any claim
questions.explanation: A life tenant must not permanently damage or destroy the property, which is called waste. The remainderman has an interest to protect and may sue.
questions.common_trap: Treating a life tenant as the full owner.

questions.stem: Land is given 'to Hui Min for life, then to Jia Wei if he qualifies as a lawyer'. What kind of interest does Jia Wei hold in the meantime?
options: A vested remainder, because his interest is already certain to take effect
A reversion, because he stays connected to the original owner
A contingent remainder, which takes effect only if the condition is satisfied
A freehold estate that is registered in his name today
questions.explanation: His right depends on an uncertain event, which makes it a contingent remainder. A vested remainder is held by an identified person with no condition left to meet.
questions.common_trap: Mistaking an interest that depends on a condition for a vested one.

questions.stem: Which four unities must be present for a joint tenancy?
options: Possession, interest, title and time
Possession, ownership, survivorship and time
Possession, interest, title and registration
Occupation, interest, payment and time
questions.explanation: The four unities are possession, interest, title and time. Survivorship is a consequence of joint tenancy, not one of the unities.
questions.common_trap: Listing survivorship or registration as one of the unities.

questions.stem: Two buyers acquire their interests in a house by separate transfers on different dates. Which unity is missing, so that they cannot be joint tenants?
options: Unity of possession
Unity of title
Unity of time
Unity of interest
questions.explanation: Joint tenants must take their interests at the same time. Where the interests vest at different times, the owners can only hold as tenants in common.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that being on the same title is enough for a joint tenancy.

questions.stem: Mei Ling and Hui Min buy a flat, with Mei Ling owning 70% and Hui Min 30%. How must they hold the flat?
options: As joint tenants, because they are both named on the same title
As tenants in common, because unequal shares rule out a joint tenancy
As joint tenants, because they bought the flat at the same time
As sole proprietors, since each holds a separate physical part
questions.explanation: Joint tenants have identical interests, so unequal shares point to a tenancy in common. Being on one title and buying at one time is not enough.
questions.common_trap: Thinking that same title and same time are enough, ignoring unity of interest.

questions.stem: Farhan and his wife own their private flat as joint tenants. Farhan dies, leaving a will that gives his 'half' of the flat to his nephew. Who owns the flat after his death?
options: The wife and the nephew as tenants in common in equal shares
The nephew alone, since the will takes effect on the death of the testator
Farhan's estate, until the court issues a grant of probate
The wife alone, since survivorship overrides his will
