questions.explanation: On the death of a joint tenant, the survivor takes the whole by survivorship and nothing passes under the will. The nephew's gift fails unless the tenancy was severed before death.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a will can dispose of a joint tenant's share.

questions.stem: A co-owner of a private flat dies while holding a distinct 40% share as a tenant in common. What happens to that share?
options: It passes automatically to the other co-owners by survivorship
It passes under his will, or under the intestacy rules if he left none
It is shared out equally between all the other co-owners
It reverts to the State because the co-owner no longer exists
questions.explanation: A tenant in common's share forms part of his estate and passes by will or intestacy. There is no right of survivorship.
questions.common_trap: Applying survivorship to a tenancy in common.

questions.stem: When a joint tenant of registered land dies, what does the surviving joint tenant lodge with the Singapore Land Authority to update the title?
options: A notice of death
A transmission application supported by a grant of probate
A fresh transfer of the deceased's share to the survivor
A caveat against the deceased's estate
questions.explanation: Survivors lodge a notice of death, because the deceased's interest ends automatically. A transmission application with a grant is for a tenant in common's share, which passes into the estate.
questions.common_trap: Treating a joint tenant's death like a tenant in common's death.

questions.stem: Jia Wei and her brother own their flat as joint tenants. Jia Wei signs a declaration to sever the joint tenancy and posts a copy to her brother by registered post, but she never registers it. She then dies. Who owns the flat?
options: Jia Wei's estate as to a half share, since her declaration was served on him
The brother and Jia Wei's estate in equal shares, from the day he received the post
The brother alone, since the unregistered declaration did not sever the tenancy
Jia Wei's heirs alone, because she signed the declaration before she died
questions.explanation: For registered land, severance by unilateral declaration needs an approved-form declaration, proper service and registration. As it was not registered, the joint tenancy continued and survivorship applied.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a signed and served notice alone severs the tenancy.

questions.stem: Which event severs a joint tenancy of a private flat?
options: One joint tenant makes a will leaving his share to a nephew
One joint tenant moves out and stops living in the flat
One joint tenant gets married to a person who is not a co-owner
The joint tenants agree in writing to hold as tenants in common
questions.explanation: Severance can occur by mutual agreement, by a course of dealing, or by an act that disposes of a joint tenant's own share. A will only speaks on death and so cannot sever; moving out and marriage also do not sever.
questions.common_trap: Believing a will, or moving out, can sever a joint tenancy.

questions.stem: Raj and Mei Ling hold a shophouse as joint tenants. Raj is adjudged bankrupt. What is the effect on the joint tenancy?
options: It continues, because only Mei Ling's consent can sever it
It is severed, and Raj's share vests in the Official Assignee
It ends, and the Official Assignee takes the whole shophouse
It continues until Raj and Mei Ling sign a new agreement
questions.explanation: Bankruptcy operates on the bankrupt's own share and severs the joint tenancy. The Official Assignee takes Raj's share only, not Mei Ling's.
questions.common_trap: Assuming a creditor or trustee in bankruptcy can reach the whole property of a joint tenancy.

questions.stem: Which unity must be present in a tenancy in common?
options: Unity of interest, meaning every owner holds an equal share
Unity of title, meaning all owners must derive title from the same document
Unity of possession, meaning each owner is entitled to enjoy the whole land
Unity of time, meaning all owners must acquire title at the same moment
questions.explanation: A tenancy in common needs only unity of possession, so no co-owner can claim a physical part as his alone. The other three unities may be absent.
questions.common_trap: Thinking tenants in common need the same four unities as joint tenants.

questions.stem: Farhan holds a 40% undivided share in a private flat as a tenant in common. Which statement is correct?
options: He may sell or mortgage his share without the others' consent
He may sell his share only if all the other co-owners agree
He can claim sole possession of 40% of the rooms in the flat
His share must pass to the other co-owners when he dies
questions.explanation: A tenant in common owns a distinct, undivided share that can be sold, mortgaged or left by will. The land stays undivided physically, and survivorship does not apply.
questions.common_trap: Confusing an undivided share with a divided physical portion.

questions.stem: Farhan contributes 60% and Raj 40% of the purchase price of a private flat. Farhan wants his share to pass to his wife on his death. Which form of holding suits him best?
options: Joint tenancy, since they bought on the same day and from the same seller
Joint tenancy, so that his wife takes his share by survivorship
Tenancy in common in equal shares, so that each has the same entitlement
Tenancy in common in 60:40 shares, so his share passes under his will
questions.explanation: A tenancy in common lets each co-owner hold shares in line with contributions and leave their share by will. Joint tenancy would pass his share to Raj by survivorship.
questions.common_trap: Choosing joint tenancy without realising survivorship benefits the other co-owner.

sections.title: Restrictions on Capacity to Hold Land

questions.stem: For the purpose of holding land in Singapore, a person is treated as a minor until reaching which age?
options: 18 years
19 years
25 years
21 years
questions.explanation: The age of majority in Singapore is 21, so anyone below 21 is a minor and cannot hold land absolutely in his or her own right.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the age of majority is 18 as in many other countries.

questions.stem: Mr Ong buys a condominium unit as a gift for his 15-year-old daughter, Hui Min, and wants her to be the owner. How is the legal title usually held?
options: In Hui Min's sole name, with her school principal signing documents for her
In the name of the Public Guardian until Hui Min turns 18
By trustees, such as her parents, on trust for her until she turns 21
By the Housing and Development Board until Hui Min completes her studies
questions.explanation: A minor can have the beneficial interest, but the legal title is held by trustees on her behalf. The trust ends when she reaches 21.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a minor can be the registered proprietor if an adult signs on the minor's behalf.

questions.stem: Mr Rahim, aged 78, has mild memory lapses. His nephew says Mr Rahim cannot be allowed to sell his flat. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2008, what is the starting position?
options: He is presumed to lack capacity because he is over 75 years old
He is presumed to have capacity unless shown otherwise
He is presumed to lack capacity until a doctor certifies otherwise
His nephew may decide for him once memory lapses are noticed
questions.explanation: The first principle of the Act is that an adult is presumed to have capacity. Age or a diagnosis alone does not remove that presumption.
questions.common_trap: Treating old age or memory lapses as proof of incapacity.

questions.stem: Jia Wei, who fully understands the transaction, sells his shophouse unit to a friend for 20% below valuation. His brother argues that this proves Jia Wei lacks mental capacity. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2008, is the brother right?
options: Yes, because nobody with capacity would accept a price below valuation
No, an unwise decision alone does not show a lack of capacity
Yes, because any sale made below valuation is automatically voidable
No, but only if the friend buying the unit is related to Jia Wei
questions.explanation: One of the Act's principles is that a person is not treated as unable to decide merely because the decision is unwise. The test looks at the ability to decide, not the quality of the outcome.
questions.common_trap: Equating a poor bargain with a lack of mental capacity.

questions.stem: Madam Chua can explain the terms of the proposed sale of her flat and why she chose the buyer, but she needs reminders of the details after an hour. What is the effect of this under the Mental Capacity Act 2008?
options: Short retention alone does not show that she is unable to decide
She lacks capacity because she cannot retain the details for long
She lacks capacity unless she signs the contract within the hour
She keeps capacity only if a deputy attends to remind her
questions.explanation: The ability to retain information for a short period is enough; short retention alone does not show incapacity. The test also asks whether she can understand, weigh and communicate her decision.
questions.common_trap: Believing the person must remember every detail indefinitely to have capacity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a deputy with a donee under a Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA)?
options: A deputy is chosen by the donor beforehand, but a donee is appointed by the court after capacity is lost
Both are appointed by the Public Guardian after the family files an application for them
Both are chosen by the person before losing capacity, though a deputy has wider powers
A deputy is appointed by the court after capacity is lost, but a donee is chosen by the donor beforehand
questions.explanation: An LPA is the donor's own advance choice of donee, made while he has capacity. A deputy is a court appointment, made when the person has already lost capacity and no LPA is in place.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up who appoints the decision-maker and when.

questions.stem: A donee under an LPA who has been given powers only over property and affairs wants to consent to major surgery for the donor. What is the position?
options: He can, because property powers extend to every decision the donor could make
He can, if the surgeon recommends the operation in writing
He cannot, unless the LPA also grants personal welfare powers
He cannot, because a donee is never allowed to make healthcare decisions
questions.explanation: An LPA can cover property and affairs, personal welfare, or both. Healthcare decisions fall within personal welfare, so they must be expressly granted.
questions.common_trap: Assuming one LPA automatically covers every kind of decision.

questions.stem: Madam Goh, 62 and in good health, fears she may develop dementia. She wants her daughter to be able to sell her condominium unit for her care costs if that happens. What is the best step to take now?
options: Sign an ordinary power of attorney, which would continue after she loses capacity
Wait for a diagnosis, then ask the Land Titles Registry to appoint her daughter
Make an LPA now, naming her daughter as the donee
Wait for a diagnosis, then transfer the unit into her daughter's name
questions.explanation: An LPA is designed to survive the donor's loss of capacity, but it can only be made while the donor still has capacity. An ordinary power of attorney would generally stop being effective once she loses capacity.
questions.common_trap: Believing an ordinary power of attorney remains valid after the donor loses mental capacity.

questions.stem: Mr Wee is the sole director and shareholder of Wee Holdings Pte Ltd, which owns a shophouse unit. Mr Wee dies. Who owns the shophouse unit?
options: Mr Wee's estate, because he was the only shareholder of the company
The company, as a separate legal person that continues to exist
The Registrar of Companies, until a new director is appointed
Mr Wee's beneficiaries directly, who take it as joint tenants
questions.explanation: A company has its own legal personality and can hold land in its own name. The death of its only director does not move the company's assets; only the shares form part of Mr Wee's estate.
questions.common_trap: Treating the owner of all the shares as the owner of the company's property.

questions.stem: A club or association must be registered under the Societies Act if it has how many members or more?
options: 10 members
5 members
7 members
20 members
questions.explanation: The Societies Act defines a society as a club, company, partnership or association of 10 or more persons, and such a body must be registered unless exempted.
questions.common_trap: Recalling the threshold as 5 or 20 members.

questions.stem: The Bukit Gombak Chess Society, a registered society, wants to buy a small clubhouse unit. In whose name can the title be registered?
options: The society's own registered name, since it can sue and be sued in that name
The names of all its members as joint tenants
The name of the Registrar of Societies as custodian
The names of trustees who hold the unit for the society
questions.explanation: A registered society can sue and be sued in its name but cannot hold land itself, so land is held through trustees. The right to sue does not give it the capacity to own land.
questions.common_trap: Reasoning that the power to sue in its own name means the society can also be the registered owner.

questions.stem: Tan and Kaur run a design firm as a general partnership and buy an office unit for the business. How should the title be registered?
options: In the firm's business name, because the firm is a separate legal person
In Tan's name alone as absolute owner, because he is the senior partner
In the name of ACRA, which holds it as nominee for the firm
In their names as individuals, on trust for the partnership
questions.explanation: A general partnership has no separate legal personality, so land must be held by the partners as individuals on trust for the firm. Registering a business name does not change this.
questions.common_trap: Believing registration of the business name gives the partnership a legal identity separate from its partners.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares a limited liability partnership (LLP) with a general partnership regarding the holding of land?
options: Both can hold land in the firm's name once they are registered with ACRA
Neither of them can hold land, so both must use trustees as owners
An LLP can hold land in its own name, but a general partnership cannot
A general partnership can, but an LLP must use its partners as trustees
questions.explanation: An LLP is a body corporate with its own legal personality and can buy and hold land in its own name. A general partnership has no such personality.
questions.common_trap: Assuming every registered business structure has separate legal personality.

questions.stem: Rani runs a bakery under the registered business name Rani's Treats and buys a shop unit for it. Whose name appears on the title?
options: Rani's Treats, because that name is registered with ACRA
Rani's own name, as a business name is not a separate person
The bakery's employees, who act as trustees for the business
Rani's Treats Pte Ltd, formed automatically on registration of the name
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship is the owner personally. Registering a business name does not create a separate legal person.
questions.common_trap: Thinking a registered business name creates a separate legal entity.

questions.stem: A couple who have held Singapore permanent resident status for eight years want to buy a terrace house. Under the Residential Property Act, how are they classified?
options: As foreign persons, since only citizens and Singapore entities are excluded
As non-foreign persons, because they have lived here for over five years
As non-foreign persons, because permanent residents rank as citizens for land
As foreign persons only if they hold passports of certain restricted countries
questions.explanation: A foreign person is anyone who is not a Singapore citizen, Singapore company, Singapore LLP or Singapore society. Permanent residents are therefore foreign persons for this Act.
questions.common_trap: Assuming permanent residents are treated like citizens under the Residential Property Act.

questions.stem: Without any special approval, which purchase is a foreign person able to make?
options: A unit in a private condominium development
A 99-year leasehold semi-detached house
A vacant plot of residential land
A townhouse in a strata landed project that is not an approved condominium
questions.explanation: Apartments and condominium units are non-restricted. Landed houses, vacant residential land and strata landed houses outside approved condominium developments are restricted and need approval.
questions.common_trap: Treating any strata-titled home as non-restricted.

questions.stem: Farhan, a foreigner, takes a 3-year lease of a bungalow with an option to renew for a further 3 years. Is approval needed under the Residential Property Act?
options: Yes, because any lease of landed property is a restricted dealing
Yes, because the renewal option makes the lease longer than 5 years
No, but only if he chooses not to exercise the renewal option
No, as the total term including the renewal option is within 7 years
questions.explanation: A leasehold of landed residential property for up to 7 years, counting any renewal option, is non-restricted. Approval would be needed once the total could exceed 7 years.
questions.common_trap: Counting only the initial term and ignoring the renewal option.

questions.stem: How is a foreign person's ability to buy an HDB flat or an Executive Condominium unit decided?
options: By the Land Dealings Approval Unit, using the same test as for landed property
By the Controller of Residential Property, once an application fee is paid
By HDB's own eligibility rules, not by LDAU approval under the Act
By URA, which sets a quota of foreign buyers for each project
questions.explanation: HDB flats and Executive Condominium units are outside the LDAU approval regime and follow HDB's eligibility conditions instead.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the Residential Property Act covers every type of housing.

questions.stem: When assessing a permanent resident's application to buy a landed house, which factor does the Singapore Land Authority look at?
options: Whether he can show a higher income than the average Singapore citizen buyer does
Whether he has been a PR for five years or more and shows exceptional economic contribution
Whether he has already sold all of the property that he holds overseas by then
Whether he agrees to pay the Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty upfront in cash form
questions.explanation: Applications are judged case by case. SLA expects permanent residency of at least five years together with an exceptional economic contribution.
questions.common_trap: Believing that being able to pay, or paying extra stamp duty, is enough for approval.

questions.stem: Wei Hong, a permanent resident, is approved to buy a bungalow. After moving in, he rents the basement room to a student. What is the position?
options: It is allowed, as long as the rent is below the market rate
It breaches the owner-occupation condition, which bars letting any part
It is allowed, because the ban applies only to letting the whole house
It is allowed once he has lived in the house for two years
questions.explanation: Approved purchases may be used only as a dwelling for the owner and family. Letting out even part of the house is prohibited.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the ban applies only if the entire property is let.

questions.stem: A foreign person is approved to buy a completed terrace house. For how long must he hold the property before he is allowed to sell it?
options: Five years from legal completion
Two years from legal completion
Three years from legal completion
Seven years from legal completion
questions.explanation: One of the approval conditions is a five-year non-disposal period, running from legal completion (or, for a property still under construction, from the earlier of TOP or CSC).
questions.common_trap: Mixing this period up with the 2-year disposal deadline after loss of PR status.

questions.stem: Priya, approved to buy a bungalow as a permanent resident, gives up her permanent resident status and does not become a citizen. By when must she sell the property?
options: Within 6 months of losing her PR status
Within 1 year of losing her PR status
Within 5 years of losing her PR status
Within 2 years of losing her PR status
questions.explanation: A person who stops being a permanent resident, without becoming a citizen, may not keep restricted property and must sell within 2 years. Failing to do so is an offence.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the 2-year deadline with the 5-year period applicable to inheritance.

questions.stem: Madam Lim, a Singapore citizen, died on 10 March 2026 leaving a bungalow to her son, a foreign person who has no approval to keep it. By what date must the personal representatives dispose of his interest?
options: 10 March 2027, which is 1 year from the date of death
10 March 2028, which is 2 years from the date of death
10 March 2031, which is 5 years from the date of death
10 March 2036, which is 10 years from the date of death
questions.explanation: Where a foreign beneficiary cannot acquire the restricted property, the personal representatives have 5 years from the date of death to dispose of the interest, with extensions available on application.
questions.common_trap: Applying the 2-year rule for loss of PR status to inherited property.

questions.stem: Who must obtain a Qualifying Certificate under the Residential Property Act?
options: A foreigner who buys a private condominium unit to live in as his own home
A Singapore citizen who buys a bungalow as a long-term investment
A foreign developer buying restricted residential land to build homes for sale
A foreign investor who buys an HDB shophouse for rental income
questions.explanation: The Qualifying Certificate regime applies to housing developers who are foreign (or Singapore entities without a clearance certificate) and who intend to build homes for sale on restricted land.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the certificate is a personal permit for any foreign homebuyer.

questions.stem: A foreign developer's Qualifying Certificate is issued on 1 June 2026. It obtains TOP on 30 September 2030. What is the latest date by which it must sell all the units?
options: 1 June 2033, which is 7 years after the certificate was issued
30 September 2032, which is 2 years after TOP
30 September 2031, which is 1 year after TOP
30 September 2035, which is 5 years after TOP
questions.explanation: The developer must complete within 5 years of the certificate and sell all units within 2 years after TOP or CSC, whichever is earlier. The 7-year figure is only the outer limit if TOP comes at the last moment.
questions.common_trap: Treating 7 years from the date of the certificate as a fixed deadline.

questions.stem: A foreign developer buys a residential site for S$180 million and obtains a Qualifying Certificate. What is the minimum banker's guarantee it must provide?
options: S$18 million
S$9 million
S$36 million
S$54 million
questions.explanation: The banker's guarantee must be at least 10% of the land purchase price, so 10% of S$180 million is S$18 million. It can be forfeited if the conditions are not met.
questions.common_trap: Using the wrong percentage of the land price.

questions.stem: A foreign developer cannot sell all its units within the 2-year period and applies for a time extension. What is the extension charge for the first year, as a percentage of the land purchase price?
questions.explanation: The extension charge is 8% of the land price for the first year, 16% for the second and 24% for the third year onwards, taking the number of unsold units into account.
questions.common_trap: Confusing the first-year charge with the 10% banker's guarantee.

questions.stem: A foreign owner rented out a restricted residential property in breach of the conditions and earned S$24,000 in rent over the period of breach. What is the maximum financial penalty under the Residential Property Act?
options: S$10,000, which is the fixed penalty for unauthorised rental
S$24,000, which is equal to the rent earned
S$200,000, which is the maximum fine for unauthorised disposal
S$72,000, which is three times the rent earned
questions.explanation: The financial penalty can be up to three times the rental income earned, or S$10,000, whichever is higher. Three times S$24,000 is S$72,000.
questions.common_trap: Using the S$10,000 figure without comparing it with three times the rent.

questions.stem: Which pairing of land-use plan and review cycle is correct?
options: The Concept Plan is reviewed about every 5 years, and the Master Plan about every 10 years
Both plans are reviewed about every 10 years
Both plans are reviewed about every 5 years
The Concept Plan is reviewed about every 10 years, and the Master Plan about every 5 years
questions.explanation: The Concept Plan (now presented by URA as the Long-Term Plan) looks 50 years ahead and is reviewed about every 10 years. The Master Plan turns it into detailed plans for the next 10 to 15 years and is reviewed every 5 years.
questions.common_trap: Swapping the two review cycles.

questions.stem: Hui Min is considering a site and wants to find out its permitted land use and the intensity allowed by the Government. Which document should she check?
options: The Concept Plan, which shows the zone and plot ratio of each lot
The Government Land Sales programme, which lists approved uses of private land
The Master Plan, which sets zoning and gross plot ratio for each parcel
The Land Titles Register, which states the permitted plot ratio
questions.explanation: The Master Plan is the statutory plan showing land use zones and intensities, such as gross plot ratio, for each parcel. The Concept Plan is only strategic and does not set lot-level controls.
questions.common_trap: Looking to the Concept Plan for detailed lot-level controls.

questions.stem: Which statement about the current Master Plan is correct?
options: Master Plan 2025 was gazetted in 2019 and guides development for 40 to 50 years
Master Plan 2025 was gazetted on 1 December 2025 for the next 10 to 15 years
Master Plan 2025 is still only a draft exhibited to the public, with no legal effect
Master Plan 2025 replaced the Concept Plan and will be reviewed every 10 years
questions.explanation: URA gazetted Master Plan 2025 on 1 December 2025, so it is the statutory plan guiding development over the next 10 to 15 years. The much longer 50-year horizon belongs to the Long-Term Plan, which was formerly called the Concept Plan.
questions.common_trap: Using the older Master Plan 2019 as the current plan.

questions.stem: How does the Government Land Sales (GLS) programme make state land available for private development?
options: Sites are allocated to developers by ballot at a fixed price
Sites are put up for tender, on a Confirmed List or a Reserve List
Sites are transferred by URA to developers on request, with no tender
Sites are sold only to buyers who first obtain a Qualifying Certificate
questions.explanation: GLS releases land by tender. Confirmed List sites are released for tender on a fixed timeline, while Reserve List sites are released when a developer commits to bid at least a minimum price.
questions.common_trap: Thinking GLS land is allocated administratively rather than by tender.

questions.stem: A site is zoned Residential with Commercial at 1st Storey. What does this mean?
options: Housing is the main use, and commercial uses are permitted only on the first storey
Commercial uses are permitted on any floor, and housing is limited to the first storey
Housing and commercial uses are each allowed on up to 50% of the GFA
Housing is allowed only if the developer also builds a hotel
questions.explanation: This zone is mainly for housing, with commercial uses such as shops allowed only on the ground floor. It is narrower than Commercial & Residential or White zones.
questions.common_trap: Mixing it up with Commercial & Residential, which is a wider mixed zone.

questions.stem: What is the main feature of a site zoned White in the Master Plan?
options: It is reserved for open space and parks, so it cannot carry any buildings at all
It allows only industrial and warehouse uses, with no residential component
It allows only residential use, but at a higher plot ratio than other zones
It allows mixed uses such as commercial, hotel and residential, alone or combined
questions.explanation: A White zone gives flexibility, so the developer may choose among compatible uses, such as commercial, hotel, residential and sports and recreation, or combine them.
questions.common_trap: Reading White as meaning no development.

questions.stem: How does a Business 2 (B2) zone differ from a Business 1 (B1) zone?
options: B2 allows only residential uses, while B1 allows industrial uses
B1 allows heavy polluting industry, while B2 allows only light industry
B2 allows general industry in addition to the uses allowed in B1
B1 and B2 are identical, but B2 has a higher plot ratio
questions.explanation: B1 is for clean, low-impact industry and related uses. B2 permits everything B1 allows and also general industrial uses that may cause more disamenity.
questions.common_trap: Assuming B1 is the heavier category.

questions.stem: How does a Business Park-White zone differ from a Business Park zone?
options: Business Park-White bans all White uses, which a Business Park zone allows
Business Park-White allows only residential use, with no business park use
Business Park-White allows a bigger share of White uses, set by location
Business Park-White places no limit on White uses at any location at all
questions.explanation: In a Business Park zone, White uses are capped at 15% of the overall GFA. A Business Park-White zone allows more than that, with the share depending on factors such as nearness to MRT stations.
questions.common_trap: Believing White zones have no cap on White uses.

questions.stem: How is plot ratio defined?
options: The ratio of site area to gross floor area
The ratio of gross floor area to site area
The ratio of net lettable area to gross floor area
The ratio of building footprint to site area
questions.explanation: Plot ratio is gross floor area divided by site area. It controls the total quantum of floor space allowed on a site.
questions.common_trap: Confusing plot ratio with site coverage, which relates to the building footprint.

questions.stem: A developer buys a site of 2,500 sq m zoned with a gross plot ratio (GPR) of 2.8. What is the maximum GFA allowed?
options: 892 sq m
questions.explanation: Maximum GFA equals site area multiplied by GPR, so 2,500 x 2.8 is 7,000 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Dividing by the plot ratio instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: An approved scheme allows 9,600 sq m of GFA at a GPR of 1.6. What is the site area?
questions.explanation: Site area equals GFA divided by plot ratio, so 9,600 divided by 1.6 is 6,000 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Multiplying the GFA by the plot ratio instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A building has 12,000 sq m of GFA on a site of 4,000 sq m. What is its plot ratio?
questions.explanation: Plot ratio is GFA divided by site area, and 12,000 divided by 4,000 is 3.0.
questions.common_trap: Inverting the fraction and arriving at 0.33.

questions.stem: A 5,000 sq m site has a GPR of 2.1. The existing building has 7,800 sq m of GFA. How much additional GFA can still be built, if the plot ratio is the only limit?
questions.explanation: The maximum GFA is 5,000 x 2.1, which is 10,500 sq m. Deducting the existing 7,800 sq m leaves 2,700 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Stopping at the maximum GFA and forgetting to deduct the GFA already built.

questions.stem: A developer has a 3,000 sq m residential site with a GPR of 1.4. If the average unit has 105 sq m of GFA, what is the largest number of units that fits within the plot ratio?
options: 29 units
40 units
44 units
126 units
questions.explanation: The maximum GFA is 3,000 x 1.4 = 4,200 sq m, and 4,200 divided by 105 gives 40 units.
questions.common_trap: Using site area instead of allowable GFA to divide by unit size.

questions.stem: How is the gross floor area of a building generally measured?
options: Covered floor space measured to the middle of external walls, excluding voids
Usable floor space measured from the inside face of walls, excluding all wall thickness
Footprint of the building at ground level multiplied by its number of storeys
Floor space that can be let to tenants, excluding all common areas
questions.explanation: URA defines GFA as the total covered floor space, measured to the middle of external walls and excluding voids. It counts regardless of whether the space is usable or lettable.
questions.common_trap: Treating GFA as the same as usable or lettable area.

questions.stem: A mall tenant sets up an uncovered outdoor dining deck for its restaurant. For GFA purposes, how is the deck treated?
options: It counts as GFA, because uncovered areas used commercially are deemed GFA
It is excluded from GFA because it has no roof over it
It is excluded from GFA because it is not enclosed by any walls
It counts only if the deck exceeds 20% of the mall's total GFA
questions.explanation: GFA covers covered floor areas as well as uncovered areas used for commercial purposes. Not having a roof does not exempt a commercial area.
questions.common_trap: Assuming that only covered space counts as GFA.

questions.stem: How are bay windows treated for GFA purposes in new development applications since 1 January 2009?
options: They are exempt if they are cantilevered and raised 500 mm above the floor
They are exempt if the projection from the wall is below 600 mm
They count as GFA in landed housing only, but not in condominiums
They count as GFA, whatever their size or materials
questions.explanation: From 1 January 2009 bay windows are no longer exempt from GFA. This applies to development types generally, whatever their size.
questions.common_trap: Believing a design feature such as being cantilevered gives GFA exemption.

questions.stem: Since 12 January 2013, how are private enclosed spaces and private roof terraces in new non-landed residential developments treated?
options: They are fully exempt from GFA as semi-outdoor spaces
They are exempt provided they are on the top floor
They count towards GFA, like balconies
They are exempt only for Executive Condominiums
questions.explanation: URA counts private enclosed spaces and private roof terraces approved on or after 12 January 2013 as GFA, as balconies already are. They may still qualify as capped bonus GFA under the Balcony Incentive Scheme, and earlier approvals stayed under the old rules.
questions.common_trap: Thinking semi-outdoor spaces remain exempt from GFA.

questions.stem: Under the harmonised floor area definitions of URA and SLA, how are voids (such as double-volume spaces) treated in a unit's strata area?
options: All voids are excluded from the unit's strata area
Voids are included in strata area but excluded from GFA
Only double-volume voids are included in the strata area
Voids are included only if the buyer pays an extra charge
questions.explanation: Under the harmonised definitions, all voids are excluded from strata area, and floor areas are measured to the middle of the wall. Older sales material may still quote strata areas that included voids, so buyers should read the area breakdown.
questions.common_trap: Relying on the older practice where void space could be included in the quoted strata area.

questions.stem: How does net lettable area differ from gross floor area?
options: NLA is the covered floor space of the building, with external wall thickness
NLA is the space that can be let to tenants, without common areas
NLA is always larger than the gross floor area of the same building
NLA includes lift lobbies and staircases but leaves out the tenants' space
questions.explanation: NLA is the lettable space within a tenancy, excluding common areas such as corridors and lobbies. GFA is a planning measure that includes covered areas of the building.
questions.common_trap: Treating NLA and GFA as interchangeable.

questions.stem: An office building has 6,000 sq m of GFA, of which 18% is made up of common and service areas that cannot be let. What is the net lettable area?
questions.explanation: The non-lettable area is 18% of 6,000, which is 1,080 sq m. Deducting it leaves 4,920 sq m of lettable space.
questions.common_trap: Reporting the deducted portion instead of what remains.

questions.stem: What does a street block plan provide?
options: A list of the tenants who are allowed in each shophouse of the street
The land betterment charge that is payable on each lot in the street
The approved tender price for state land in the street block concerned
Detailed guidance on setbacks and storey and building heights in the area
questions.explanation: Street block plans set out urban design controls like setbacks and heights so that buildings in a street block fit together.
questions.common_trap: Seeing it as a financial or tenancy document.

questions.stem: Outside a Good Class Bungalow area, what is the minimum plot size for a new bungalow (detached house)?
options: 200 sq m
300 sq m
400 sq m
questions.explanation: A new bungalow outside a Good Class Bungalow area needs a plot of at least 400 sq m and a width of at least 10 m. The 1,400 sq m figure applies to Good Class Bungalows.
questions.common_trap: Using the GCB size for ordinary bungalows.

questions.stem: Mr Teo owns a 1,250 sq m plot inside a Good Class Bungalow area and wants to rebuild. What is the key issue under URA's guidelines?
options: There is no issue, because the minimum is 1,000 sq m in every landed area
He must first amalgamate land to reach 4,000 sq m, as for condominiums
A GCB plot generally needs 1,400 sq m, so his plot is below the minimum
The only requirement is a minimum plot width of 8 m, with no area limit
questions.explanation: Bungalows in a Good Class Bungalow area generally need a plot of at least 1,400 sq m and a width of 18.5 m. URA may consider in-fill plots already below that size, but an ordinary rebuild does not get the lower limit.
questions.common_trap: Applying the lower ordinary bungalow limit to GCB plots.

questions.stem: What is the minimum plot size for a semi-detached house of the common side-to-side type?
options: 80 sq m
200 sq m
150 sq m
400 sq m
questions.explanation: A side-to-side semi-detached house needs at least 200 sq m of land and 8 m width. Terrace houses can be smaller and bungalows larger.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the minimum for terraces with that for semi-detached houses.

questions.stem: A Good Class Bungalow must keep what setback from its side and rear boundaries, compared with a non-GCB bungalow?
options: 3 m, compared with 2 m
2 m, compared with 3 m
1 m, compared with 2 m
7.5 m, compared with 3 m
questions.explanation: A Good Class Bungalow must be set back 3 m at the sides and rear, whereas other detached houses need 2 m. The front setback is 7.5 m on a Category 3 to 5 road.
questions.common_trap: Assuming the 7.5 m front setback applies to the sides as well.

questions.stem: How is the number of storeys of a landed house controlled in landed housing estates?
options: There is no storey control for landed houses, only a plot ratio limit
By a uniform limit of 5 storeys that applies to all landed houses
By the developer's own choice, as long as the height is below 10 m
By envelope control, which sets a 2-storey or 3-storey envelope for the estate
questions.explanation: Landed housing follows envelope control, which limits houses to 2 or 3 storeys depending on the estate, with an attic allowed within the envelope.
questions.common_trap: Assuming landed houses may use the same storey limits as flats.

questions.stem: A non-GCB bungalow plot is 500 sq m. Under URA's current site coverage rules, what is the maximum bulk of the house, measured up to the external facade (the 40% sub-control)?
options: 150 sq m
225 sq m
250 sq m
200 sq m
questions.explanation: The sub-control for bungalows is 40% of the plot, and 40% of 500 sq m is 200 sq m. The overall limit is 50%, or 250 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Using the overall 50% figure for the sub-control.

questions.stem: What is the minimum site area for a condominium development, and how does it compare with flats?
options: 1,000 sq m for condominiums, compared with 4,000 sq m for flats
4,000 sq m for both condominiums and flats
4,000 sq m for condominiums, compared with 1,000 sq m for flats
400 sq m for condominiums, compared with 100 sq m for flats
questions.explanation: A condominium needs at least 0.4 ha (4,000 sq m) because it must have communal and recreational facilities. Flats need at least 1,000 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Mixing up the figures for flats and condominiums.

questions.stem: A developer assembles a 3,200 sq m residential site and wants to build a condominium. What is the likely outcome?
options: A condominium is allowed, because the minimum site area is 3,000 sq m
A condominium is not allowed, but flats may be, as the site exceeds 1,000 sq m
Neither is allowed, because both need a site of at least 4,000 sq m
A condominium is allowed if the project has fewer than 100 units
questions.explanation: Condominium status requires at least 4,000 sq m of net site area. The site is large enough for flats, which need at least 1,000 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Believing the number of units can substitute for minimum site area.

questions.stem: Under URA's default controls for residential-only sites, what is the maximum number of storeys for a flat or condominium site with a GPR of 1.4?
options: 5 storeys
4 storeys
8 storeys
12 storeys
questions.explanation: For a residential-only site, URA's storey control rises with GPR. A GPR of 1.4 is linked to 5 storeys, 1.6 to 12 and 2.1 to 24, subject to local controls.
questions.common_trap: Assuming storey limits do not vary with the plot ratio.

questions.stem: In a single-user Business 1 or Business 2 industrial development, what is the use quantum control?
options: At least 60% of GFA must be for industrial use, and up to 40% may be ancillary uses
At least 40% of GFA must be for industrial use, and up to 60% may be ancillary uses
100% of GFA must be industrial, with no ancillary use allowed
At least 60% must be for offices, and up to 40% for industry
questions.explanation: B1 and B2 developments need at least 60% of GFA for industrial use. The rest, up to 40%, may be ancillary, such as ancillary offices.
questions.common_trap: Reversing the 60:40 split.

questions.stem: A single-user B2 industrial development has 8,000 sq m of GFA. What is the maximum GFA that can be ancillary uses?
questions.explanation: Ancillary uses are capped at 40% of GFA, so 40% of 8,000 is 3,200 sq m. At least 4,800 sq m must be used for industrial purposes.
questions.common_trap: Taking the 60% industrial figure as the ancillary cap.

questions.stem: A Business Park (non-White) development has a total GFA of 20,000 sq m. What is the maximum GFA that can be allowed for White uses?
questions.explanation: In a Business Park zone, White uses are capped at 15% of the proposed GFA, and 15% of 20,000 is 3,000 sq m.
questions.common_trap: Applying the 40% ancillary limit to White uses.

questions.stem: Mei Ling owns a conserved shophouse in the Joo Chiat conservation area and plans to repaint the facade. Repainting a building is generally on URA's exemption list. What is the position here?
options: The exemption applies, as repainting never needs permission anywhere in Singapore
The exemption does not apply, as exemptions exclude conservation areas
The exemption applies if the owner first informs the neighbouring owners
The exemption applies only if the new paint colour chosen is white
questions.explanation: The exemption list excludes national monuments, conservation buildings and sites in conservation areas, where specific guidelines must be followed. Owners should check with URA first.
questions.common_trap: Applying the general exemption to conserved buildings.

questions.stem: How many use classes are there under the Planning (Use Classes) Rules, after the 2016 revision?
questions.explanation: The 2016 revision added Commercial School as the 18th class, separating it from Office.
questions.common_trap: Remembering an older, smaller number of classes.

questions.stem: A restaurant in a shophouse changes hands and the new operator opens a different restaurant in the same premises, with no works. Is planning permission needed for the change of use?
options: No, as a change within the same use class is not treated as development
Yes, because every change of operator counts as a change of use
Yes, because opening a new restaurant always needs written permission
No, because a change of use never needs any kind of permission
questions.explanation: URA states there is no need to apply for planning approval for a change from one use to another within the same Use Class, unless special planning conditions apply. Permission is needed when the use moves to a different class unless exempted.
questions.common_trap: Believing any change of tenant or business needs permission.

questions.stem: A unit approved for office use in a commercial building is to be turned into a tuition centre that counts as a commercial school. Is planning permission needed?
options: No, because both are used for business purposes
No, because Commercial School remains part of the Office class
Yes, but only if the unit is larger than 200 sq m
Yes, because Commercial School is a separate use class from Office
questions.explanation: URA treats a commercial school as a use separate from office, so changing between them is a change of use that needs a change of use application or lodgment. Both being business uses does not exempt it.
questions.common_trap: Assuming schools are still counted within the Office class.

questions.stem: What does 'development' mean for the purpose of requiring planning permission?
options: Only the construction of a brand-new building from the ground up
Only the sale or transfer of land from one owner to a new owner
Building or other operations on land, or a material change in its use
Only building works costing more than a fixed amount of money
questions.explanation: Development covers building, engineering and other operations as well as material changes of use. Planning permission is generally required for it, unless exempted or authorised.
questions.common_trap: Thinking development means new construction only.

questions.stem: Under URA's Plan Lodgment scheme, what is the role of the Qualified Person (QP)?
options: To grant planning permission on URA's behalf for the owner's proposal
To pay the development charge to the State on behalf of the owner
To declare that the proposal fully complies, so declared works are deemed authorised
To certify to the buyer that the land is free from any caveats
questions.explanation: Under the scheme, the QP self-declares compliance, and proposals properly declared are treated as authorised without a separate application. URA can reject a lodgment if the declaration is not in order.
questions.common_trap: Thinking the QP replaces URA as the approving authority.

questions.stem: How long does a Provisional Permission last, and how long does a Written Permission last, before lapsing without extension?
options: Provisional Permission lapses after 2 years, and Written Permission lapses after 6 months
Provisional Permission lapses after 6 months, and Written Permission lapses after 2 years
Both lapse after 12 months
Both remain valid indefinitely once granted
questions.explanation: A Provisional Permission lapses 6 months after grant, and a Written Permission 2 years after grant. Extensions can be applied for about 2 months before expiry.
questions.common_trap: Swapping the two periods.

questions.stem: What is a development charge?
options: A charge to the State when permission raises land value; rates are revised half-yearly
A fee paid to URA for filing any development application, revised yearly
A tax on rental income from developed properties, collected by IRAS
A levy on foreign developers who fail to sell their units in time
questions.explanation: Development charge is the levy on the enhancement in land value when the State approves a higher-value development proposal. DC rates are reviewed half-yearly in consultation with the Chief Valuer.
questions.common_trap: Mistaking it for a filing fee or an income tax.

questions.stem: Estate agency work in Singapore is regulated mainly under which Act, and who polices it?
options: The Estate Agents Act 2010, policed by the Singapore Land Authority
The Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act 1965, policed by the Council for Estate Agencies
The Estate Agents Act 2010, policed by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
The Estate Agents Act 2010, policed by the Council for Estate Agencies
questions.explanation: Estate agency work falls under the Estate Agents Act 2010 (EAA), which the Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) enforces. It may be carried out only by a licensed estate agent, or by a registered salesperson acting through one.
questions.common_trap: Candidates pick the right Act but pair it with another government body they know from property work, such as SLA or IRAS.

questions.stem: Zhi Wei is registered with CEA under Agency A. He also starts closing deals under the name of Agency B at the same time. Which rule is breached?
options: A registered salesperson can act on behalf of only one estate agent at a time
A salesperson must not act for both sides in the same transaction
A salesperson must hold professional indemnity cover for at least 1 year
A salesperson must complete 16 hours of CPD in each calendar year
questions.explanation: An RES holds a registration through CEA and can be attached to only one EA at any one time. Working for two agencies at once breaches this rule.
questions.common_trap: The dual representation rule sounds similar because two parties are involved, but it is about acting for both sides of one deal, not about two agencies.

questions.stem: Who is eligible to be the Key Executive Officer (KEO) of an estate agent?
options: A sole proprietor, director or partner of the agency who has the valid exam credentials and track record
Any registered salesperson in the agency who has at least 10 years of experience
An administrative manager of the agency, as long as he or she holds the RES examination pass
An external compliance consultant appointed by the agency for its annual audit
questions.explanation: The KEO is the person accountable for corporate compliance and must be a sole proprietor, director or partner. The KEO must also hold valid exam credentials and meet the minimum transaction track record.
questions.common_trap: Seniority or experience tempts candidates to think any veteran salesperson can be KEO, but the position must be an owner-level role.

questions.stem: What minimum track record must a Key Executive Officer have?
options: At least 30 transactions within the last 5 years
At least 30 transactions within the last 3 years
At least 20 transactions within the last 3 years
At least 50 transactions within the last 2 years
questions.explanation: A Key Executive Officer needs a track record of at least 30 transactions over the preceding 3 years. The other route is 3 or more years of experience running a licensed agent's business, alongside a recent exam pass and an owner-level role.
questions.common_trap: Neighbouring numbers (30 in 5 years, 20 in 3 years) look natural, so candidates misremember either the count or the period.

questions.stem: Which statement about the CEA Public Register is correct?
options: Consumers can use it to verify an agent's registration and to view the agent's recent residential transactions
Consumers can use it to verify an agent's registration, but past transaction records are not shown
It is open only to estate agents and CEA officers and is not available to consumers
It lists transaction records of agents but does not confirm whether the agent is currently registered
questions.explanation: The Public Register lets consumers check that an agent has a valid registration, see any disciplinary records, and view the residential transactions the agent facilitated in the last two years and which parties were represented. It is open to the public.
questions.common_trap: The second option is tempting because many candidates assume the register is just a name list with no transaction information.

questions.stem: Jason is 20 years old, holds 5 GCE O-Level passes, has passed the RES examination, has no criminal record and has PII arranged. Which baseline requirement does he fail?
options: The minimum number of GCE O-Level passes
The fit-and-proper test
The professional indemnity insurance requirement
The minimum age requirement of 21
questions.explanation: A salesperson applicant must be at least 21, hold at least four GCE O-Level passes (or an accepted equivalent), have passed the RES examination and be covered by valid PII. Jason meets all of these except the age requirement.
questions.common_trap: Candidates sometimes call any failure a fit-and-proper failure, but age is an administrative requirement and is not part of that test.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of GCE O-Level passes (or approved equivalent) required to register as a salesperson?
questions.explanation: The baseline academic requirement is at least 4 GCE O-Level passes or an approved equivalent. It is an administrative requirement, not a fit-and-proper criterion.
questions.common_trap: Candidates confuse this with the 5 O-Level passes commonly asked in other contexts, or settle for a lower number.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the fit-and-proper test for registration?
options: A conviction involving dishonesty or fraud
Being an undischarged bankrupt
Having at least 4 GCE O-Level passes
A conviction under the Estate Agents Act
questions.explanation: Fit-and-proper looks at character issues such as convictions for dishonesty, fraud or EAA offences and bankruptcy. Age, O-Level passes and the RES exam are administrative requirements and sit outside the test.
questions.common_trap: Because O-Levels are a requirement for registration, candidates assume they belong to the fit-and-proper test as well.

questions.stem: Which of the following would count against an applicant under the fit-and-proper test?
options: Having passed the RES examination only on the second attempt
Having exactly 4 GCE O-Level passes
A civil judgment against the applicant for breach of fiduciary duty
Having PII arranged through the agency's group policy
questions.explanation: Civil judgments for breach of fiduciary duty or fraud are listed as fit-and-proper disqualifiers. The other options are either administrative requirements or normal arrangements.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think only criminal convictions matter, overlooking that civil judgments are also relevant.

questions.stem: Kumar meets every administrative requirement for registration but also holds an active moneylender licence. What is the position?
options: He can register because a moneylender licence is unrelated to estate agency work
He can register but must disclose the licence in writing to the agency's KEO
He cannot register, because a salesperson must not hold a moneylender's licence
He can register but his PII premium must be set at a higher tier
questions.explanation: CEA's registration conditions bar an applicant who holds a moneylender's licence, or who is an employee, director or partner of a licensed moneylender. This is a separate registration condition, not one of the fit-and-proper disqualifiers in the Act.
questions.common_trap: Candidates treat the moneylending licence as a separate industry and assume it is only a disclosure matter, or lump it into the fit-and-proper test.

questions.stem: Which statement about the fit-and-proper test is correct?
options: The minimum age of 21 is one of the fit-and-proper criteria
Age, O-Level passes and the RES exam are administrative requirements and are not part of the test
Passing the RES examination is assessed as part of the fit-and-proper test
Only criminal convictions are considered, never civil judgments
questions.explanation: Age, O-Level passes and the RES exam pass are separate registration requirements and are not part of the fit-and-proper test. The test looks at conduct and integrity such as convictions, civil judgments and bankruptcy.
questions.common_trap: The word 'criteria' makes candidates lump all registration requirements into one test.

questions.stem: Over what period does the annual CPD training cycle run?
options: 1 April to 31 March
1 July to 30 June
12 months starting from the salesperson's registration date
1 January to 31 December
questions.explanation: The CPD cycle is a calendar year, running from 1 January to 31 December.
questions.common_trap: Candidates often assume a financial-year or anniversary-based cycle.

questions.stem: How many total CPD hours must a salesperson complete each year?
options: 16 hours
8 hours
12 hours
20 hours
questions.explanation: A salesperson must complete 16 CPD hours per year, made up of 12 structured hours and 4 self-directed hours.
questions.common_trap: The figure 12 is tempting because it is the structured component, not the total.

questions.stem: How many of the annual CPD hours must be structured hours?
options: 12 hours
4 hours
8 hours
16 hours
questions.explanation: Of the 16 CPD hours, at least 12 must be Structured Learning, and at least 4 are Self-directed Learning.
questions.common_trap: Candidates pick 4 or 16 by mixing up the self-directed portion and the total.

questions.stem: Under the CPD requirements, which type of hours must cover the mandatory prescribed essentials such as AML/CFT and agency ethics?
options: Self-directed hours
Structured hours
Either structured or self-directed hours, as the salesperson prefers
Neither, because these topics are tested only in the RES examination
questions.explanation: Structured Learning includes at least 4 hours of Prescribed Essentials from CEA-accredited courses (Laws, Regulations and Ethics, plus a topic CEA sets each year, which is anti-money laundering for 2026) and at least 8 hours of Professional Competencies. Self-directed hours cover general competencies.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think the 4 self-directed hours are enough to cover compliance topics because they are more flexible.

questions.stem: By 31 December, Mei Ling has done 10 structured hours and 6 self-directed hours. How does this compare with the CPD requirement?
options: She has the 16 total hours but is short of the 12 structured hours required
She has met the requirement because the total is 16 hours
She is short of the 4 self-directed hours required
She has met the requirement because self-directed hours can replace structured hours
questions.explanation: The requirement is at least 12 Structured Learning hours plus at least 4 Self-directed hours, and hours earned in one category cannot count toward the other. With 10 structured hours, Mei Ling is 2 short.
questions.common_trap: Looking only at the headline total of 16 hours hides the split between the two categories.

questions.stem: What does professional indemnity insurance (PII) protect against?
options: The salesperson's loss of commission when a transaction falls through
Damage to the agency's office and equipment
A client's loss caused by a fall in property prices after purchase
Consumers' financial loss arising from a salesperson's professional negligence or omissions
questions.explanation: PII protects the estate agent and its salespersons against legal liability for claims arising from professional errors or omissions, so a consumer who suffers loss through negligence can be compensated.
questions.common_trap: Candidates confuse PII with income protection or general business insurance.

questions.stem: How is PII for salespersons arranged?
options: Each salesperson buys an individual policy directly from CEA
Each client buys cover before signing the estate agency agreement
Under an agency-wide master group policy
CEA pays the premium from the industry fund for all salespersons
questions.explanation: PII is arranged under an agency-wide master group policy, so salespersons are covered through their agency.
questions.common_trap: Candidates assume registration with CEA means the cover is bought from or paid by CEA.

questions.stem: The PII policy is described as 'cost-inclusive'. What does this mean?
options: Legal defence fees are paid on top of the full cover amount
Legal defence fees count towards the total cover, reducing what remains to pay the claim
The policy covers only the legal defence fees and not the claim itself
The premium is included in the salesperson's registration fee
questions.explanation: Under the regulations, the insured amount may include the costs and expenses of defending or settling a claim. In a cost-inclusive policy, defence costs therefore use up the same limit, leaving less to pay the consumer's claim.
questions.common_trap: The first alternative sounds sensible because many assume defence costs are separate, but cost-inclusive means the opposite.

questions.stem: For how long must the PII cover remain active from the date of registration?
options: At least 6 months
At least 2 years
At least 1 year
At least 3 years
questions.explanation: A salesperson must be covered by professional indemnity insurance valid for at least one year when applying for registration.
questions.common_trap: Candidates pick 2 years or 6 months because they mix this with other periods in other CEA rules.

questions.stem: What is the maximum penalty for acting as an estate agent without a valid licence?
options: A fine of up to $75,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $25,000, imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both
A fine of up to $50,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $100,000, imprisonment of up to 5 years, or both
questions.explanation: Acting as an estate agent without a licence carries the heaviest court-track penalty: up to $75,000, 3 years' imprisonment, or both.
questions.common_trap: The $25,000 and 12 months figures belong to the salesperson-level offences, and the $50,000 figure belongs to false information.

questions.stem: Daniel does estate agency work without being registered as a salesperson. What is the maximum penalty he faces in court?
options: A fine of up to $75,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $50,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment of up to 6 months, or both
A fine of up to $25,000, imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both
questions.explanation: Acting as a salesperson without registration is punishable by up to $25,000, 12 months' imprisonment, or both. The higher $75,000 and 3 years apply to acting as an estate agent without a licence.
questions.common_trap: Candidates apply the unlicensed estate agent penalty to any unlicensed activity.

questions.stem: An estate agent appoints and uses an individual who is not a registered salesperson to do estate agency work. What is the maximum court penalty for the agency's offence?
options: A fine of up to $75,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $50,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $200,000 only, with no imprisonment
A fine of up to $25,000, imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both
questions.explanation: An estate agent that appoints or employs an unregistered salesperson commits an offence punishable by up to $25,000, 12 months' imprisonment, or both. The $200,000 figure is the Disciplinary Committee cap for an agency, which cannot impose jail.
questions.common_trap: Candidates may think the agency, as the larger party, faces the same penalty as an unlicensed agent or the DC cap.

questions.stem: Of the following offences, which carries the highest maximum fine in the court track?
options: Acting as a salesperson without registration
Acting as an estate agent without a valid licence
An estate agent employing or paying an unregistered individual
Practising without a valid written agreement with an estate agent
questions.explanation: Acting as an estate agent without a valid licence carries up to $75,000. The other offences listed here carry lower maximum fines.
questions.common_trap: Candidates may pick the agency-side offence, assuming a company always faces the larger penalty.

questions.stem: Mei, a registered salesperson, left her agency but kept working on listings without a valid written agreement with any estate agent. How is this treated?
options: It is not an offence as long as her registration is still valid
Only her former agency can be held liable for her conduct
It is only a civil matter and CEA cannot take any action
It is an offence to practise without a valid written agreement with an estate agent
questions.explanation: A registered salesperson must work through an estate agent under a valid written agreement. Practising without one is a statutory offence, punishable by up to $25,000, 12 months' imprisonment, or both.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think registration alone is enough to practise, forgetting the written agreement with an EA.

questions.stem: Alicia submits a forged O-Level certificate to obtain her registration. What is the maximum penalty for providing false information to secure credentials?
options: A fine of up to $25,000, imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both
A fine of up to $75,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
A fine of up to $5,000 with no imprisonment
A fine of up to $50,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both
questions.explanation: Giving false information to secure or renew credentials carries up to $50,000, 3 years' imprisonment, or both.
questions.common_trap: The $25,000 and 12 months pairing is the most common figure in the table, so it is the default guess.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of panel members in a Disciplinary Committee?
questions.explanation: A Disciplinary Committee comprises at least 3 panel members.
questions.common_trap: Candidates pick 5 by assuming larger panels for serious matters.

questions.stem: Which of the following can a Disciplinary Committee NOT do?
options: Suspend a salesperson's registration
Revoke a salesperson's registration
Impose a jail term
Attach operational conditions to a registration
questions.explanation: The DC can revoke or suspend registrations, attach conditions and impose financial penalties, but it cannot issue jail terms. Imprisonment comes only from the court track.
questions.common_trap: Because DC penalties are serious, candidates assume jail is available.

questions.stem: What is the maximum financial penalty per case that a Disciplinary Committee can impose on an estate agent (agency)?
questions.explanation: The DC cap is $200,000 per case for an agency and $100,000 per case for an individual salesperson.
questions.common_trap: The $100,000 figure is the individual cap and is easily swapped with the agency cap.

questions.stem: What is the maximum financial penalty per case that a Disciplinary Committee can impose on an individual salesperson?
questions.explanation: The DC cap for an individual salesperson is $100,000 per case. The cap for an agency is $200,000.
questions.common_trap: The $200,000 figure is the agency cap and is easily swapped with the individual cap.

questions.stem: A salesperson has been convicted and fined in court for an offence under the EAA. CEA also brings disciplinary proceedings. How do the two tracks relate?
options: The Disciplinary Committee track is independent of court rulings, so both can proceed
The Disciplinary Committee cannot act once a court has dealt with the matter
The Disciplinary Committee must wait for the court and adopt the court's sentence
The court fine automatically revokes the registration and ends the disciplinary process
questions.explanation: The DC track runs independently of the court track. A salesperson can face court penalties and also disciplinary action such as suspension, revocation or financial penalties.
questions.common_trap: Candidates assume double jeopardy applies, but the two tracks serve different purposes.

questions.stem: A minor infraction is dealt with by a Letter of Censure. Which statement is correct?
options: It may carry a financial penalty of up to $1,000 per case and is kept confidential
It may carry a financial penalty of up to $5,000 per case and is published on the register
It may carry a financial penalty of up to $20,000 per case and is kept confidential
It carries no financial penalty and is not published on the register
questions.explanation: A Letter of Censure is the minor-breach track. It may be issued with or without a financial penalty, capped at $5,000 per case, and sanctions under it are publishable in the CEA Public Register.
questions.common_trap: Candidates assume a minor sanction is private, but Letter of Censure sanctions are publishable on the register (a warning letter, by contrast, is not).

questions.stem: Within how many days of being notified of a Council or Disciplinary Committee decision must a Notice of Appeal be lodged with the Appeals Board?
options: 7 days
14 days
21 days
30 days
questions.explanation: A Notice of Appeal must be lodged within 14 days of being notified of the decision. The Petition of Appeal then follows within 21 days after that deadline.
questions.common_trap: The 21-day figure belongs to the later Petition of Appeal, and 30 days is a common appeal period in other contexts.

questions.stem: A salesperson's registration is suspended by CEA. What happens to the registration fees paid for it?
options: A pro-rated refund is given for the suspension period
They are non-refundable
A full refund is given because CEA withdrew the registration
Half the fees are refunded regardless of how long the suspension lasts
questions.explanation: Registration fees are non-refundable, so no refund is given when a registration is suspended or revoked.
questions.common_trap: Candidates assume fairness requires at least a pro-rated refund.

questions.stem: Ravi is asked by a buyer and a seller to act for both of them in an HDB resale flat transaction, and both agree in writing. What is the position?
options: He may act for both if both parties consent in writing
He must not act for both sides, even with written consent
He may act for both if he collects commission from only one party
He may act for both if the buyer and seller are related
questions.explanation: An agent cannot be appointed by both buyer and seller (or landlord and tenant) for the same transaction, and written consent does not cure this. An agent may help the other party with paperwork only if that party consents and is told the agent neither acts for nor is paid by them.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think disclosure and consent solve the problem, as they do for some conflict of interest situations.

questions.stem: A potential conflict of interest is deemed to exist for a salesperson in which of these situations?
options: The opposing salesperson works for a competing agency that you know well
The property is in the same estate as one of your earlier deals
The other party, or the other party's salesperson, is related to you, such as a spouse, parent, sibling or business partner
The opposing party is a first-time home buyer
questions.explanation: CEA's Professional Service Manual deems a potential conflict where the other party or their salesperson is related to the salesperson, for example a spouse, relative or partner. It also requires written disclosure to the client if the other side is from the same estate agent.
questions.common_trap: Treating any familiarity or shared estate as a deemed conflict.

questions.stem: Priya acts for a seller and collects commission from the seller. The buyer is unrepresented, and she also asks the buyer to pay her a fee. Which rule is breached?
options: The co-broke split must be agreed in writing before marketing begins
A salesperson may not receive commission from more than one party to the same transaction
Signed copies of documents must be given to clients on execution
A salesperson must not hold transaction monies
questions.explanation: A salesperson can take commission from only one side of a deal. Charging both the seller and the buyer is a breach, even if the buyer has no agent of their own.
questions.common_trap: Candidates focus on co-broking rules, but no other agent is involved here.

questions.stem: When should the co-brokerage fee between the two agents' salespersons be agreed?
options: Upfront, before the transaction is closed
Only after the sale completes
When the commission invoice is issued
It need not be agreed, because the buyer's agent sets it
questions.explanation: CEA's guidelines say the sharing of commission is an agreement between the agents and salespersons involved. To prevent disputes, the co-brokerage fee must be mutually agreed upfront, before the transaction is closed.
questions.common_trap: Leaving the split until the deal is done.

questions.stem: Under what condition can a salesperson receive a co-broking fee from the other party's agent?
options: Her own client has agreed to pay her only half of the usual fee
The other salesperson agrees to pay her in cash
The transaction value is above $1 million
Her own client is not paying her any fee for the transaction
questions.explanation: If an agent takes commission from his own client, he cannot also take a commission or co-broking fee from the other party or that party's agent. A co-broking fee is therefore possible only when his own client is not paying him a fee.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think a reduced fee from the client still allows a co-broke fee on top.

questions.stem: Wei and Sam are from different agencies and have agreed a co-broke split. Wei offers to hand Sam his share in cash. What is the position?
options: Allowed if both sign a receipt for the cash
Allowed if the amount is below $1,000
Allowed if the payment is made by PayNow from Wei's personal account
Not allowed, because co-broke payments must go directly between the licensed estate agents
questions.explanation: Co-broke payments must go straight from one licensed estate agent to the other. A salesperson must never pay a co-broking colleague's share in cash, or transfer it to that salesperson directly.
questions.common_trap: A receipt or a traceable payment method seems to make it safe, but the problem is the channel, not the record.

questions.stem: When must a salesperson give the client a signed copy of a document?
options: Within 3 working days of execution
Only when the client asks for it
Immediately upon execution of the document
Only for the option to purchase or the lease agreement
questions.explanation: Under the Code of Ethics, the client must receive a copy of every form or document signed, right away or as soon as practicable afterwards. This applies to all documents, not just the major ones.
questions.common_trap: Candidates assume a short grace period or limit it to key documents.

questions.stem: Which of the following marketing claims is permitted?
options: "Property King of the East"
"Top Transactor in Singapore", with no records to support it
"Expert in all HDB matters"
"Sold 14 units in this block in Q1", backed by clear records
questions.explanation: Advertisements must be accurate and verified and must not be false or misleading, so unprovable titles and claims without records are not allowed. A factual metric backed by clear records is acceptable.
questions.common_trap: 'Top Transactor' sounds like a factual claim, but without records to prove it the claim is unsubstantiated.

questions.stem: What is the general rule on transaction monies for a registered salesperson?
options: An RES may handle them if the client gives written consent
An RES may handle them up to a total of $1,000
An RES should not handle transaction monies
An RES may hold them in the agency's account for up to 7 days
questions.explanation: The general rule is that RESs should not handle transaction monies. Only limited, specified reimbursement situations are exceptions.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think consent or a small amount makes it acceptable.

questions.stem: At a viewing, a buyer hands Lina a cheque for the option fee so she can pass it to the seller. What should Lina do?
options: Accept it and pass it to the seller on the same day
Accept it because the option fee is part of her commission
Accept it as long as the cheque is crossed
Decline it, because an RES should not handle the option fee
questions.explanation: Money moving in a transaction (option fee, exercise fee, down payment, stamp duties, deposits, sale proceeds, legal fees) should not pass through the RES's hands.
questions.common_trap: Same-day handover and crossed cheques feel safe, but the issue is the RES touching the money at all.

questions.stem: Which statement about commission and transaction monies is correct?
options: Commission is transaction money and the RES may hold it on behalf of the client
Commission is not transaction money in general and is paid to the estate agent, not directly to the RES
Commission is paid directly to the RES, who then passes it to the estate agent
Commission is transaction money and must be paid through a lawyer's CVY account
questions.explanation: Commission is generally not treated as transaction money. It is paid to the estate agent, not directly to the RES.
questions.common_trap: Candidates assume all money in a deal is transaction money and that the salesperson collects it personally.

questions.stem: A landlord of an HDB flat asks the salesperson to collect the monthly rent from the tenant for convenience. What is the position?
options: He may collect it if he issues a receipt to the tenant
He may collect it if he passes it on within 3 days
He should not collect it, because an RES should not handle rental deposits or monthly rent
He may collect it if the rent is below the HDB rental cap
questions.explanation: In HDB rentals, the RES should not handle rental deposits or monthly rent. The landlord and tenant should deal with those payments directly.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think a receipt or quick transfer solves the problem.

questions.stem: Which statement about reimbursement for lease stamping is correct?
options: An RES may collect the estimated stamp duty from the tenant first and pay IRAS later
An RES may pay first and seek reimbursement, but must not collect the fee before stamping
An RES may never pay such a fee, even from his own pocket
An RES may collect stamp duty in cash only if the amount is below $500
questions.explanation: There are limited situations, such as certain lease stamp-duty reimbursements, where the RES can pay first and be reimbursed afterwards. The RES must not collect the fee before stamping.
questions.common_trap: Candidates think collecting in advance is more practical, but advance collection is prohibited.
